sources.name: the Voice at our Lord's baptism; our Lord's prayer
sources.quote: How I have both glorified my Name and I will glorify it again
sources.use: Illustrates The Name speaking and working its change; Christ needing new strength by its utterance ('Father, glorify thy Name'; 'Now is my soul troubled').

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.quote: Take that matter which is gold
sources.use: Supports: the matter thrown into bottomless Mercury, glossed as finding the magical earth at one's own center.

sources.name: Book of Wisdom
sources.use: Supports: the best description of Wisdom as man's exemplar.

sources.name: Job
sources.quote: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth Thee; therefore I abhor myself and repent in dust and ashes
sources.use: Illustrates the contrast between the perfection of the Law of Light and human defection.

sources.name: Kirchberger
sources.use: Supports: names 'the physical problem', making the invisible spirit visible.

sources.name: Chaldaic Oracles
sources.quote: There is room for the image also in the circumlucid place. Every way to the unfashioned soul stretch the reins of fire
sources.use: Supports: the soul as the place of manifestation of the law of Light.

sources.name: Stanley
sources.use: Reference only, for the Chaldaic Oracles.

sources.name: Kant
sources.use: Criticized: never got beyond the negative margin of intellectual intuition.

sources.name: Fichte
sources.use: Contrasts: broke through into the Absolute ground, seeing but without experiencing.

sources.name: Schelling
sources.use: Contrasts: as Fichte.

sources.name: Hegel
sources.use: Named among modern metaphysicians who took their starting point from the Mystics.

sources.name: Oken
sources.use: Contrasts: appears to have had an inspiration into the science of created nature.

sources.name: Kirchberger
sources.quote: the Divine Will makes use of the human voice as an organ for conducting the Light, through the fire
sources.use: supports: endorsed; Atwood glosses the fire as our chaotic will.

sources.name: Arndt
sources.use: illustrates: the one Mystic who recognizes the depth of the Psalms.

sources.name: the Psalms
sources.use: praised for 'surpassing depth of Divine experience', neglected by the Mystics.

sources.name: unattributed scriptural phrase
sources.quote: eternal purpose, purposed in Christ Jesus, our Lord
sources.use: supports: the Fall accords with a purpose of greater restoration.

sources.name: St Martin
sources.quote: in the true pronunciation of the two great names
sources.use: supports: foundation of both Testaments, glossed as the revealed utterance of the life of God in man.

sources.name: Old and New Testaments
sources.use: illustrates: founded on the revealed utterance; the New fulfils the Old's promise and gives another.

sources.name: our Lord, on the language of David
sources.quote: I have said ye are gods, if (says our Lord) ye called them gods unto whom the Word of God came
sources.use: illustrates: powers subordinate to God evolved where the Word comes, with the danger of self-centers.

sources.name: the First and Second Commandments
sources.use: interpreted: graven images (Second) as the practical result of self-centering (violating the First).

sources.name: the ancient prophets
sources.use: impugned both inner and material idolatry.

sources.name: the Masons
sources.use: is criticized: ape the words of power but lost the magic Key; outward form absurd, kept alive by a secret response of commonsense to the original mystery.

sources.name: the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus
sources.use: supports: carefully prepared the magic Key to open the door into the Hermetic garden.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: Haste is the Devil’s part
sources.use: supports: Hermetists war against over-haste.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.use: supports: warns against haste under the similitude of red poppies.

sources.name: Behmen
sources.use: supports/contrasts: with de St Martin, source of 'the Crown'; contrasted with Engelbrecht as penetrating surfaces; in him the body was swallowed up with Light.

sources.name: de St Martin
sources.use: with Behmen, source of the phrase 'the Crown'.

sources.name: Engelbrecht
sources.use: is criticized: visionary without education of the intellect, little gauge for truth; perhaps misconceived the Evester.

sources.name: Swedenborg
sources.use: compared: Engelbrecht lived like him in the visionary sphere.

sources.name: Paracelsus
sources.use: source of the name 'Evester' for the analogical sphere.

sources.name: Vaughan, the Welshman
sources.use: illustrates: 'very elegantly depicts the play of that ether'.

sources.name: De St Martin
sources.quote: Numerical numbers are merely the bark of things
sources.use: supports: numbers as outer bark; extended to outer nature and scriptural tradition.

sources.name: Pythagorus
sources.quote: the source, as he called it, of ever-flowing Nature
sources.use: supports: his Tetractys, obtained by theurgic multiplication, as the kind of ens underlying the stone.

sources.name: the Iliad
sources.use: illustrates: after the death of Patroclus, the connate spirit deprived of its understanding spirit.

sources.name: Hercules and Hylas
sources.use: illustrates: Hercules' grief for Hylas, same point as the Iliad.

sources.name: Se St Martin
sources.quote: the earth is the crucible for souls as well as bodies
sources.use: supports: the residuum of the sensual medium giving body to the regenerate soul.

sources.name: the Smaragdine Tablet
sources.quote: The power is integral if it be turned into earth
sources.use: supports: the earth/residuum point.

sources.name: Festina lente, Ne quid nimis (sayings)
sources.quote: Festina lente, Ne quid nimis
sources.use: supports: against haste and excess in the work, higher or lower.

sources.name: Solomon
sources.quote: Be not righteous overmuch
sources.use: supports: do not exceed the capacity given.

sources.name: Pharisees, Katharoi, Devotes, Puritans
sources.use: illustrates: religious self-will in history.

sources.name: Bacon
sources.quote: Man is the servant and interpreter of Nature
sources.use: His lucid style illustrates that clear language seems mystical when turned to the a priori ground (¶111); his dictum is accepted only for outward seeking and qualified: turned within, man can be Nature's revealer and master (¶120).

sources.name: Kirchberger
sources.quote: there is no true government but a Theocracy
sources.use: Says this 'for de St Martin'; Atwood calls it a great truth but qualifies it. Kirchberger himself is criticized as an intellectual seeker who did not convert wholly into the Light.

sources.name: de St Martin
sources.use: Cited on a perfect law working by degrees; praised as having entered the center of substantial life; his answers to his friend's particular enquiry illustrate universal truth exploding questions, like the Hermetic inquisition.

sources.name: Kant
sources.use: Listed as having 'saw that'; the antecedent is not stated, presumably the preceding point (¶116) on intellect and the Universal Reason.

sources.name: Hegel
sources.use: Same list ('saw it').

sources.name: Fichte
sources.use: Same list ('knew it').

sources.name: Schelling
sources.use: Same list ('saw it').

sources.name: Boehme
sources.use: Knew it and proved it by experienced in-seeing whereby he became it.

sources.name: St Paul
sources.use: Example: better understood in the atmosphere of the higher Mystics than through professed commentators.

sources.name: the higher Mystics
sources.use: Their atmosphere opens St Paul's depths; contrasted with commentators.

sources.name: Hermetic Riddle
sources.quote: omnia in omnibus
sources.use: Its 'omnia in omnibus' identified with the Universal Ether.

sources.name: the masters
sources.quote: benedicta viriditas
sources.use: Their term, applied to the green/purple vegetative life.

sources.name: Song of Sol.
sources.use: Reference only, attached to the benedicta viriditas.

sources.name: Behmen
sources.use: Said to surpass the Neo-Platonists in revelations of the Life Center (as Newton's astronomy to Ptolemy's).

sources.name: Neo-Platonists
sources.use: Contrast: delivered principles scientifically and underwent long-perfected Initiation, but did not declare the inner experience of the Mystae and Teleioi; confined to psychological investigation; surpassed by Behmen.

sources.name: Ptolemy
sources.use: Comparison only (his astronomy to Newton's).

sources.name: Newton
sources.use: Comparison only.

sources.name: Apuleius
sources.use: Illustrates the coruscation of released light: the midnight sun seen when initiated by the Goddess Isis.

sources.name: the Alchemists
sources.use: Their Vulcan decoded as Motion.

sources.name: the Myths
sources.use: Represent Vulcan as lame, explained as halting motion.

sources.name: our Lord
sources.quote: Seek ye first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness and all these things shall be added unto you
sources.use: Supports: seeking the Universal first is the shortest and truest road in the Hermetic Art.

sources.name: 1st and 2nd Commandments
sources.use: Supports: stopping in finite gifts is idolatry.

sources.name: the philosophers
sources.quote: The First Matter is not to be found on earth, as the philosophers say
sources.use: Supports: the First Matter is sought inwardly, not on earth.

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.quote: a recessure of reason behind itself into the indefinite intermediate between reason and the Absolute
sources.use: Praised but qualified: gives only the metaphysic of the First Matter's generation, never realized so.

sources.name: Holy Scripture
sources.use: The Work revealed there is the analogue of the Hermetic Work; the Stone is the analogue of the Chief Corner Stone.

sources.name: Virgil
sources.use: Illustrates: advice to Aristaeus on binding Proteus alludes to the First Matter's changing forms; Aristaeus's lost bees are the soul's faculties; Aeneas's Golden Bough is the aurific seed; Virgil wrote on initiated ground, the Georgics an allegory of celestial and spiritual agriculture, the Aeneid (6th Book markedly) the same truths.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.use: Reference only (cf. for Virgil's Aristaeus and Proteus).

sources.name: St Paul
sources.quote: the letter killeth
sources.use: Interpreted by Atwood: the living letter of the law is too powerful a test for man's spirit.

sources.name: St Paul
sources.quote: It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption
sources.use: Supports: seed of spirit grows to spirit; the law of regeneration of the anima media.

sources.name: unattributed Latin verse
sources.quote: Felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas
sources.use: Called 'a grand declaration of a deep Hermetic truth': the light of life lodged in its causal center frees the threefold life.

sources.name: Behmen
sources.quote: the bitter anguish of the driving wheel of existence
sources.use: Illustrates the bitterness of self-life from which nature shields us.

sources.name: unattributed couplet
sources.quote: Art, then, what nature left in hand doth take, And out of one a twofold work doth make.
sources.use: Supports: Alchemy advances nature beyond her created state.

sources.name: Homer
sources.use: The Hermetic is the only true key to them.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.use: Supports: develops the ontological basis of the Iliad.

sources.name: David
sources.quote: as wax before the fire
sources.use: Illustrates the dispelling of the alien when the Divine presence arises.

sources.name: Van Helmont
sources.use: Speaks of the White Light as the Quellem, 'in a very superficial way' (qualified).

sources.name: the Kabalists
sources.use: Celebrate the White Light as belonging to the Ancient of Days, the primeval Light.

sources.name: unattributed saying
sources.quote: The ransom of a man’s life are his riches
sources.use: Supports: the seeker gives up the riches set before him.

sources.name: Grecian fables (Midas)
sources.use: Illustrates: Midas as the will starved in possession of the aurific life.

sources.name: Bishop of Oxford (Wilberforce)
sources.quote: Nature, as the Bishop of Oxford (Wilberforce) says, is as much the voice of God as Revelation is
sources.use: Agreed with, then qualified: since the fall Nature distorts that voice.

sources.name: the Bible / Revelation
sources.use: Revelation rectifies man and Nature; the science-versus-Bible question is left on its own ground.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.quote: there are two pairs of eyes; those which are beneath are closed, when those which are above are opened
sources.use: Supports the alternating inner sight of the Matter.

sources.name: Aeneid (author not named here)
sources.quote: Strictamqu Aeneas aciem venientibus offert
sources.use: Illustrates the reason's light confronting and dispersing the images in the vital chaos; Aeneas, the Golden Bough, Tartarus and Elysium read as stages of the work.

sources.name: Homer
sources.use: Proteus' last subterfuge, transformation into a tree, identified with the Golden Bough's tree; illustrates the elusive Protean life.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: enters into the Magian School but he wanders awhile in the region of Chimaeras
sources.use: Supports: every seeker passes through a phase of illusory images that must be destroyed.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.use: Praised: Time as a participation of the Paradigm by the image, against the addressee's relational view and modern metaphysicians.

sources.name: modern metaphysicians
sources.use: Contrasted: they make Time a condition of thought.

sources.name: Virgil
sources.quote: Quis deus hac musae quis nobis extudet artem?
sources.use: The Aristaeus myth is said to bear altogether on the Vital transmutation in an advanced stage.

sources.name: unattributed words: 'the fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom'
sources.quote: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom
sources.use: Their meaning becomes clear on contact with universal power, the initial of regenerate life.

sources.name: Emily Bronte
sources.use: Criticized: a Saturnine mass of power in potentiality wanting the clearing Jupiter element; Emily called Saturn.

sources.name: Charlotte Bronte
sources.use: Said to be Jupiter and Lune; ought to have reworked her sister's book.

sources.name: Anne Bronte
sources.use: Said to be Venus and Lune.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: conversant with the soul in her philosophy
sources.use: Supports: alchemy understood only by those working the philosophic (separative) process.

sources.name: unattributed Latin tag
sources.quote: Visitabis interiore terrae, etc.
sources.use: Reference only; appended to the account of successive dissolutions.

sources.name: Herman Conringius
sources.work: De Hermetica Aegyptior, vetere et Paracelsior. Nova Medicina.
sources.use: Criticized: tried to slight alchemy as a recent invention.

sources.name: A. Kircher
sources.work: Oedipus Aegyptiacus; de Lapide Philos. Dissert.
sources.use: Supports alchemy's antiquity; also source of the Latin rendering of the Smaragdine Table from Arabic and Greek copies.

sources.name: Olaus Borrichius
sources.use: Supports alchemy's antiquity ('the learned Dane').

sources.name: Robert Vallensis
sources.work: De Veritate et Antiquitate Artis Chemiae (in the first volume of the Theatrum Chemicum)
sources.use: Supports alchemy's antiquity.

sources.name: the best Greek Authors, historical and philosophic
sources.use: Provide collateral probability for alchemy's antiquity.

sources.name: Plutarch
sources.quote: by the word Chemia, says Plutarch, the seeing pupil of the human eye was also designated
sources.use: Illustrates etymology: Egypt called Cham/Chemia for black soil; Chemia also the pupil and black matters.

sources.name: Suidas
sources.work: de Verbo Chemiae; in Verbo Chemeia
sources.quote: Chimia est auri et argenti confectio
sources.use: Dating of Hermes before the Pharoahs, about 400 years before Moses; n8 cites his entry on Chemeia (on our translation, defining Chimia as the making of gold and silver).

sources.name: Terullianus
sources.use: Reference only (attached to Hermes' 'spiritual intelligence of all things').

sources.name: Hermes (Trismegistus)
sources.use: Starting point of the Hermetic story; adept king credited with the Hermetic writings.

sources.name: Clemens Alexandrinus
sources.use: Names in detail the books attributed to Hermes.

sources.name: Jamblicus
sources.work: Jamblichus de Mysteriis, sect viii, cap. iv
sources.use: Supports judging Hermes' lost books by the surviving Asclepian Dialogues and Poimander.

sources.name: Asclepian Dialogues
sources.quote: Oh, Egypt! Egypt! Fables alone shall remain of thy religion
sources.use: Theosophic Hermetic book; source of the prophecy of Egypt's fall, which Atwood defends as authentic.

sources.name: Divine Poimander
sources.use: Praised for sublimity of doctrine; concerns divine capabilities and regeneration rather than their physical ground.

sources.name: Ficinus
sources.use: Latin version of the Asclepian Dialogues and Poimander.

sources.name: Dr Everard
sources.use: English translation of the Hermetic books, praised.

sources.name: Tractatus Aureus
sources.work: Hermetis Trismegisti Tractatus Aureus de Lapidis physici secreto (Golden Treatise, seven chapters)
sources.use: Gives the physical ground and practical method of alchemy.

sources.name: Smaragdine Table
sources.quote: that which is above is as that which is below
sources.use: Quoted in full as comprehending the working principle and total subject of the art; the only Egyptian remnant of the Sacred Art.

sources.name: Herodotus
sources.use: Historian who recorded Egypt's remaining splendour after Cambyses.

sources.name: T. Taylor
sources.work: rendering of the Asclepian Dialogue; notes to the Prophecy, in Plotinus' Select Works
sources.use: Translation used for the prophecy; reference for Augustine's view.

sources.name: Apuleius
sources.use: Contrasts: hypothetical forger of the prophecy, a theory Atwood rejects.

sources.name: Lactantius
sources.use: Supports authenticity of the prophecy: mentions it without doubt.

sources.name: St Augustine
sources.quote: instinctu fallacies spiritus
sources.use: Supports authenticity (mentions it without doubt), though he 'esteemed it instinctu fallacies spiritus' (ours: by prompting of a deceiving spirit), which Atwood attributes probably to the popular notion and thinks he might later have revised.

sources.name: Pliny
sources.work: Hist. Nat. (Hostor. Nat.) lib. xxx, cap. I; lib. 33, cap. 4
sources.quote: Plenum miraculi et hoc pariter utrasque artes effloruisse, medicinam dico, magiciemque eadem aetate
sources.use: Supports: Ostanes brought the Persian spirit to Greece; Democritus' experimental fame and occult practice; Caligula's failed attempts.

sources.name: Ostanes
sources.use: Persian sage (per Pliny) who first brought the Persian spirit into Greece.

sources.name: Thales, Pythagoras
sources.use: Early Greek philosophers who sought eastern wisdom; their writings are lost.

sources.name: Democritus of Abdera
sources.work: book of Sacred Physics (de Arte Sacra)
sources.use: Supports: treats the Hermetic art and the occult discovery under ancient philosophy. Named as acquainted with the divine water.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.work: in Democritum Abderitam de Arte Sacra
sources.use: Commentary on Democritus; supports the work's standing.

sources.name: Nicholas Flamel
sources.use: Gave extracts from Democritus; supports the work's standing.

sources.name: Hippocrates
sources.use: Named in Pliny as the illustrator of medicine, contemporary with Democritus' magic.

sources.name: Seneca
sources.quote: his artificial confection of precious stones
sources.use: Supports Democritus' making of artificial precious stones.

sources.name: Petronius Arbiter
sources.use: Reference only, for Democritus spending his leisure on hyperphysical researches.

sources.name: Maria
sources.work: Sapientisima Maria de Lapide Philosophica Praescripta; Maria Practica
sources.use: Hebrew woman advanced in the Hermetic Art, associated with Democritus at Memphis; her treatises are extant.

sources.name: Syncellus
sources.use: Reference only (Democritus and Maria).

sources.name: Anaxagorus / Anaxagoras
sources.use: Celebrated as an alchemist; praised by Norton as the plainest writer. His metaphysics agrees with Aristotle's.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: Yet Anaxagoras wrote plainest of them all In his boke of Conversions Naturall;
sources.use: Supports: masters wrote under coverts; Anaxagoras wrote plainly; Aristotle envied him.

sources.name: Ashmole
sources.use: Reference only, as the location of Norton's Ordinal.

sources.name: Hermes, Rasis, Geber, Avicen, Merlin, Hortolan, Democrit, Morien, Bacon, Raymond
sources.quote: Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.
sources.use: Named in Norton's verse as masters who wrote obscurely.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.work: epistles to Alexander the Great on the Philosophers' stone (de Lapide ad Alexandrum Magnum); Secreta Secretorum; book of Meteors
sources.use: Criticized by Norton and the adepts for envy and veiling; Atwood qualifies this. His works are cited as evidence of hidden knowledge, but she declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher without more evidence.

sources.name: Heraclitus
sources.use: His metaphysics agrees in essentials with Aristotle's.

sources.name: Plato
sources.work: Phaedrus, Philebus, seventh book of Laws, Parmenides, Phaedo, Banquet, Timaeus; Epistles (Epistle II); treatise on the philosophers' stone (doubtful)
sources.quote: it is a parturition respecting this ingenerated in the soul, from which he who is not liberated will never in reality acquire truth
sources.use: Illustrates hyperphysical, veiled philosophy and dread of writing the truth. Atwood suggests the science behind it was practical but declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher.

sources.name: Dionysius of Syracuse
sources.use: Plato's correspondent, drawn to him by a science Atwood thinks was practical.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.work: Plato's Works, vol. v; notes to his Pausanias, vol 3
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Theatrum Chemicum
sources.use: Reference only. It preserves the Aristotle and Plato treatises, the lamp inscriptions and the Bononian Enigma.

sources.name: Suidas
sources.use: Supports: the Emperor's burning of chemical books because the Egyptians made gold and silver; explains antiquity's silence about the Egyptian Art.

sources.name: Cleopatra
sources.use: Illustrates the art's revival in Egypt: the earring dissolved in philosophic vinegar, and chemical treatises attributed to her.

sources.name: Virgil, Ovid, Horace, Vitruvius
sources.use: Augustan men accused of sorcery; illustrates Rome's limited achievement.

sources.name: Pancirollus
sources.use: Describes several perpetual lamps.

sources.name: St. Augustin
sources.use: Mentions an inextinguishable lamp consecrated to Venus.

sources.name: Maximus Olybius
sources.quote: Namque elementa gravi clausit digesta labore
sources.use: Maker of the perpetual lamp found near Alestes; his inscription speaks of elements digested by laborious art.

sources.name: petri Apiani
sources.use: Reference only, for the inscriptions.

sources.name: Hermolaus Barbarus
sources.work: corollary to Dioscorus, or some other (text is uncertain)
sources.quote: There is a celestial, or rather a divine water of the chemists
sources.use: Supports: the existence and nature of the divine water.

sources.name: Trismegistus
sources.use: Named as acquainted with the divine water.

sources.name: H. Khunrath
sources.quote: the ether in this praeter-perfect aqueous body will burn perpetually
sources.use: Cites an ancient author on the perpetually burning ether in the water.

sources.name: ancient author of the Apocalypse of the Secret Spirit of Nature
sources.work: Apocalypse of the Secret Spirit of Nature
sources.use: Cited by Khunrath on the divine water.

sources.name: Bononian Enigma
sources.quote: Nec vir, nec mulier, nec androgyna,
sources.use: Claimed by the adepts as referring to the occult material of the art.

sources.name: Kircheri
sources.use: Reference only, for the Bononian Enigma.

sources.name: The Critic
sources.use: Source of the English epitaph translations (1845).

sources.name: Michael Maier
sources.use: Detailed the whole allusion of the epitaph.

sources.name: N. Barnaud
sources.work: commentary in the Theatrum Chemicum (n32: Commentariolum in Enigmaticum quoddam Epitaphium Bononiae studiorum)
sources.use: Commented on the epitaph.

sources.name: St John, the Evangelist Apostle
sources.use: Cited as practising the Occult Art for the poor (healing, making gold, silver, gems).

sources.name: St Victor
sources.use: Relates the particulars of St John's practice.

sources.name: Greek Catholics' hymn for St John's day
sources.quote: Qui de virgis fecit aurum Gemmas de lapidibus
sources.use: Illustrates the tradition of St John making gold and gems.

sources.name: Alexander Beauvais
sources.use: Reference only (for the hymn).

sources.name: Thomas Vaughan
sources.use: Supports: story of an early Christian mission to China spreading faith by works of healing and purification.

sources.name: Plotinus, Philo-Judaeus, Proclus, Porphyry, Jamblicus, Julian, Apuleius
sources.use: Alexandrian revival figures professing Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge; to be quoted later.

sources.name: Heliodorus, Olympiodorus, Synesius, Athenagoras, Zosimus, Archelaus
sources.use: Extant treatises on the stone.

sources.name: Dufresnoy
sources.work: Hist. De l’Art Hermetique, vol. 3, Cat. Gr. Mss.
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Hypatia
sources.use: Taught Synesius the occult truths of the philosophy.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.work: Epistola 36, 142; Alchemical commentary on Democritus; The True Book of Synesius, on the Philosophers’ Stone
sources.use: Example of a bishop-adept who guarded the mysteries and bound initiation by oath.

sources.name: Democritus
sources.use: Subject of Synesius's commentary (before mentioned).

sources.name: Artephius
sources.work: celebrated treatise on the philosophers’ stone (n42: Artefii Antiquissimi Philosophi de Arte Occulta atque Lapide Philosophorum Liber secretus)
sources.quote: I except one thing only, which it is not lawful that I should write, because it can be revealed truly only by God, or by a master
sources.use: Quoted at length: long life by the quintessence; publishes all but one unwritable point.

sources.name: Flamel
sources.use: Reference only (Synesius's piece appended to it).

sources.name: Basil Valentine
sources.work: Chariot of Antimony (n36: The Triumphal Chariot of Antimony)
sources.use: Reference only (published with Synesius in English).

sources.name: Kirchringius
sources.use: Called 'the adept'; his commentaries are 'useful'.

sources.name: Troics
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Heliodorus
sources.use: Mystical romance attributed to him; he resigned his bishopric of Tricca rather than disavow it.

sources.name: Zosimus
sources.use: Egyptian, reputed a great practitioner.

sources.name: Athenagoras
sources.use: Shows practical knowledge of the art it allegorizes.

sources.name: Asclepian prophecy
sources.use: Post-640 decline seen as something like its fulfilment, but worse than predicted.

sources.name: Geber
sources.work: The Investigation of Perfect, The Sum of the Perfect Magistery, Testament (n37: Gebri Arabum Summa Perfectionis magisterii in sua Natura)
sources.use: Greatest after Hermes per adepts; his obscure recipes defended as deliberate veils.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.use: Standard of greatness (Geber ranks after him); Artephius learned the art from his books.

sources.name: Albertus Magnus, Lully
sources.use: Adepts who revered and cited Geber.

sources.name: Faraday Society, opening meeting address (1846)
sources.quote: from whose peculiar and mysterious style of writing we derive the word geber or gibberish
sources.use: Is criticized: modern view of alchemists as deluded crucible-brooders.

sources.name: Rhasis
sources.use: Arabian alchemist famous for public transmutation displays.

sources.name: Roger Bacon
sources.use: Contains extracts from Rhasis; appears to credit Artephius's tale.

sources.name: Morienus (Morien)
sources.work: dialogue with Calid (n38: Morienus Eremita Hierosol. De Transfiguratione Metallorum)
sources.use: Example of a disciple of an adept (Adfar) who later initiated King Calid.

sources.name: Morienus's biographer
sources.use: Relates Morienus's story; too long to extract.

sources.name: Adfar
sources.use: Solitary adept of Alexandria, Morienus's master.

sources.name: Calid
sources.work: Liber Secretorum, or Secret of Secrets
sources.use: King initiated and converted; wrote treatises.

sources.name: Theatr. Chem. vol. 5; Salmon’s Practical Physic; Le Bibliotheque des Philosophes Chimiques
sources.use: Reference only (n39; no marker for it appears in the main text).

sources.name: Averroes
sources.use: Named as demanding notice; nothing more said.

sources.name: Avicenna
sources.work: Avicenna de Tinctura Metallorum; Porta Elementa; de Mineralibus (attributed)
sources.use: Reputed practitioner of transmutation and magic; remains neither lucid nor numerous.

sources.name: Paracelsus
sources.use: Compared to Avicenna's ill-directed genius; appears to credit Artephius's tale.

sources.name: Pontanus
sources.use: Appears to credit Artephius's tale.

sources.name: Artephius
sources.use: Illustrates: a link in alchemy's history as it passed from Asia to Europe.

sources.name: Roger Bacon
sources.work: Speculum Alchimiae Rogerii Bachonis; De Mirabilibus Potestatibus Artis et Naturae; Fr. Bachonis Anglici libellus cum influenctiis Coeli
sources.quote: truth ought not to be shown to every ribald, for then that would become most vile, which, in the hands of a philosopher, is the most precious of all things
sources.use: Supports: an adept who produced gold; his maxim justifies concealment of the practice; conscience led him to withhold his gift.

sources.name: Albertus Magnus (Albert)
sources.work: De Mineralibus; Libellus de Alchemia; Concordanditia Philosophorum de Lapide; Secretum Secretorum; Breve Compendium
sources.quote: De transmutatione horum corporum metallicorum et mutatione unius in aliud non est physici determinare, sed artis quae est Alchimica
sources.use: Supports: proof Albert was a practising alchemist who described the first matter and commended alchemy as the best means of inquiry; example of renunciation of worldly advantage.

sources.name: Aquinas
sources.work: Thesaurus Alchimiae (Tractatus D. Thomae Aquino datus fratri D. Reinaldo de Arte Alchimiae); Meteorum, lib. Iv; De Esse et Essentia; Secreta Alchimiae
sources.quote: Metalla transmutari possunt unum in aliud
sources.use: Supports: transmutation affirmed by a confessed adept; his deliberate obscurity and his warnings to keep the secret from worldly seekers; points to the art's higher theosophical purpose. Atwood criticizes his 'false panegyrists'.

sources.name: Abbot Reginald
sources.use: Addressee of Aquinas' Thesaurus Alchimiae.

sources.name: Scotus Erigina
sources.use: Listed among confessed adepts.

sources.name: Arnold di Villa Nova
sources.work: Rosarium Philosophicum; Speculum; Carmina; Questiones ad Bonifacium; Testamentum
sources.use: Supports: confessed adept whose skill, including projections with transmuting powder, is attested by contemporaries.

sources.name: Raymond Lully
sources.quote: Converti una vice in aurum 50 millia pondo argenti vivi, plumbi, et stannic.
sources.use: Supports: confessed adept of known Christian zeal; story of 50,000 pounds of gold produced for Edward II.

sources.name: John Reuchlin
sources.use: Listed among those blending alchemy and therapeutics with neoplatonism and cabala.

sources.name: Ficinus the Platonist
sources.use: Listed as above.

sources.name: Picus di Mirandola
sources.use: Listed as above.

sources.name: Spinoza
sources.use: Named as a metaphysician and speculator on the same experimental ground.

sources.name: Alain de l’Isle (Alani Philosophi; Alanai de Insulis)
sources.work: Dicta de Lapide; commentary on the Prophecies of Merlin (Prophetia Anglicana Merlini, Francf. 1608)
sources.use: Supports: said to have obtained the Elixir; example of editors suppressing alchemical testimony.

sources.name: Merlin (St Ambrose)
sources.use: Listed among the great spirits; his Prophecies reported to refer solely to Hermetic arcana.

sources.name: John Trithemius
sources.use: Listed among the great spirits.

sources.name: Cornelius Agrippa
sources.use: Listed as Trithemius' pupil among the great spirits.

sources.name: Norton
sources.work: Ordinal of Alchemy, Preface, in Ashmole’s Theat. Chem. Brit.
sources.quote: Quod inter mille millia, vix subt tres electi
sources.use: Supports: few are chosen; covetousness disqualifies.

sources.name: Chronicon Magnum Belgicum
sources.quote: magnus in magia, major in philosophia, maximus in theologia
sources.use: Supports: praise of Albert at his death.

sources.name: John Andre (J. Andraeas)
sources.work: in addit. ad Speculum Rub de crim. Falsi
sources.quote: Nostris diebus habuimus magnum
sources.use: Supports: testifies to Arnold's conversion of iron bars into gold at Rome.

sources.name: Oldradus (Oldranus)
sources.use: Supports: praised the Hermetic Art and Arnold's wisdom.

sources.name: Abbot Panorimitanus
sources.use: Supports: praised the Hermetic Art and Arnold's wisdom.

sources.name: R. Vallensis
sources.work: de Veritate, etc., in Theat. Chem., vol. 1
sources.quote: Haec ille Andaeas
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: D. Fabianus de Monte, S. Severin
sources.work: Tractatu de Emptione et Venditione, Quest 5
sources.quote: Alchimia est ars perspicaci
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: John Cremer, Abbot of Westminster
sources.use: Illustrates: a long-labouring seeker misled by the adepts' enigmas who found enlightenment by seeking Lully.

sources.name: Theatrum Chemicum
sources.use: Reference only: collection containing works of Bacon, Albert, Aquinas, Arnold and Alain.

sources.name: Cremer
sources.use: Supports the Lully story; Cremer openly condemns the king's breach of faith.

sources.name: Camden
sources.use: Supports: describes the Nobles of the Rose coins.

sources.name: Lully
sources.use: His own declarations cited as evidence for the England story; his alchemical writings described as obscure but numerous and favorable to the art.

sources.name: Lully
sources.work: Theoriea et Practica (in the third volume of the Theat. Chem.)
sources.quote: appears to us one of the very best pieces of Alchemical philosophy extant
sources.use: Atwood recommends it highly.

sources.name: Olaus Borrichius
sources.work: de Ortu et Progressu Chemiae, 4 to., p. 242
sources.quote: Aureas illas Anglorum primum...
sources.use: Supports the Lully story / the English gold coins.

sources.name: R. Constantius
sources.use: Cited as containing allusions supporting the Lully story.

sources.name: l’Englet Dufresnoy
sources.work: Histoire Hermetique (Hist. Herm.), vol. 2 p. 11; vol 3
sources.use: Supports the Lully story; his catalogue lists about 200 of Lully's alchemical treatises; reference for the laws forbidding transmutation.

sources.name: Dickenson
sources.use: Relates the discovery of powder of transmutation in Lully's Westminster cell.

sources.name: Arnold
sources.use: Mentioned as possibly having convinced Lully by exhibiting transmutation in his presence.

sources.name: Rupicessa, De Meun, Flamel, John Pontanus, Basil Valentine, Ripley
sources.use: Listed with Lully and Cremer as genuine seekers entering the lists, contrasted with the spurious brood of idlers.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: For it is most profounde philosophye This subtill science of holy Alkimy
sources.use: Illustrates the universal craze for alchemy across all estates, the ruin of hasty seekers, the need for learning, and the damage done by a monk's book of false receipts.

sources.name: the adept
sources.quote: they have blasphemed the Sacred Science, and by their errors have brought contempt on men philosophizing
sources.use: Supports Atwood's condemnation of fraudulent books; the adept is not named.

sources.name: acts of Parliament; Pope’s Bull’s
sources.use: Illustrates the legal suppression of transmutation, which only drove the pursuit into secrecy.

sources.name: Pope John XXII
sources.use: Said to have practised the art he interdicted and enriched the treasury by it; illustrates continued secret pursuit.

sources.name: Nicholas Flamel
sources.quote: I had now the prima material, the first principles, yet not their preparation
sources.use: His own account is quoted at length as a remarkable, well-known case: the book, its explanation, the preparation, projection, and the moral effect of the Stone.

sources.name: Flamel
sources.use: Sources of the preceding Flamel relation.

sources.name: chronicle
sources.quote: the evidence of his charitable deeds remained and the symbols of the art
sources.use: Supports the lasting visibility of Flamel's charities and symbols in Paris as late as 1740.

sources.name: Flamel
sources.work: La Sommaire Philosophique; Le Desir desiree; Le Grand Eclaircissement
sources.use: Listed among Flamel's writings; the Sommaire is in French verse, translated in the Theatrum Chemicum.

sources.name: Theatrum Chemicum
sources.use: Called 'an esteemed work'; contains a translation of the Sommaire with important annotations; also cited for Picus' de Auro.

sources.name: Histoire Hermetique; Lives of the Adepts; Les Hieroglyphiques de N. Flammel
sources.work: Histoire Hermetique, vol. 1; Lives of the Adepts; Les Hieroglyphiques de N. Flammel
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: The Isaacs (J. I. Hollandus, I. Hollandus)
sources.use: Dutch adepts, father and son, said to have worked successfully; works given as reference.

sources.name: Boorhaave
sources.use: Supports the Isaacs' reputation; he lauds them and seems acquainted with occult science.

sources.name: Basil Valentine
sources.work: Chimische Schriften (Hamburg edition, 1717); Triumphal Chariot of Antimony; Stone of Fire; Twelve keys
sources.use: Praised as the star of the 15th century, credited with a new method for the Red Elixir; editions and translations assessed.

sources.name: Kirchringius
sources.use: His Latin version with 'admirable commentary' is the basis of the only good English translation of Valentine.

sources.name: Bibliotheque des Philosophes Chimiques
sources.work: Bibliotheque des Philosophes Chimiques, second edition
sources.use: Contains the Twelve Keys.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: Till the white medicine be fully wrought;
sources.use: Supports the rarity of the Red Stone and the order white-before-red; the Ordinal is praised as candid and orderly except for the concealed Subject Matter.

sources.name: Albertus Magnus, the Black Freere
sources.use: Named in Norton's verse as lacking understanding of multiplying the Red Stone.

sources.name: Freer Bacon
sources.use: Named in Norton's verse with Albertus; also 'Friar Bacon', whose example Agrippa followed in proving principles.

sources.name: Elias Ashmole
sources.quote: I know enough to hold my tongue, but not enough to speak
sources.use: His collection praised; his preface cited to show secrecy and the need for practical experience; also cited on incredulity as a punishment.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.use: The Twelve Gates criticized as disorderly and misleading. Separately, Ripley is cited (via Ashmole) for verses against those who prate 'Of Robin Hood, and of his Bow' without practice; the chunk does not name the work.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.work: Erroneous Experiments (An Admonition of Erroneous Experiments, Theat. Chem. Brit., p. 189)
sources.quote: But profytt found I right none therein.
sources.use: Illustrates the failures of ignorant practice on vulgar substances.

sources.name: Eirenaeus Philalethes
sources.use: Criticized: practically explanatory for the initiated but sophistical to beginners.

sources.name: Pierce, the Black Monke
sources.use: Among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole's collection.

sources.name: Bloomfield
sources.use: Among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole's collection.

sources.name: Philosophy and Experience
sources.use: Among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole's collection.

sources.name: Ficinus
sources.work: Liber de Arte Chemica (Marsilii Ficini Florent.)
sources.use: Translator of Plato and of the works imputed to Hermes; explained the art theoretically.

sources.name: Plato
sources.use: Mentioned only as translated by Ficinus.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.use: Translated from Greek into Latin by Ficinus.

sources.name: Picus, prince di Mirandola
sources.work: de Auro; Opus Aureum de Auro
sources.use: Supports the link of Alchemy with profound metaphysical science.

sources.name: Cornelius Agrippa
sources.work: three books of Occult Philosophy; Vanity of the Sciences (De Vanitate Scientiarum)
sources.quote: I could tell many tings of this art, if I had not sworn to keep silence
sources.use: Supports the oath of secrecy and the singleness of the subject; Atwood argues the Vanity is a consummation, not a recantation.

sources.name: Abbot Trithemius
sources.use: Agrippa's source for the means and principles of Occult Science.

sources.name: Celsus
sources.use: 'Celsus’ ladder' used as an image of ascending knowledge.

sources.name: the monks
sources.use: Criticized for promulgating Agrippa's Vanity as a recantation.

sources.name: Theophrastus Paracelsus
sources.work: three Addresses to the Athenians; Aurora
sources.use: Criticized for deliberately misleading writings; best works named; his death discussed.

sources.name: J. Crollius
sources.use: Disciple of Paracelsus; his book carries the Addresses to the Athenians in English; named among worthy disciples.

sources.name: J. Grasseus
sources.work: Water Stone of the Wise Men
sources.use: Published with the Aurora.

sources.name: Lives of the Alchemists
sources.use: Reference only (on Paracelsus' death).

sources.name: Van Helmont, Crollius, Fludd, Helvetius, Faber
sources.use: Named as intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus.

sources.name: a modern adept
sources.quote: this bushel being placed over the light, the darkness of it invited ignorance abroad
sources.use: Supports the claim that hiding the truth let ignorance spread.

sources.name: Erasmus
sources.use: His burlesques illustrate the alchemical mania of the age.

sources.name: Chaucer
sources.work: the tale of the Chanon’s Yeoman
sources.use: Illustrates the boastings and beliefs of ignorance.

sources.name: Geber
sources.quote: as one of Geber’s cooks
sources.use: Named in Ripley's verse; failed practitioners as 'Geber’s cooks'.

sources.name: Alexander Seton
sources.work: Open Entrance [Correction: Philalethes]; n73: Introitus Apertus ad Occlusum Regis Palationem, cap. xiii
sources.quote: a continual banishment: deprived of the society of friends and family
sources.use: Illustrates the persecution of true adepts and the danger of even healing with the medicine. The bracketed correction in the text attributes the work to Philalethes.

sources.name: Michael Sendivogius
sources.work: Novum Lumen Chemicum / The New Light of Alchemy
sources.use: His imprisonment illustrates persecution. His book is praised as attractive but deliberately disordered, needing repeated study. He is also identified by some with Philalethes and with 'Alexander Seton'.

sources.name: Khunrath (Henry Khunrath)
sources.work: n84: Ampitheat. Sapientiae Eternae; Magnesia Catholica
sources.use: Pious adept embittered by mistreatment. Listed among the German adepts.

sources.name: George Von Welling
sources.use: A persecuted adept and friend of Fichtuld. Listed.

sources.name: Herman Fichtuld (Fichtuld)
sources.use: A persecuted adept. Listed.

sources.name: Ambrose and Phillip Mueller (Muller)
sources.work: n78: Philippi Mulleri Miracula et Mysteria Medico-Chemica; Amb. Muller's Paradeis-Spiegel
sources.use: Persecuted adepts. Listed among the German writers.

sources.name: Harprecht
sources.use: A persecuted adept, sometimes confused with Philalethes.

sources.name: Rosicrucian Fraternity
sources.use: A secret association into which some adepts carried their work for protection.

sources.name: Thomas Vaughan
sources.work: English rendering of the Rosicrucian Fame and Confession, with preface and appendix
sources.use: Translator and commentator on the Rosicrucians. Sometimes confused with Philalethes.

sources.name: Dee (Dr Dee)
sources.quote: Master E. Kelly did open the great secret to me, God be thanked.
sources.use: Source for Kelly's projection and for the possible discovery of the secret.

sources.name: Kelly (Sir Edward Kelly)
sources.use: Example of an adept who reportedly possessed the Powder. His book is judged of little value, and his lavishness is criticized.

sources.name: A True and Faithful Relation of what passed for many years between Dr John Dee and some Spirits
sources.work: A True and Faithful Relation ..., London 1659
sources.use: Reference for Dee and Kelly's spirit conversations, which Atwood calls 'ludicrously mundane and abortive'.

sources.name: Ashmole
sources.use: Relates the warming-pan story and judges Kelly profuse beyond a sober philosopher.

sources.name: Theat. Chem. Brit.
sources.work: notes appended to the Theat. Chem. Brit.
sources.use: Reference only (n75; its marker does not appear in the text).

sources.name: Bloomfield
sources.use: Witness to rings made of Kelly's gold.

sources.name: Jacob Boehme
sources.work: The Aurora, or Day Spring; The Discourse of the Three Principles; The Mysterium Magnum; The Tree of Life; The Turned Eye, or 40 Questions Concerning the Life of Man; Epistles (n77: Boehme's Works, edited by Law and others, 4 vols.)
sources.use: Supports: the plainest exponent of the mystery from experience, with explicit pointers to the physical basis of magic and the material of the stone. Qualified: his revelation is theosophical, not intellectual.

sources.name: Pordage and Lead school
sources.use: Not to be undervalued; on the same original track as Boehme.

sources.name: manuscript eulogy found in a volume of Boehme's works
sources.quote: In Boehme’s wondrous page we view, Discoverd and revealed anew
sources.use: Praises Boehme as renewing all ancient wisdom. It names Eastern Magi, Orpheus, Hermes, Confucius, Zoroaster, Pythagoras, Plato, Socrates and Epictetus. Atwood accepts it with the qualification 'theosophically, but not intellectually'.

sources.name: the Greeks
sources.use: Their doctrine of Wisdom is held up as unequalled, to be discussed later.

sources.name: J. Crollius
sources.work: n81: Philosophy Reformed, transl. By Pinnel
sources.use: Listed adept.

sources.name: the Van Helmonts, father and son
sources.use: Listed adepts.

sources.name: Grasseus
sources.work: the Water Stone (n83: Das Wasser-Stein des Weissens; Arca Arcano; Lillium inter Spina)
sources.use: Reputed author of the Water Stone and a personal friend of Boehme. Listed.

sources.name: Andrew Libavius
sources.quote: A ponderous compilation.
sources.use: Listed.

sources.name: J.J. Beccher
sources.work: n86: Physica Subterranea; Oedipus Chemicus Aperius Mysteria; Laboratorium Chemicum
sources.use: Listed.

sources.name: J. Tollius
sources.work: n87: Tollii Fortuita; Manudcutio ad Coelum Chemicum; Sapientia Insanies, sive Promissa Chemica
sources.use: A Dutchman and an elegant classical expositor on the same ground.

sources.name: Faber
sources.use: Listed.

sources.name: Michael Maier
sources.work: n89: Symbola Aurea Mensae; Ulysees; Septimana Philosophica
sources.use: Ranks first among those who explained ancient fable by the Hermetic key, though profoundly guarded.

sources.name: John French
sources.work: The New Light of Alchemy (translation); n90: French's Art of Distillation
sources.use: A practitioner who translated Sendivogius, with a 'bold and striking' preface.

sources.name: Paracelsus
sources.use: Published together with French's New Light, 1650.

sources.name: Digby (John Digby)
sources.work: n91: Sendivogius' New Light of Alchemy, London 1722
sources.use: Translator of the French edition, which adds the Treatise on Salt and an instructive Dialogue.

sources.name: Dufresnoy
sources.quote: les Anglois n’ecrivent sur la science hermetique avec beaucoup de lumiere et de profondeur
sources.use: Supports: a skeptic's testimony to the depth of English Hermetic writing.

sources.name: Eirenaeus Philalethes (Eiranaeus)
sources.work: An Open Entrance to the Shut Palace of the King; Ripley Revived; The Marrow of Alchemy; Metallorum Metamorphoses; Brevis Manuductio as Rubinum Coelestum; Fons Chemicae Veritatis
sources.use: Presented as the most celebrated later adept, a 'perfect artist', whose identity is unknown.

sources.name: Starkey
sources.quote: I saw
sources.use: Testimony that Philalethes possessed the White and Red elixir, and an account of Starkey's own wasteful projection.

sources.name: Boyle
sources.use: Rumoured to have been intimate with Philalethes (uncertain).

sources.name: Museum Hermeticum / Musaeum Hermeticum
sources.use: Collection containing works by Philalethes and the Water Stone.

sources.name: Manget's collection
sources.use: Collection containing works by Philalethes and Grasseus.

sources.name: Thomas Vaughan
sources.work: Magia Adamica; Coelum Terrae; Anthroposophia Theomagica; Anima Magia Abscondita; Euphrates, or Waters of the East; Lumen de Lumine
sources.use: Supports: praised as showing the Art of vital perfectibility most clearly of English authors; pseudonym Eugenius Philalethes; death by overdose of the elixir.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.use: Contrasts: the 'foregoing' adept with whom Vaughan is confounded.

sources.name: Virgil
sources.use: Illustrates: his death compared to Vaughan's.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.use: Illustrates: account of Alexander the Great's death by the venom of the waters of the Styx, paralleling Vaughan's.

sources.name: Petri Norelli
sources.use: Reference only: for the count of 4000 authors.

sources.name: Borricius
sources.use: Supports: counts 2500 authors; also cited for transmutation stories.

sources.name: L’Englet Dufresnoy
sources.work: Histoire Hermetique, tom. iii, in Catalogue Raisonnee des Ecrivains de cette Science, Paris, 1762
sources.use: Criticized: reduced the count of authors, ignorant of the subject, excluding by title rather than matter; also cited (hist. Herm., vol. 2) for transmutation stories.

sources.name: Van Helmont
sources.quote: I have seen the Stone and handled it
sources.use: Supports: eyewitness projection on quicksilver yielding gold; powder received from the stranger Butler.

sources.name: Paracelsus
sources.quote: Our tincture of gold
sources.use: Supports: describes the tincture's astral fire, signs and transmuting and medicinal power.

sources.name: Friar Bacon
sources.use: Supports: said he saw and touched the perfect thing transmuting.

sources.name: Lully
sources.use: Supports: same testimony.

sources.name: Arnold
sources.use: Supports: same testimony.

sources.name: Geber
sources.work: Epilogue to the Investigation of Verity, Russel’s Geber
sources.quote: we have searched out and found, and have seen with our eyes and handled with our hands
sources.use: Supports: work verified by experiment and reason; completed magistery handled.

sources.name: Pico di Mirandola
sources.quote: I have seen it and done it myself
sources.use: Supports: a friend made gold and silver in his presence.

sources.name: Gustavus Adolphus
sources.use: Supports: transmutation before him in 1620, gold coined into medals.

sources.name: king of Prussia
sources.use: Supports: transmutation at Berlin, 1710.

sources.name: Kircher
sources.use: Supports: explicit transmutation story.

sources.name: Helvetius
sources.use: Supports: explicit transmutation story.

sources.name: unattributed verse
sources.quote: vaguely opinable, But clean, experimental and determinable
sources.use: Illustrates: the evidence of Alchemy was concrete.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.quote: Never trewly for merke nor for pounde Make yt I common
sources.use: Supports: offered to show his king the Stone's working, conditionally; argues against wilful deceit.

sources.name: H. Khunrath
sources.quote: I write not fables
sources.use: Supports: tangible Azoth; received the universal tincture and healed with it; argues against self-deception.

sources.name: Lord bacon
sources.use: Supports: reportedly experimented toward the philosophers' stone and recognized its possibility in the Advancement of Learning; did not condemn the tradition.

sources.name: Sir Isaac Newton
sources.use: Supports: recognized the possibility; did not condemn the tradition.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: Every and each of them disclosed but a parte
sources.use: Supports: the parts of the work are set out of order and divided among authors.

sources.name: Artephius
sources.quote: he that takes the philosophers’ saying according to the outward sense and signification has already lost the clue to Ariadne
sources.use: Supports: the art is cabalistic and must not be read literally.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.work: Preface of the Twelve Treatises (n109: New Light of Alchemy, preface)
sources.quote: this Art is for the wise, not for the ignorant
sources.use: Supports: read from the possibility of nature, not the words; the art is for the wise; montebanks deceived the world.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.quote: it being the custom of philosophers to use them; thou hast need of them
sources.use: Supports: indirect teaching by reasons and examples; deliberate contradictions.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.quote: In horrid metaphors veiled are an art most plain
sources.use: Supports: a plain art concealed in metaphor to protect it from the unworthy.

sources.name: Roger Bacon
sources.quote: operate according to the blood; i.e., according to the understanding
sources.use: Supports: leave off experiments until understanding is attained.

sources.name: Basil Valentine
sources.use: Cited among adepts who warn against practice before full understanding; 'Basil's' receipts also named among those that misled literal readers.

sources.name: Eiranaeus
sources.use: Cited among adepts who warn against practice before full understanding.

sources.name: Geber
sources.use: His receipts, read literally, misled seekers into laboratory practice.

sources.name: Glauber
sources.use: His receipts, read literally, misled seekers into laboratory practice.

sources.name: Dufresnoy
sources.use: Reference only; no marker for n1742 appears in the chunk text.

sources.name: Turba
sources.quote: Est in Mercurio quicquid quaerunt Sapientes
sources.use: Chapter epigraph; the maxim that all the wise seek is in Mercury, taken up again in I.2 ¶12.

sources.name: Arnold di Villanova
sources.quote: there abides in nature a certain pure matter
sources.use: Supports: the basis of the whole theory.

sources.name: Arnold
sources.work: Liber Perfect. Magist.; Speculum Alchymiae Arnoldi, Octava Dispositio
sources.quote: Species non transmutari sed individual specierum
sources.use: Supports: species are indestructible, so the subject must be freed by artificial reduction.

sources.name: Friar Bacon
sources.work: Radix Mundi et Speculum Alchemiae (n1, as 'Roger Bacon')
sources.quote: Species non transmutantur, sed subjecta specierum optime et propriisime
sources.use: Supports: subject-matter, not species, is transmuted; the first work is Solution.

sources.name: the author of the Rosarium
sources.work: Rosar. Abbrev., Tract ii. De Lapide in Thet. Chem., vol iii
sources.quote: Adverte carissime...
sources.use: Supports: Solution as first preparation; subjects of species must be reduced to first matter; analogy of glass-making.

sources.name: Avicenna
sources.work: Sciant Artifices Alchimiae, Lib. ii, Tractat. i, Cap. iv, De Operat.Med. Sing.
sources.use: Cited as concurring on species; reference only.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.work: Metoer lib. iii cap. iv (the 'Book of Meteors')
sources.quote: Metalla autem omnia...
sources.use: Cited as concurring, via Ripley's verse: metals not transmutable unless reduced to their beginning.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.quote: Without they be reduced to their beginning materiable
sources.use: Supports: reduction to first matter; liquable bodies may be mercurized; the science is true.

sources.name: Raymond
sources.use: Named in Ripley's verse as having determined the science true.

sources.name: Lully
sources.quote: Elementiva habent vera conditiones et una species se non transmutet in aliam
sources.use: Apparent contradiction explained: he denies only a false position of the art.

sources.name: the adept (Vaughan)
sources.quote: It is the Light only that can be truly multiplied
sources.use: Supports: the Light as multiplying agent; every body has passive principles; nothing borrowed from gold or silver.

sources.name: Lucerna Solis (n10: 'Lucerna Salis, from the Latin verse')
sources.quote: A certain thing is found in the world
sources.use: Illustrates the one universal matter, called the Sages' salt.

sources.name: the monk in his Rosary
sources.work: Rosar., Abbrev. Tract. iii and iv
sources.quote: The Stone is one
sources.use: Supports: Stone and medicine are one; nothing is added or taken away.

sources.name: Geber
sources.quote: All is made of Mercury
sources.use: Supports: all from Mercury; the Stone is foetant spirit and living water, dry water.

sources.name: Aquinas
sources.work: Roasrium Abbrev. Tract. iii and v
sources.quote: It is Mercury alone which perfects in our work
sources.use: Supports: Mercury alone suffices; it is the root of gold and silver and works itself.

sources.name: the Greeks and eastern sages; Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, and Peripatetics
sources.quote: a certain pure and hidden fire
sources.use: Supports: ancient doctrine of the Ether as universal source.

sources.name: Virgil
sources.quote: Spiritus intus alit
sources.use: Illustrates: the spirit nourishing heaven, earth and stars.

sources.name: the Ethnics
sources.use: Their Anima Mundi doctrine is said to agree in substance with Hebrew doctrine.

sources.name: Hebrew doctrine
sources.use: Compared: differs from the Ethnic Anima Mundi only in words.

sources.name: Homberg, with Boerhaave, Boyle
sources.quote: this mighty Ether moreover is always at hand
sources.use: Supports: moderns who held with the alchemists a universal Ether; but they lacked proof.

sources.name: Bishop Berkeley
sources.quote: a pure invisible fire
sources.use: Supports: universal material called ether, source of air's vitalizing power.

sources.name: Mesmerism
sources.use: Contrasts: its phenomena revive belief in an Odic Force, which Atwood does not assume here.

sources.name: the Kabalists
sources.quote: Lumen Vestimenti, the Vehicle of Light
sources.use: Supports: a name for the pure Quintessence.

sources.name: the Greeks
sources.quote: the Free Ether
sources.use: Supports: name for the essence freed from gross matter.

sources.name: Zeno
sources.quote: Ignem esse artificiosum, ad gignendum progredientem via
sources.use: Supports: the ether as plastic, generating fire.

sources.name: Cicero
sources.quote: coelestis alstissima aethereaque natura
sources.use: Supports: the ether as igneous nature begetting all things.

sources.name: Euripides
sources.quote: The viewless Ether in his genial arms Clasping the earth; Him call thou Lord and Jove
sources.use: Illustrates: Ether as all-nourishing, called Jove.

sources.name: Blackwells’s Letters on Mythology
sources.use: Reference only (for the Euripides verse).

sources.name: Lully
sources.work: Lullii Theorica et Practica in Theat. Chem., vol. iv; R. Lullii Theorica et Practica, cap. iii. De Forma Minori
sources.quote: Imo argentums vivum nostrum est aqua alterius naturae
sources.use: Supports: the subject is of another nature and needs human art; describes it as Hyle, a clear compounded water.

sources.name: Arnold
sources.work: Arnoldi Speculum, Octava Dispositio; Speculum Alchimiae, Octava Dispositio
sources.quote: Converte elementa et quod quaeris invenies
sources.use: Supports: conversion of elements as reduction of natures to first root; describes argent vive as stone and no stone, One Thing.

sources.name: Lord Bacon
sources.work: De Sapientia Veterum, Fable of Proteus
sources.quote: torture and vex it in order to its annihilation
sources.use: Supports (via Democritus) the torture-and-restoration principle; criticized for proposing mechanical dissolution and for not knowing the Great Art or its subject.

sources.name: Lord Bacon
sources.work: Sylva Sylvarum; History of Rarity and Density
sources.quote: particular digesters applied to the fire
sources.use: Is criticized: such instruments expel the prized nature.

sources.name: Democritus
sources.use: Supports: his proposal (as reported by Bacon) to reduce matter near annihilation and free the spirit; endorsed by Atwood.

sources.name: Paracelsus
sources.work: To the Athenians, book i, text 9; book ii, text 2 and 5
sources.quote: The greatest miracle of all in philosophy is separation
sources.use: Supports: natural magic of separation; true element as spirit of life and First Matter of the elements.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.quote: The elements of Mercury being separated
sources.use: Supports: separation and recombination of Mercury's elements make the elixir.

sources.name: Tractatus Aureus
sources.use: Reference only; its marker (25) does not appear in the text.

sources.name: Orpheus
sources.quote: Fortis subtilis Pan, integer et generalis
sources.use: Illustrates: Pan as the whole of nature.

sources.name: Albertus Magnus
sources.work: De Mineralibus, cap. ii; Breve Compendium in That. Chem. vol. ii
sources.quote: a watery element, cold and moist, a permanent water
sources.use: Supports: definition of the mercury of the wise and first material of metals.

sources.name: Atrephius
sources.quote: a white fume, in substance like to pure silver
sources.use: Supports: description of the subject.

sources.name: Belus

sources.quote: this very permanent water is the stone, but whilst it is water it is no stone
sources.use: Supports: explains 'stone and no stone'.

sources.name: Lucerna Salis Phil.
sources.quote: It is a stone and no stone, In which the whole art consists;
sources.use: Supports/illustrates: verse on the stone, its growth, Red Lyon and red Sulfur.

sources.name: adepts
sources.use: Supports: doctrine that nature's ordinary manifestation contradicts her perfect law; the goddess known only in action.

sources.name: Basil Valentine
sources.work: De Prima Materia, in Museo Hermetico
sources.quote: Corpus anima spiritus in duobus existit
sources.use: Supports: First Matter is like no particular and indescribable without experience; verse on its one-yet-three nature; calls it a third thing (¶42).

sources.name: Rupecissa
sources.use: Supports Basil Valentine's view.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.quote: Aquosa substantia sicca reperta
sources.use: Supports: First Matter as a middle substance; calls it a third thing.

sources.name: Lully
sources.use: Supports: calls it tertium, compounded; a third thing.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: the First Matter is indeed the union of masculine and feminine spirits
sources.use: Supports, as 'a modern authority': definition of the First Matter.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.work: New Light of Alchemy, Tract 10, Of the Supernatural Generation; Tract. 3
sources.quote: Our water is heavenly, not wetting the hands, not of the vulgar, but almost rain water
sources.use: Supports: heavenly water; 'matter of the metals is twofold', which Atwood reinterprets as relation within the Ethereal being.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.work: the ancient book of Synesius (treatise of Synesius)
sources.quote: a clear Light, which fills with true virtue every mind that has once perceived it
sources.use: Supports: long summary passage concluding the 'verbal instructions' on the Matter (with the New Light).

sources.name: the New Light
sources.use: Co-source of the summary passage.

sources.name: the Enigma
sources.use: Illustrates: celebrates the Laelia Aelia as comprehending all.

sources.name: unattributed verse on Proteus

sources.use: Illustrates the one omniform subject.

sources.name: Democritus
sources.use: Earlier cited for 'Pan contains Proteus'.

sources.name: the Orphic oracles
sources.use: Supports: Pan evolves every property and form out of his central will, of necessity.

sources.name: hymn to Mercury (source not stated)
sources.quote: Hear me, O Mercury, and Son of Maia; the bright expositor of things!
sources.use: Illustrates Mercury 'with like allusion'.

sources.name: Georgics (author not named)
sources.quote: Et, quanto illa magis formas se vertet in omnes,
sources.use: Illustrates: the more the shape-changer turns into all forms, the tighter the bonds.

sources.name: Bloomfield
sources.work: Camp of Philosophy, book I, in Ashmole
sources.quote: It is a privy quintessence; keepe it well in minde
sources.use: Illustrates the many names of the subject.

sources.name: Geber
sources.quote: the thing which perfects in minerals, is the substance of argent vive and sulfur, proportionally commixt in the bowels of clean inspissate earth
sources.use: Reinterpreted: not literal sulfur/mercury/earth but relations of the Ethereal being.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.work: Tract. Aur., cap. i, prop. v
sources.quote: the separation of the ancient philosophers is made upon Water, dividing into four substances
sources.use: Reinterpreted: the Water is the ethereal body, not common water.

sources.name: Thales
sources.use: Comparison: his water from which all is generated is not common water.

sources.name: Moses
sources.use: Comparison: the waters on which the Spirit of God moved are not common water.

sources.name: the Arabian
sources.quote: to which we add nothing different or extract, only in the separation removing superfluities
sources.use: Supports: nothing is added; separation only removes superfluities.

sources.name: the moderns / empirical chemists
sources.quote: as the empirical chemists formerly imagined
sources.use: Contrasted/criticized: their elements and distilled waters are not what the adepts mean.

sources.name: all these philosophers
sources.use: Supports: their combined evidence yields the definition of the stone as purified Ethereality.

sources.name: the adept
sources.work: Rosarium, Democritus Phil. Artis. Auriferae, vol. ii
sources.quote: the seed of gold, says the adept, is a fiery form of Light inspissate, and this is the Stone of Fire
sources.use: Supports: seed of gold is fiery Light, the Stone of Fire; Latin line on the stone as fire.

sources.name: Eiranaeus
sources.quote: This Form is Light, the source of central heat
sources.use: Supports: verse on Light as inward agent and Form begetting a seed.

sources.name: Hunt
sources.use: Supports: modern science admits the unexplained nature of light.

sources.name: the Emerald Table
sources.quote: That which is below is as that which is above
sources.use: Supports: unity of agent and patient after dissolution; the One Thing.

sources.name: the adepts
sources.use: Supports: all things derive from the same Spirit; gold is nearest to it; ice in warm water simile.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.work: New Light of Alchemy, Preface to the Phil. Enigma
sources.quote: you must seek for that hidden thing, out of which is made, after a wonderful manner, such a moisture or humidity which doth dissolve gold without violence or noise
sources.use: Supports: the hidden matter dissolving gold, mother of gold.

sources.name: Geber
sources.quote: In metals,says Geber, is lesser perfection than in animals
sources.use: Supports: metals, being less perfect, can be perfected more freely. In-text marker printed as (57), footnote is n47.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.quote: Vulgar gold Sendivogius compares to a herb without seed
sources.use: Supports: metals hindered by crude earth; art via fire or heat; body must be dissolved and pores opened.

sources.name: Augurellus
sources.use: Reference only (cited with Sendivogius).

sources.name: Nuysement

sources.use: Supports: power of the pure mineral spirit (introduced as 'another').

sources.name: the ancients
sources.use: Supports: they assert surpassing realities known in intellect and experiment.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.work: Tractatus Aureus, or Golden Treatise of Hermes, concerning the Physical Secret of the Philosopher’s Stone
sources.use: Introduced as an ancient epitome of the whole Art, of doubtful authorship, to be translated next.

sources.name: Eiraneaeus (the adept)

sources.use: Supports: alchemical books not written for casual or covetous readers.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: This subtill science of holy Alkimy
sources.use: Illustrates: the profundity of the Art.

sources.name: Hermes Trismegistus

sources.use: The primary text of the chapter, given in full and glossed in Atwood's footnotes. Also named as the first to declare that Mercury cannot be mortified alone ('Hermes the King').

sources.name: the Scholiast
sources.quote: not corporally but spiritually and wisely
sources.use: The main glossator, cited throughout with approval ('our Scholiast', 'the wise Scholiast'). Interprets the elements, colours, recipe, Mercury, vulture, mountain, and fire and bird.

sources.name: Geber
sources.quote: he who knows the principles and the way of generation, which consists according to the intention of nature, is but a very short way from the completement
sources.use: Supports the need for theory and a 'true root' before experimenting.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: If one evil man had hereof his will, All Christian peace he might easily spill;
sources.use: Supports the duty of secrecy, since evil men could misuse the art (n15). Elsewhere a reference only.

sources.use: Reference only (cap. 8, 4 and 5, 3).

sources.use: Reference only.

sources.use: Reference only, on secrecy.

sources.use: Reference only.

sources.use: Reference only (p. 3).

sources.use: Reference only (p. 22 in n30).

sources.use: Reference only (for the King gloss).

sources.use: Illustrates: his writings alarmed alchemists by applying alchemy openly to human life.

sources.name: Rosicrucians
sources.use: Illustrates: certain Rosicrucians were alarmed by Agrippa's and Paracelsus' disciples' books.

sources.name: Paracelsus’ disciples
sources.use: Illustrates/supports: applied alchemy to human life and suggested 'the method and medium of attraction'.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.quote: Whosoever, therefore, shall know himself, shall know all things in himself
sources.use: Supports: soul freed from the senses comprehends all; man as image of God and microcosm; self-knowledge gives knowledge and attraction of all things.

sources.name: the Moorish philosopher
sources.quote: contains not so great mysteries and excellences as Man reformed by God into his image
sources.use: Supports: man himself is the best subject and can draw the Central Salt of nature.

sources.name: Trismegistus / Hermes
sources.quote: the work is both in us and about us
sources.use: Supports: the work is within man; also moral requirements of the operator (¶14) and the black-to-white sequence (¶23).

sources.name: Geber
sources.quote: he has not the true root in him whereon to base his labor and intention
sources.use: Supports: the root is in the operator himself.

sources.name: Basil (the monk)
sources.work: Stone of Fire (n8: 'See the Stone of Fire, Kirchringius; Ed. Webster’s Hist. of Minerals, the Extract.')
sources.quote: all metals and minerals have one root from whence their descent is
sources.use: Supports: one root and one thing containing mercury, salt, sulfur.

sources.name: Crollius
sources.quote: the same is the generating spirit of all creatures
sources.use: Supports: gold-producing vapor is in man; describes the true physician.

sources.name: Paracelsus
sources.use: Mentioned as calling Crollius a natural divine; 'salem Paracelsi' in the Latin.

sources.name: Albertus Magnus
sources.quote: fire, which is the true aurific principle in the life of all, burns more than all glorious in him erect
sources.use: Supports: highest mineral virtue is in man.

sources.name: Tract. Aureus. Text et Scholium
sources.quote: Our Mercury is philosophic, fiery, vital
sources.use: Reference for the 'Our Mercury' passage.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.quote: Out of hy myner by arte yt most be brought
sources.use: Supports: man is the mine of the natural mercury.

sources.name: Reymond
sources.quote: Of our Soon and Moone, wyse Reymond seyd so
sources.use: Cited within Ripley's verse as authority.

sources.name: Maria
sources.use: Cited for the shortness of the work as reason philosophers say little.

sources.name: Aliphili (the Arabian)
sources.quote: even thou art he who through the breath and power of the water and earth in thyself, conjoinest the elements
sources.use: Supports: man produces the true fiery water.

sources.name: Theat. Chem. Brit.
sources.quote: For blood is the principle matter of each thing
sources.use: Illustrates: blood as principal matter.

sources.name: Morien
sources.work: De Transm. Metal. Artis Auriferae, vol. 1 end
sources.quote: The thing, O king, is extracted from thee
sources.use: Supports: the matter is taken from man himself.

sources.name: Bohme / Jacob Boehme
sources.work: on the Generation of the Three Principles
sources.quote: the agent in the preparation of this spirit, continues Bohme, is the Invisible Mercury
sources.use: Supplies the three-principle account, the Antimonial Spirit and Invisible Mercury, and the disorder of arterial blood.

sources.name: Phillips
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Arcanum Liquaris Alkahest
sources.quote: sanquinis salem per urinaceum fermentum sic transmutari debere
sources.use: Latin on transmuting salt of blood.

sources.name: our modern exponent
sources.quote: in three months circulation, says he, by digestion, the powder becomes black
sources.use: Confirms and illustrates Hermes' process in terms of the three principles.

sources.name: the more modern class of adepts
sources.quote: a pure, naked, and unmingled fire of infinite capability
sources.use: Supports: man's life as fire capable of improvement.

sources.name: Kirchringius
sources.work: Stone of Fire (as given in n8)
sources.use: Reference only (n8, for Basil's passage).

sources.name: Webster
sources.use: Reference only (n8).

sources.name: Boehme
sources.work: Tract. Aur., cap. 3 (n20); Epistles; Forty Questions; Discourse of the Three Principles (n23)
sources.quote: the Work is easy and simple, but the wisdom therein is great and the greatest mystery
sources.use: Supports: describes the white and red stages, the future of the adepts, concealment under the Seal of God.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.use: Cited as reiterating the process of the Vital Spirit, and as witness that the art must be entrusted.

sources.name: Democritus
sources.use: Cited with Hermes as reiterating the process of the Vital Spirit.

sources.name: the adept
sources.quote: if the process fails in any stage, an addition of the same will renew it
sources.use: Supports: renewal and multiplication of the powder.

sources.name: Nuysement
sources.quote: Auru ex se virtutem...
sources.use: Footnoted source for the passage on gold's magnetical virtue and the names Microcosmic Sun, Stone of Fire.

sources.name: Basil Valentine
sources.quote: how that extraction should be made, is a principal secret in which the whole art of Alchemy consists
sources.use: Supports: the true tincture is not common antimony; extraction is the secret.

sources.name: Kirchringius
sources.work: Triumphal Chariot of Antimony, English edition
sources.use: Reference for the Basil Valentine passage and/or the Latin line.

sources.name: M. Dunstani
sources.use: Reference only ('In init.').

sources.name: Arnold
sources.use: Witness, with Hermes, that the art must be entrusted by one to another.

sources.name: the apostle
sources.quote: He is not far off from every one of us; for in Him we live, and move, and have our being
sources.use: Supports: the principle of being is near us and is to be sought.

sources.name: (unattributed)
sources.quote: Seek and ye shall find, knock and it shall be opened unto you
sources.use: Illustrates the promise that God may be found, though it remains hidden.

sources.name: Vaughan ("that Philalethean Welshman")
sources.quote: change their abstractions into extractions
sources.use: Supports: practical Protochemic Artifice as only way to the foundation; Spirit in nature; uniting Particular Spirit to Universal.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.quote: in us, I say, is the Operator of miracles
sources.use: Supports, endorsed by Atwood as alluding to Alchemy: the pure mind laid asleep and brought into its divine nature; the Operator is within us.

sources.name: Apuleius
sources.use: Called to witness by Agrippa.

sources.name: Epistle to Trithemius
sources.work: Epistle to Trithemius, at the end
sources.quote: But the Spirit begetting all doth in us dwell
sources.use: Supports: the all-begetting Spirit dwells in us.

sources.name: Manilius
sources.quote: Quid mirum noscere mundum
sources.use: Supports (per our translation): men contain the world within and are each a small image of God.

sources.name: cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience
sources.quote: man, say they, is demonstrated to be a compendium of the whole created nature
sources.use: Reported view: man's rank rests on a Divine Reason and a latent Faculty of Wisdom; Atwood says this was once proved but is now beyond present evidence.

sources.name: our metaphysicians
sources.use: Contrast: they lamented the inadequacy of natural reason but could not free it from dependence on sense.

sources.name: Locke
sources.quote: Intuitive faith is certain beyond all doubt, and needs no proof beyond itself
sources.use: Supports: intuition is the highest certainty. Locke's 'sensual system' is also criticized.

sources.name: Victor Cousin
sources.use: Supports: he used the truth of intuitive certainty to shake the sensual system of Locke and Condillac.

sources.name: Condillac
sources.use: Criticized: his sensual system, along with Locke's.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom is the highest science, drawn from what is universal in oneself.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom is the true being of Intellect, small in bulk but surpassing in energy.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.quote: True Intellect, he says, is that which is essentially the most essential of that which is most essential
sources.use: Supports: mystical exercises bring the understanding into contact with its cause; intellect is identical with the intelligible.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.use: Illustrates: Universals compared to colors needing the sun; human reason called 'intellect in capacity'.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: to know oneself is Wisdom and the highest virtue of the soul
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom is self-knowledge; the soul entering itself beholds Deity.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: on the Theology of Plato, lib. 1, cap. 3
sources.use: Reference only (with the First Alcibiades). Elsewhere named among the Neoplatonists who dilate on the same ground.

sources.name: Socrates
sources.quote: Wisdom is generative of truth and intellect
