sources.use: Supports: Wisdom generates truth, perfects imperfect things and calls forth latent Intellections.

sources.name: Diotima
sources.quote: that mind which is become wise needs not to investigate any further
sources.use: Supports: the wise mind possesses its object within itself.

sources.name: Archytas (the Pythagorean)
sources.work: Fragment given by Taylor in his Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagorus
sources.quote: he will have conjoined ends with beginnings
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom contemplates the whole and discovers the Principles of Being, leading to a vision of Divinity.

sources.name: Crito
sources.quote: gave him a sight called Intellect, which is capable of beholding God
sources.use: Supports: Intellect is a God-given sight; mortals lack it through generation.

sources.name: Pythagoras
sources.quote: the science of truth which is in all beings
sources.use: Supports: a definition of Wisdom.

sources.name: Iamblicus
sources.work: life of this Samian (Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagorus by Taylor, chap 2)
sources.quote: it is truly a science which is conversant with the first and most beautiful objects
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom deals with undecaying first objects, by participation in which other things are beautiful.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.use: Reference only: the edition used for the Pythagorean fragments.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.use: Supports: named among the Neoplatonists who dilate on the same ground.

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.use: Supports: 'the graceful Plotinus', named among the Neoplatonists.

sources.name: Neoplatonists
sources.use: Supports: a latent Principle of Universal Science, cognizable under conditions.

sources.name: the Egyptians
sources.quote: that Man should know himself
sources.use: Supports: self-knowledge, meant 'experimentally and ontologically'.

sources.name: Hebrew Kabalists / Rabbis
sources.use: Supports: absolute Idealism; creation's fall and reunion; reason over authority; self-inquiry.

sources.name: Liber Zohar
sources.quote: beams with the revelation of the celestial prototype in humanity
sources.use: Supports: reveals the celestial prototype in humanity and the covert fire in Holy Writ.

sources.name: Holy Writ / Pentateuch / Old Testament
sources.use: Illustrates: read by the Kabalists as divine symbols.

sources.name: Kabalists
sources.use: Supports: their elevation of man as containing the prototype of creation.

sources.name: Rabbi Ben Jochai
sources.quote: The Form of man, says the Rabbi Ben Jochai, contains all that is in the heaven and earth
sources.use: Supports: man as Celestial Prototype and image of God; reads 'The Eternal has founded the earth upon his wisdom' as referring to the human prototype. Atwood endorses.

sources.name: Philo (the Jew Philo)
sources.work: De Praemiis et Poenis; De Nobilitate; De Profugis; De Plantatione Noe
sources.quote: God dwells, says the Jew Philo, in the rational part of man as in a palace
sources.use: Supports: the rational part of man as God's temple; the soul as impression of the Logos-seal.

sources.name: Hermes (the ancient Hermes)
sources.quote: For this Mind in men is God
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom as the good and blessed Eternity; Mind in men is God.

sources.name: the Stagyrite
sources.quote: It is essentially, the most essential of that which is most essential.
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom as the most essential reality, not an abstraction ('before cited').

sources.name: Solomon (the wise king)
sources.quote: Wisdom, says the wise king, is more moving than any motion
sources.use: Supports/illustrates: panegyric of Wisdom as pure, all-pervading, renewing, entering holy souls.

sources.name: Scripture
sources.use: ¶45 refers to Scripture's promise with Wisdom (following Solomon's panegyric) and says there are other such places.

sources.name: Geber
sources.work: Investig. of Perf., cap. 3; Russel's Geber
sources.quote: men have thought the confection of fold impossible, because they have not know the artificial destruction according to the course of nature
sources.use: Supports: the work fails for ignorance of the 'artificial destruction'.

sources.name: Bloomfield
sources.use: Reference only (cited in n43 with the verse at ¶48; attribution of the verse not stated).

sources.name: the philosopher
sources.quote: When the soul is situated in the body, says the philosopher, she departs from self-contemplation
sources.use: Supports: purified soul recollects what it forgot.

sources.name: Plutarch
sources.quote: the souls of men are not able to participate of the Divine nature whilst they are thus encompassed about with senses and passions
sources.use: Supports: senses and passions as impediments; rites prepare the aspirant for knowledge of the Supreme Mind. Called 'well initiated in these mysteries'.

sources.name: Isis (the old mythology)
sources.use: Illustrates: the divine beauty Isis pursues; 'the Goddess' whose temple is Reason.

sources.name: Psellus
sources.quote: there is no other means of strengthening the vehicle of the sold but by material Rites
sources.use: Supports: the soul perfected by material rites and divine illumination.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: calls the magic of Zoroaster the service of the gods
sources.use: Supports: magic as divine service.

sources.name: Zoroaster
sources.use: His magic described as the service of the gods.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.use: Supports: efficacy of Divine Works.

sources.name: the Emperor Julian
sources.work: arguments preserved by Cyril; Julian's Arguments (Greek extract)
sources.quote: without such assistance the Divine union is neither effected not rightly understood
sources.use: Supports: Divine union requires such assistance.

sources.name: Cyril
sources.use: Reference only: preserved Julian's arguments.

sources.name: Eleusian Mysteries (accounts of)
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom as offspring of a vital experiment into nature.

sources.name: Archytas
sources.quote: If you investigate rightly, says Archytas, discovery will be easy for you
sources.use: Supports: right method of investigation is the key; mankind has not known how to investigate.

sources.name: the Platonic Successor
sources.work: Iamblichus on the Mysteries; Taylor's Notes
sources.quote: has given us observation through Sacred Arts, by which we have at hand sufficient assistance
sources.use: Supports: Sacred Arts replace lost spontaneous revelation.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.use: Reference only (cited in footnotes).

sources.name: Oracle of Apollo, from Eusebius
sources.quote: The Path by which to Deity we climb Is arduous, rough, ineffable, sublime;
sources.use: Epigraph: the path to Deity is hard and was disclosed by Egyptians and other ancient peoples.

sources.name: Alexandrians
sources.use: Their enthusiasm for the Mysteries cited as evidence of their high regard.

sources.name: Iamblichus / Iamblicus
sources.work: Iamblicus on the Mysteries; Taylor, p. 109
sources.quote: by certain ineffable and sublime media that Theurgists became cognizant partakers in the Wisdom of true Being
sources.use: Supports: the rites worked by divinely potent arts, not contemplation or representation; also listed among Neoplatonists who describe the Mysteries.

sources.name: St Augustine
sources.use: Church Father who adopted the language and rites of the Mysteries; quotes many lost Neoplatonist books.

sources.name: Cyrillus / St Cyrillus
sources.quote: except in obscure terms, in such a manner, however, as that the faithful who are initiated may comprehend, and the rest be discouraged
sources.use: Church Father adopting the Mysteries' rites; supports that the church veiled its mysteries in enigmas.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.use: Church Father adopting the Mysteries' rites; also among writers who describe the Mysteries.

sources.name: Clemens Alexandrinus
sources.quote: O mysteries truly sacred, O pure light!
sources.use: Supports: called the Mysteries 'blessed'; describes the Greater Mysteries as unveiling nature, the Lord as hierophant.

sources.name: Warburton
sources.use: Criticized: saw the Mysteries as political fraud; his notions obsolete. Divine Legation also cited as reference in n8.

sources.name: Sainte Croix / St Croix
sources.use: Criticized: thorough research but astronomical and superficial reading.

sources.name: Gebelin
sources.use: Criticized: agricultural interpretation.

sources.name: La Pluche
sources.use: Criticized: agricultural interpretation.

sources.name: the author of Antiquity Unveiled
sources.work: L’Antiquitie devoilee par ses Usages, etc.
sources.use: Criticized: saw the Mysteries as a depository of religious melancholy of the first men.

sources.name: Thomas Taylor
sources.work: Dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic Mysteries (footnote attached to his sentence)
sources.use: Qualified: examined philosophically but still treated the rites as immaterial ceremonies representing abstract truths. Taylor also named in n7 alongside 'Iamblicus on the Mysteries'.

sources.name: the Platonist
sources.use: Supports (previously cited): the Mysteries were called Initia.

sources.name: Psellus
sources.use: Supports (previously cited): the Mysteries were called Initia.

sources.name: Cicero
sources.use: Supports: Initia as beginning of a life of reason and virtue and hope of immortality.

sources.name: the Pythagoreans
sources.use: Supports: Greater Mysteries induce assimilation and final contact with the first principle.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: better worth than 10,000 corporeal eyes
sources.use: Supports: assimilation through the Greater Mysteries; the divine eye.

sources.name: Heraclitus
sources.use: Supports: the theurgic media are medicines of imperfect souls.

sources.name: temples of Esculapius
sources.use: Illustrates: bodily healing extensively practised with minor physico-magical arts.

sources.name: Strabo
sources.use: Supports: philosophy was the object of the Eleusinian rites.

sources.name: Servius, commenting on Virgil
sources.quote: Libris patris sacra ad purgationem animarum pertinebant
sources.use: Supports: Bacchic rites served purification of souls.

sources.name: Euripides
sources.quote: I was blessed when I got a sight of the mysteries
sources.use: Illustrates: the people placed chief felicity in the Mysteries; first quote spoken 'by Hercules', second from Bacchis.

sources.name: Sophocles
sources.quote: Life only is to be had there, all other places are full of misery and evil
sources.use: Illustrates the same.

sources.name: Praetextus
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Des Septchenes / De Septchenes
sources.use: Reference only; source of extracts for Clemens and Cyrillus.

sources.name: writers on Animal Magnetism
sources.use: Qualified: rightly link Trance to temple mysteries but do not go beyond therapy.

sources.name: Zoist
sources.use: Reference only, for mesmeric cures.

sources.name: De Mainaduc, Puysegur, Colquhoun, Elliotson, Townshend, Dupotet
sources.use: Praised as faithful pioneers of Mesmerism, since whom the science has retrograded.

sources.name: the Neoplatonists: Plotinus, Proclus, Porphyry, Synesius, Iamblicus
sources.use: Supports: their surviving writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.quote: This Etherial Spirit, he says, is situated on the confines of the rational and brutal life
sources.use: Supports: describes the Etherial/phantastic Spirit, the need for desire, will and assent, the purification of the imaginative soul, and the trials (Hercules). Atwood endorses the passage as 'beautifully suggestive' and calls his an account of 'the life that is operated upon' and 'the artifice'.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.use: Reference only: source of the Synesius extract (vol. 2) and of the History of the Restoration of the Platonic Philosophy.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.work: History of the Restoration of the Platonic Philosophy
sources.use: Reference only, for the Synesius passage in ¶13.

sources.name: Pythagoras
sources.use: Illustrates: long preparations and ordeals before admission to deeper mysteries, and purification of disciples' souls.

sources.name: his biographer (of Pythagoras)
sources.use: Reports that Pythagoras healed and purified his followers' souls by divine arts.

sources.name: Iamblicus
sources.quote: dense thickets, which are full of briars
sources.use: Supports: the uninitiated mind is obstructed, and souls must be cleansed before receiving doctrine (dyer analogy). Elsewhere: Theurgic rites follow immutable intellectual canons, and the mundane spirit fashions the soul's powers.

sources.name: Olympiodorus
sources.quote: The phantasy, says he, is an impediment to our intellectual conception
sources.use: Supports: phantasy opposes divine enthusiasm, and perceiving Universals proves the soul can act without it. Called 'The Egyptian Olympiodorus'.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.use: Reference only (with Taylor), for the Olympiodorus passage.

sources.name: Plato
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom assigned to old age (meaning intuitive Intellect without imaginative error), and the 'two-fold ignorance' he condemns.

sources.name: the ancients
sources.quote: one and the same in all, where difference is merged in objective union
sources.use: Supports: the truth is the same experience in all; the worst evil is not perceiving one's evil; they warn about the treatment of the Spirit.

sources.name: the Sacred Discourse
sources.quote: the Spirit grows heavy and sinks into profound Hades
sources.use: Supports: the labours of Hercules as the trials of whoever contends for liberty, and the Spirit's sinking when the will inclines downward.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.quote: it folds itself about the indivisibility of true intellect (which is in its center)
sources.use: Supports: describes the mundane/phantastic spirit as enfolding intellect and conforming to all forms.

sources.name: the oracles
sources.use: Cited as teaching that the impure perceptive medium needs 'alternation and solution' for discerning good and evil.

sources.name: the Alchemists
sources.use: Atwood links their condemnation of the defiled vulgar Matter, and its preparation into the Mercury of the Philosophers, to the purification of the Spirit.

sources.name: Albertus Mangus
sources.work: Secret. Tact. Alberti, in fine; Artis Auriferae
sources.quote: The first rule of the work is a perfect solution
sources.use: Supports: wash the occult Arcanum ('our brass') until pure; perfect solution is the first rule.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.use: Supports: his 'passive intellect' names the Mundane Spirit as first revealed in humanity.

sources.name: the Alchemists aforesaid
sources.quote: a thing indifferent, abject, and exposed in all hands
sources.use: Supports: their description of the subject-matter fits the Common Soul.

sources.name: the adept
sources.quote: It is what the world cares not for, as the adept says, but disesteems it
sources.use: Supports: the subject is common and despised, yet those who know the Art and have the medium will be richest.

sources.name: Aquarium Sapientum
sources.use: Reference only (footnote to the adept's words).

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.use: Reference only (footnote to the adept's words).

sources.name: Lord Bacon
sources.use: Raises a difficulty: his supposition that the understanding is too polluted by the fall to reflect total reason, in which case introspection would be useless.

sources.name: the ancients
sources.use: Supports: they warn against passive dreaming in the phantasy and require the mind to be cleared and made passive before contemplation.

sources.name: the Greek philosophers
sources.use: Supports, in part: their authority grounds the inference that the Mysteries were real and efficacious.

sources.name: Eastern temples / the priests at Eleusis
sources.use: Illustrates: where the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries were celebrated.

sources.name: Philalethes
sources.quote: Few, very few, Philalethes said, there were in his day
sources.use: Supports: few understand the principle's full scope.

sources.name: Reuchlin
sources.quote: Ex natura et divino factum est
sources.use: Supports: the purified principle, as medium of divine experience, is 'Ex natura et divino factum est'; the rest of the sense rests on our translation only.

sources.name: the Greek Aristhenes
sources.quote: Take that which is least, and draw it by artifice into the true ferment of philosophers
sources.use: Supports: the subject is least valued and outwardly dead but alive within, and preparation removes superfluities.

sources.name: Aristiteles
sources.use: Reference only (footnote n18: 'Aristiteles in Roasrio, and in the Lucerna Salis').

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.quote: For she her secret agent doth possess, Which in the universe is only one
sources.use: Supports, in verse: nature has one secret agent, distinct through numberless species.

sources.name: Esdras
sources.quote: The earth giveth much mould, whereof earthen vessels are made, but little dust that gold cometh of
sources.use: Illustrates: few attain the work.

sources.name: Latin maxim (unattributed)
sources.quote: Nemo enim dat id, quod non habet.
sources.use: Supports: only one who has it can impart it.

sources.name: Latin verse (unattributed)
sources.quote: Non levis adscensus, si quis petat ardua, sudor
sources.use: Illustrates: the toil of the ascent.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.quote: It s necessary that the soul, when purified, should associate with its Generator.
sources.use: Chapter motto: supports the aim of the purified soul's reunion with its source.

sources.name: Roger bacon
sources.work: De Mirab. Potest. Artis et naturae, Ars Aurifera, vol 2
sources.quote: Volo ovum philosophorum dissolvere et partes philosophici hominis investare, nam hoc est initium ad alia
sources.use: Called 'the experimental Friar'; supports that the beginning is dissolving and investigating the philosophic man.

sources.name: the Alchemists
sources.quote: it ought to be dissolved
sources.use: Supports the term dissolve for the trance change; also cited for Black Saturn, mineral tree, doves.

sources.name: the author of the Rosarium
sources.quote: Corpora qui vult purgare oportet fluxa facere
sources.use: Supports dissolution: the earthy body of sense made to flow.

sources.name: Albertus Magnus
sources.quote: The beginning of the work, says Albertus Magnus, is a perfect solution
sources.use: Supports solution as beginning; dissolve and recongeal, fix and volatilize.

sources.name: Virgil
sources.quote: Facilis descensus Averni
sources.use: Main illustration: Aeneas' descent read as allegory of the Mysteries; Virgil believed initiated. Sybil's warning, golden bough, cave, reception, 'king in hell'.

sources.name: Dryden
sources.quote: Deep forests and impenetrable night Possess the middle space
sources.use: English verse rendering of the Latin in ¶6.

sources.name: Warburton
sources.use: Supports: golden bough literally part of the sacred equipage; Aeneid VI alludes to the Mysteries.

sources.name: Apuleius
sources.use: Supports: the bough connected with the Mercurial caduceus in the procession of Isis initiates.

sources.name: Raymond Lully
sources.quote: Intellectus naturam habens subtilem ad intellignedum res intellibiles
sources.use: Supports reading the golden bough as Brancha Spiritualis, the subtle intellect.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: It is necessary that a man should have his right opinion as firm as adamant in him when he descends into Hades
sources.use: Supports the need for firm reason in Hades and the danger of sleeping there.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.use: Supports (endorsed): why Theseus and Pirithous were detained in Hades.

sources.name: Claudian
sources.work: de Paptu Proserpineae / De Raptu Prosepinae
sources.quote: Jam furor humanus nostro de pectore sensus Expluit
sources.use: Illustrates entry into arcane mysteries and the advent of the deity at Eleusis.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.quote: Urinus Saturni
sources.use: Supports: another name for the Black Saturn, which waters lunar and solar plants.

sources.name: another (unnamed)
sources.quote: Ex mari meo oriuntur nebulae
sources.use: Illustrates the same matter as source of blessed waters.

sources.name: Plato
sources.use: Supports: likens the soul's descent into generation to an earthquake.

sources.name: Plato
sources.use: Illustrates: Glaucus deformed by weeds, compared to the viscous soul.

sources.name: Psellus
sources.quote: mere appearances, having no substance, and therefore not signifying anything true
sources.use: Supports: the apparitions in the Chaldaic rites, including superinspection, are empty products of the soul's passions.

sources.name: Oracula Chaldaeorum
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: the oracle (Chaldaic)
sources.quote: he apply not his mind to it, nor esteem the voice proceeding thence to be true
sources.use: Supports: do not attend to the apparitions.

sources.name: the Chaldaic oracle
sources.quote: Natura suadet esse demonas puros, et malae materiae germina utilia et bona
sources.use: Supports: there are pure demons and the products of evil matter are useful.

sources.name: the oracle
sources.quote: Let the immortal depth of thy soul be predominant, and all thy eyes extend upwards
sources.use: Supports: turn upward, away from the image-loving Hades.

sources.name: the Chaldaic oracle
sources.quote: the mortal, approaching the fire, will have a light from divinity
sources.use: Supports: the guide and the promised light.

sources.name: the poets
sources.use: Illustrates: Pan as a veil for the vaporous estate and its frightening disguises.

sources.name: Aeneid
sources.quote: Corripit hic subita trepidus formidine ferrum
sources.use: Illustrates the apparitions (Latin given untranslated; per our translation, Aeneas draws his sword on bodiless shades until warned).

sources.name: Aeneid
sources.quote: Umbrarum hic locus est, somni noctisque soporae
sources.use: Illustrates: the place of shades.

sources.name: Aeneid
sources.quote: Nunc animis opus, Aenea, nunc pectore firmo.
sources.use: Illustrates: the courage required.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: commentary on the First Alcibiades of Plato; Proclus on the Theology of Plato, vol. 1, p.9; De anima et Demona
sources.quote: In the most holy Mysteries, says he, before the presence of the god, the impulsive forms of certain terrestrial demons appear
sources.use: Supports: deceptive images precede illumination in the Mysteries; the same holds in the speculation of Wholes.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: Excerpta M. Ficini ex Graecis Procli Com. in Alcibiad.
sources.use: Reference only: on the demons' material efficacy in Divine Works.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.quote: Demons who machinate a thousand ills,
sources.use: Supports: demons keep souls in the body, forgetful of their origin.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: Proclus on the Theology of Plato, book 1,cap. 3
sources.use: Reference for the dry soul turned to itself radiating its own light.

sources.name: Basil Valentine
sources.work: Alchemical Chariot; Triumphal Chariot of Antimony, Kirchringius edit.
sources.quote: endowed with senses and understanding, know Arts, and have in themselves an occult operative life
sources.use: Supports: exterior spirits are intelligent and deceive the unwary.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.use: Reference only: regular descriptions of demoniacal natures.

sources.name: Trithemius
sources.use: Reference only: descriptions of demoniacal natures.

sources.name: Psellus
sources.use: Reference only: on the demons' material efficacy.

sources.name: Iamblicus
sources.use: Reference only: on the demons' material efficacy.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.use: Reference only: on the demons' material efficacy.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.quote: If the soul on its departure, says Porphyry, still possesses a spirit turbid from humid exhalations, it then attracts to itself a shadow and becomes heavy
sources.use: Supports: a moist spirit binds the soul to images and to earth, and leaving nature makes it a dry splendor.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.use: Supports: demons are progeny of matter at war with the truth-seeking soul.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.quote: Our viscous soul
sources.use: Supports: names the soul in its defiled state.

sources.name: Heraclitus
sources.quote: a dry soul is the wisest
sources.use: Supports: the dry, self-turned soul.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: Extract from the ray its shadow and its obscurity
sources.use: Supports: separate the watery, obscuring nature from the fire until the redness is pure.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: O Nature! The most wonderful creatrix of natures
sources.use: Supports: the Stone is generated with light and brings forth clouds and darkness.

sources.name: the sage
sources.quote: Visitabis interiora terrae rectificando
sources.use: Supports: Atwood reads the saying as referring to sense-life.

sources.name: the Alchemists
sources.quote: Ignis rubber super dorsum ignis candidi
sources.use: Supports: life is a fire imprisoned in aerial moisture; they warn of the horrors and phantoms.

sources.name: the sage in Enoch
sources.quote: there is an angel standing upon it, and that angel struggles to prevail
sources.use: Illustrates: the guarded mineral soul.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.work: Regio Phantastica of his Hieroglyphic; Lumen de Lumine, Introd. Coelum Terrae, p. 90.
sources.quote: The eye of man never saw her twice under one and the same shape
sources.use: Supports: the First Matter keeps changing form under the fire of nature.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: a certain inviolable mass
sources.use: Supports: describes the 'father' of the Seed.

sources.name: Raymond Lully
sources.quote: Spiritus fugitives in aero condensators, in forma monstrorum diversorum et animalium etiam hominum
sources.use: Supports: first principles as cloud-like monstrous spirits. Atwood reads this as known from inner self-inspection.

sources.name: the adept
sources.quote: a decompounded ens, extremely heavy, shining through the darkness like a fiery star
sources.use: Supports: describes the Seed of Spirit found in the process.

sources.name: Brethren of the Rosy Cross
sources.work: a letter circulated under the name of the Brethren of the Rosy Cross
sources.quote: There is a mountain situated in the midst of the earth or center of the world
sources.use: Illustrates: an allegory of the initiatory passage (mountain, beasts, night, guide, courage).

sources.name: Themistus
sources.quote: the initiated is seized at first with solicitude and perplexity
sources.use: Supports: the initiate's perplexity until the conductor opens the vestibule.

sources.name: Warburton
sources.use: Reference only (for Themistus).

sources.name: The adepts
sources.quote: The adepts, many of them, are at some pains to denote the peculiar disposition and appearance of this guide
sources.use: Supports: the guide.

sources.name: these famous Christian philosophers
sources.quote: When you have discovered the mountain, the first miracle that will appear is this
sources.use: Illustrates: supplies the mountain allegory (wind, earthquake, fire, calm, tincture). Atwood qualifies it, saying their promises of gold drew futile public searches.

sources.name: Aeneid
sources.use: Reference only (attached to the wild beasts).

sources.name: divine oracles
sources.use: Supports: they teach that fire obliterates the strains from generation.

sources.name: Tract. Aureus
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Eccles.
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: 1 Kings
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: the Greeks
sources.use: Contrast: they kept silent about, or poetized, the physical revealments of the Tartarean realms out of fear of vulgar curiosity.

sources.name: Arabian Nights
sources.use: Illustrates: the 'entertaining' style of the Christian philosophers' promises.

sources.name: Milton
sources.quote: That riches grow in hell
sources.use: Illustrates: human works are outdone by spirits reprobate.

sources.name: Aladdin
sources.quote: Aladdin’s rapid castle
sources.use: Illustrates how such works vanish before celestial light.

sources.name: Platonic discourses
sources.use: Reference: they describe souls' allotments in Hades and the expiatory rites. Atwood declines to linger on them.

sources.name: the Ethics
sources.use: Cited for Tartarus as the next region beyond Hades.

sources.name: Euripides
sources.quote: a dream of death
sources.use: Supports: names the threshold where the Lesser Mysteries end. The Bacchae verse (¶43-44) supports purification and initiation.

sources.name: Stoboeus
sources.quote: The mind is affected and agitated in death, just as it is in initiation into the Grand Mysteries.
sources.use: Supports: the conformity of death and the next initiation, and its stages.

sources.name: Dr Warburton
sources.use: Translator of the Stoboeus passage ('well rendered').

sources.name: Solomon
sources.quote: the fear of God is the beginning of Wisdom
sources.use: Supports: Atwood reads it as the awe of the soul perceiving itself in its source.

sources.name: the son of Dirach
sources.quote: at first she will walk with him by crooked ways, and bring fear and dread upon him
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom first tries with fear, then reveals her Secret. Atwood attributes this to the same intimate experience.

sources.name: the adept
sources.work: Hermes, Tract. Aur., cap. 2; Ripley Revived, 5th Gate
sources.quote: O happy gate of Blackness!
sources.use: Supports: the noble body that suffers first and is exalted later; the gate of blackness; Dissolution.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: it is the business of philosophers to study how to be dead
sources.use: Supports: philosophic death.

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.use: Supports: the same doctrine, while condemning suicide.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.work: Auxiliaries to the Perception of Intelligible Natures (Aux. to Intell., sect. 1, 8, 9)
sources.quote: the other peculiar to philosophers, in which the soul is liberated from the body
sources.use: Supports and explains: the twofold death, which Atwood glosses. In ¶43 (the chapter motto) the purified soul's conversion to its generator.

sources.name: the Hebrews and Academics
sources.quote: precious death
sources.use: Supports: Atwood equates their 'precious death' with the gate of blackness.

sources.name: the truth-telling Oracle
sources.quote: If thou extend the fiery mind to the work of piety,
sources.use: Supports: piety and the fiery mind preserve the body; the soul's way of return; the warning against stooping down; the soul clasping God.

sources.name: the adept
sources.quote: he that has once passed the Aquaster, and entered the Fire World
sources.use: Supports: what is seen in the Fire World (Prester and Sun, fire's descent and reascent, the Fire Spirit's root). The extent of the quotation is unclear.

sources.name: Anaxagoras
sources.quote: hands loftily
sources.use: Supports: identifies the central earth with the Salt of Saturn.

sources.name: the Epidaurian
sources.quote: I approached the confines of death, and, having trod the threshold of Proserpine, I returned from it
sources.use: Illustrates: an initiate's account of what was done in the Mysteries.

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.quote: that the supplier of life is present
sources.use: supports: the soul's participation of Deity and perception of the source of life.

sources.name: Psellus
sources.quote: the Introspection which Psellus speaks of
sources.use: supports: distinction of Introspection (formless Divine Light) from Superinspection in Hades.

sources.name: the oracle / the Oracle
sources.quote: When thou seest a Fire without Form, Shining flashingly through the depths of the World, Hear the voice of Fire
sources.use: supports: the formless Fire/Light as the true vision; cited again at ¶52–53 for 'Fire, the derivation and dispenser of Fire'.

sources.name: Sir William Jones (translator of an Indian record)
sources.quote: know that to be the mind’s maya (or image or delusion) as of light or darkness
sources.use: supports: same instruction that all mental appearances except the First Cause are image or delusion.

sources.name: Deuteronomy
sources.quote: Take good heed unto yourselves, for ye saw no manner of similitude on the say that the Lord spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire
sources.use: supports: the unfigured form of the Divine Essence.

sources.name: Zohar
sources.use: supports: Divinity has no form before descent into creation, hence no image may represent Him.

sources.name: Walker’s or Lloyd’s Eidouranion
sources.use: contrasts: the orrery explanation of the Mysteries' lights, which Atwood rejects.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: Proclus on the Theology of Plato, Vol. 1, Book 3, Chap. 18
sources.quote: Beauty shining forth astonishes those that behold it, converts the soul to itself
sources.use: supports: astonishment before the mystic spectacles; Beauty converting the soul and showing what is in the adyta.

sources.name: Apuleius
sources.quote: this knowledge sometimes shines forth with a most rapid coruscation like a bright and clear light in the most profound darkness
sources.use: supports: the inner light experienced when separated from body; his 'midnight Sun' identified with the ignited Stone (¶54).

sources.name: Plato
sources.work: seventh Epistle (Taylor, vol. 5); The Cratylus, and Timaeus
sources.quote: on a sudden a light, as it were a leaping fire, will be enkindled in the soul, and will there itself nourish itself
sources.use: supports: Intellectual Intuition as a sudden self-nourishing inner light; heaven as kindled intelligence of the First Intelligible.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.work: Hymn to Plotinus, Select Works, Preface
sources.quote: Nor was the vision like the dreams of sleep, But seen whilst vigilant you brave the deep
sources.use: illustrates: waking vision of sacred light.

sources.name: the adept (unnamed)
sources.quote: Open the compound creature; look up the elements; divide the elements, and you shall find the quintessential nature
sources.use: supports: the work as separation of the compound to its quintessence and angelical spirit.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: Qui fornacem cum vase nostro construit, novum mundum conflat.
sources.use: supports: furnace and glass make a new world, glossed as new hypostasis and stone.

sources.name: Fludd
sources.use: reference only (source for the Hermes quotation).

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: unite the heaven in triple proportion to the earth, and then apply a generative heat to both
sources.use: supports: procedure on the 'little new world' to attract the 'star-fore of nature'.

sources.name: Tabula Smaragdina Hermetis
sources.use: reference only (cited in n59 alongside Vaughan).

sources.name: Anaxagoras
sources.use: illustrates: his 'ignited Stone' identified with the inner Sun; Atwood says he was discredited through the error that he meant the visible sun.

sources.name: Helvetius
sources.use: illustrates: his 'Armed Magnet' identified with the Wheel of Fire / inner Sun.

sources.name: Ezekiel; the Hebrew prophets, Moses, David, and Zachariah
sources.use: illustrates: the Wheel of Fire, in which all things are transfigured.

sources.name: the Revelation / the Apocalypse
sources.use: illustrates: the Stone of the Apocalypse; the Stone with the new name.

sources.name: the Savior
sources.use: supports: the order to have Salt in ourselves.

sources.name: Zoroaster
sources.quote: the Prester of Zoroaster which in the Chaldean sense means the Fire Spirit of Life
sources.use: supports: Prester as Fire Spirit of Life, identified with the Stone/Salt.

sources.name: St. John
sources.quote: In Him was Life; and the Life was the Light of men.
sources.use: supports: the Word/Light shining in darkness as the same Light; also the power to become sons of God (¶55).

sources.name: Abraham
sources.work: Sepher Jezirah; Liber de Creatione, Authore Abraham, cap. 1
sources.quote: Intellige in scientia et sepias intellignetia
sources.use: supports: Abraham as example of the wisely simple who subdued will to the Law of Wisdom; closing Latin injunction.

sources.name: Isis / Osiris
sources.quote: as Isis for Osiris
sources.use: illustrates: reason constantly seeking her true Hypostasis.

sources.name: modern interpreters (unnamed, 'as some say')
sources.use: is criticized: for explaining the Mysteries' lights as orreries and astronomy.

sources.name: our doctors
sources.use: supports: the Art's perfection as multiplying the Prester and placing him in the supreme Ether.

sources.name: Zoroastri Oracula
sources.quote: It behooves thee to hasten to the Light, and to the beams of the Father
sources.use: Chapter epigraph: exhortation to the Light.

sources.name: Olympiodorus
sources.work: Commentary on the Gorgias of Plato
sources.quote: islands stand out of, as being higher than the sea
sources.use: Supports: allegorical reading of Hercules' last labour and of the Islands of the Blessed/Elysian Fields as a state above corporeal life.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.work: notes to his Pausanius, Vol. 3, p. 215; his Dissertation; p.237
sources.use: Source of the Olympiodorus extract (n1); praised for setting forth Virgil's Elysian particulars in his Dissertation; cited for Porphyry (n6).

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: On the Theology (of Plato), Bk. 4, Cap. 7
sources.quote: the plain of Truth, he says, is intellectually expanded to intelligible Light
sources.use: Supports: Hercules' purification and establishment among the gods. Also the Elysian fountains as Theurgists' chief hope of salvation, and the Meadow as the prolific power of life.

sources.name: Homer
sources.quote: A lofty gate unfolds on either side
sources.use: Illustrates: the two gates of the cave in Ithaca, read as allegory of descent and ascent.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.work: on the Cave of the Nymphs; Aid to Intelligibles
sources.quote: a fountain, not flowing outwardly, but circularly scattering its streams into itself
sources.use: Supports: northern/southern gates as descent into generation and ascent to divinity, 'immortals' as essentially immortal souls. Also illustrates the self-reflexive intellectual vision and the time/eternity distinction.

sources.name: Virgil
sources.quote: Devenere locos laetos, et amoena vireta
sources.use: Illustrates: passage from Tartarus to the Elysian Fields, and the Eridanus as flow of spirit; his Elysian scenes read as the unfolding of the embryo life.

sources.name: the Oracle
sources.use: Source of the name 'Pratum' for the meadow of Divine Ideas.

sources.name: Flammel
sources.quote: the philosophers have indeed a garden where the sun as well morning as evening remains with a most sweet dew
sources.use: Supports: the alchemists' garden and the mountain of the Seven with its royal herb.

sources.name: Maria
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.work: Preface to Famma et Confessio, R.C.
sources.quote: the rendezvous of all spirits, where Ideas as they descend from above, are conceived and incorporated
sources.use: Supports: description of the garden; adds the Apollonius passage to clarify R.C.'s account.

sources.name: Esdras
sources.use: The 'outgoings of paradise' identified with the seven mystic mountains.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.use: His 'Planetary Sphere' identified with the seven mystic mountains.

sources.name: Solomon
sources.use: The 'enclosed garden of Solomon' and sealed fountain identified with Elysium.

sources.name: Heraclitus
sources.quote: we live their death and die their life
sources.use: Supports: explains nox corporis, souls dead to this life and alive in the other.

sources.name: Empedocles
sources.quote: Heaven’s exiles straying from the orb of light.
sources.use: Supports: we desert our best life by turning to externals.

sources.name: R.C.
sources.quote: Vidi aliquando Olympicos domos
sources.use: Illustrates: philosophers visiting the Elysian place.

sources.name: Apollonius
sources.quote: I have seen, says Apollonius, the Brahmans of India dwelling on the earth and not on the earth
sources.use: Illustrates (via Vaughan): the abode of the Brahmans as like the philosophers' habitation.

sources.name: the oracle (to Amelius)
sources.quote: Ubi Amicitia est, ubi cupido visu mollis
sources.use: Illustrates: the soul of Great Plotinus is in such a place.

sources.name: the Sybil
sources.use: Illustrates: drew inspiration from rivers of supernal light.

sources.name: the Orphic poet
sources.quote: Omnia quae Phoebo quondam meditante beatus Audiit Eurotas
sources.use: Illustrates: Apollo contemplating such rivers.

sources.name: St Augustine
sources.use: Supports: three modes of human vision; the third (anagogic) placed in Elysium.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.use: His Athanor, 'before mentioned', used as comparison for the revelation of the Image of Universal Nature.

sources.name: Aristophanes
sources.quote: The sun shines but for us, exclaims the chorus of the Initiated in Aristophanes
sources.use: Illustrates: the privileged light of the initiated, who perform acts of piety and justice.

sources.name: Plato
sources.use: Via Proclus: the Meadow as the prolific power of life.

sources.name: Theurgists
sources.use: Said by Proclus to place their chief hopes of salvation in the Elysian fountains.

sources.name: Tractatus Aureus
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: ancient physiologists and alchemists
sources.use: Said to accord with the metaphysician by experimentally proving the Universal Identity of Nature.

sources.name: Apuleius
sources.quote: Moved by thy prayers, O Lucius! Behold, I am come!
sources.use: Illustrates: the appearance of the goddess (Isis/nature) in the Eleusian Fane and her mandates to the initiate.

sources.name: Apuleius
sources.quote: Thou rollest the heavens round the steady poles, dost illuminate the sun, govern the world, and tread on the dark realms of Tartarus.
sources.use: Supports: Lucius' awakening after the Isis oracle and praise of the goddess, which Atwood applies to the Universal Nature; Lucius' rosy crown and shedding the beast's hide illustrate the soul's liberation.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.work: translations cited by page; 'Taylor’s notes to his Pausanias'
sources.use: Reference only (cited by page in n10, n12, n18, n20; his Pausanias notes supply the Ascelpius extract; n19 points to his note on the Phaedrus passage, no marker in the text).

sources.name: Iamblichus
sources.quote: By no means therefore, says Iamblichus, does Divinity either transform himself into phantasms
sources.use: Supports: effect of the divine vision on the initiated (fishes image); the gods emit true illuminations, not phantasms; truth with the god as light with the sun.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.quote: entering not either into the schools of other philosophers, but into yourself, ye shall know all things
sources.use: Supports: knowledge by entering into oneself; oblivion as impediment; passage from light to light.

sources.name: the Apostle
sources.quote: and from glory to glory
sources.use: Supports Agrippa's 'light to light'.

sources.name: Aeneid
sources.quote: Spiritus intus alit
sources.use: Illustrates: Aeneas meeting his father in Elysium receives the Epopteia of Universal Nature; spirit and mind pervading the whole.

sources.name: unattributed verse (Helius)
sources.quote: To Erebus he went, and the sad realms of night
sources.use: Illustrates descent to the realm of night and the ancestors, leading to Aeneas.

sources.name: unattributed couplet
sources.quote: To find the Hero, for whose only sake We sought the dark abodes and crossed the bitter lake.
sources.use: Illustrates the descent undertaken to reach the Paternal.

sources.name: Alexandrian Platonists
sources.use: Supports: initiation to the Paternal abode opens all divine paths.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: on The Theology of Plato, Book 4, Chapter 26; Book 1, Chap. 20; Chap. 3
sources.quote: there are indeed many steps of ascent, but all of them extend to the Paternal port and the Paternal Initiation
sources.use: Supports: grades of initiation; visions unfolded from the supercelestial place; phantasms before the gods; the soul's inward conversion to the gods and the One.

sources.name: Socrates
sources.quote: For telete precedes muesis, and muesis, epopteia
sources.use: Supports the ordered grades of initiation (as explained within the Proclus passage); also narrator of Plato's ascent to Intelligible Beauty.

sources.name: Ascelpius Trallianus
sources.quote: it is a certain clearness, as being that which renders all things conspicuous
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom derived from clearness and light.

sources.name: Empedocles
sources.quote: Then all the members of the god appeared
sources.use: Illustrates concealed harmony made manifest by ether's motion ('a poet').

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.work: on the Beautiful and the Three Hypostases
sources.quote: All the gods, says Plotinus, are beautiful, and their splendour is intense.
sources.use: Supports: gods beautiful and visible through Intellect, nourished by Truth.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: resident in a Pure Light
sources.use: Supports: the blessed visions seen by pure souls freed from the body.

sources.name: Dr Warburton
sources.quote: a mere illuminated image, which the priest had purified
sources.use: Criticized: his account of the institution called absurd.

sources.name: the great theologist
sources.use: Cited within the Proclus passage for the soul's entry into the Adytum of Life.

sources.name: the experienced
sources.use: Unnamed authority Atwood relies on for our connection to the Universal Nature's fountain.

sources.name: unnamed verse
sources.quote: "The Hand that moves us is divine".
sources.use: Illustrates: the heavenly bodies proclaim a divine mover.

sources.name: the mathematician
sources.quote: En tibi Norma Poli --- ! en divae Libramina Molis!
sources.use: Illustrates: praise of the Creator's laws and foundations (Latin; our translation).

sources.name: Iamblichus
sources.quote: the perfect efficacy of ineffable works
sources.use: Supports: union comes from divine media and Synthemata, not intellectual perception. Endorsed.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.use: Reference only (page for the Iamblichus citation).

sources.name: Chaldaic Oracle
sources.quote: O how the world hath Intellectual guides inflexible!
sources.use: Supports/illustrates, in 'operative language': fire, intellectual pattern, Presters of Intellectual Fire.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.quote: the motions themselves will be dissolved through their proximity to the reasoning power
sources.use: Supports: once discipline is complete, the inferior powers submit to Reason.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.work: New Light of Alchemy, Element of Fire
sources.quote: Fire, says the adept philosopher, is the purest and most worthy of all the elements
sources.use: Supports: the nature of the divine Fire, the rational soul, and the exclusion of the compounded. Endorsed.

sources.name: Morieni
sources.work: de Trans, Metal; Ars Aurifera, vol 2
sources.quote: Scire etiam tibi convenit, O bone rex
sources.use: Supports: the magistery is God's secret of secrets, entrusted to the prophets.

sources.name: the Greeks
sources.use: Their usage is cited: Intelligible Causes are called gods.

sources.name: Orphic Fragment
sources.quote: I open a secret to the Initiated, but let the doors be shut.
sources.use: Supports: purity and contemplation of the One. Atwood qualifies its 'never seen by mortal eyes': the Initiated did behold Him.

sources.name: Musaeus
sources.use: Addressee of the Orphic fragment ('offspring of the bright Silene').

sources.name: Warburton
sources.use: Reference only (where the Orphic Fragment is found).

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: Plato beautifully unfolds the passive method of the Divine Intuition
sources.use: Supports: passive intuition and the three elevating causes of love, hope and faith. The 'head of the charioteer' phrase is called Platonic.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.quote: what else than faith is the cause of this ineffable muesis?
sources.use: Supports: initiation comes through faith-given silence, above Gnostic energy.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.quote: This, then, is the Paternal Port and the discovery of the Father, according to Proclus, viz., an undefiled union with him
sources.use: Supports: gives Atwood's account of the soul's union with the Father, the 'Paternal Port'.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.work: On the Timaeus of Plato, Vol. 1
sources.use: Reference only, for the Proclus passage (p. 254).

sources.name: the Platonic Successor
sources.quote: Now, if ever, to remove from ourselves multiform knowledge
sources.use: Supports: an exhortation to inner stilling and adoration of the First, praised by Atwood for its 'magnificence of thought and diction'.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: there are many more thrysus bearers than Bacchic souls
sources.use: Supports: the discovery is called 'difficult' as Plato alludes. Plato cites the records of the Mysteries, which Atwood reads as saying that many have the fire but cannot draw it forth.

sources.name: the Poets
sources.quote: emerging, as the Poets say, from the bosom of the ocean
sources.use: Illustrates the Sun from which the Intelligible gods proceed (inside the Platonic Successor's passage).

sources.name: the Divine Oracle
sources.quote: There is something Intelligible which it behooves thee to understand with the Flower of thy mind.
sources.use: Supports: said to ratify the Platonic instruction on how to apprehend the Intelligible.

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.quote: He comes, says Plotinus, suddenly alone
sources.use: Supports: the sudden arrival of the One and the description of the transparent ultimate state.

sources.name: unattributed Latin verse
sources.quote: Ille deum vitam accipiet, divisque videbit
sources.use: Illustrates the attainment of the life of the gods.

sources.name: unattributed Latin verse
sources.quote: Tunc ire ad mundum archetypum saepe atque redire
sources.use: Illustrates repeated going to and returning from the archetypal world.

sources.name: records of the Mysteries
sources.use: Cited by Plato as witness to the thrysus-bearers saying.

sources.name: the orphic verse
sources.quote: triumphant, and appearing in splendour to mortals
sources.use: Illustrates the radiant return of Bacchus.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.use: Reference: 'several notable examples in ths kind' of radiant transfiguration.

sources.name: Apuleius
sources.use: Reference for Socrates shining forth in ecstasy.

sources.name: the expounders
sources.quote: all this splendid delirium and transfiguration in the Mysteries was the effect of narcotic liquors
sources.use: Criticized: Atwood rejects the narcotic explanation as common sense acting 'Procrustes like'.

sources.name: Greek and Alexandrian Platonists; mystics of the middle ages; the enlightened Fathers of the Christian Church
sources.use: Supports: Atwood says their writings give much evidence that the Eleusinian rites differed widely from common report.

sources.name: early Christians; the wisest Ethnics
sources.quote: early Christians concurring with the wisest Ethnics in declaring that they proposed the noblest ends
sources.use: Supports: they agree that the Mysteries were instituted pure.

sources.name: Epictetus
sources.use: Supports: the Mysteries become venerable when one believes they were provided for the perfection of human life.

sources.name: Tractatus Aureus
sources.quote: Naturam in primisimitabere in arte, magister.
sources.use: Chapter motto: imitate Nature in the art; on our tentative reading of the corrupt Latin, outer fire only excites, an inner ethereal agent perfects all.

sources.name: the Greeks / Greek philosophy
sources.use: Supports: they substantialize mind as substratal matter of existence; their ethereal hypostasis parallels the alchemists' first matter.

sources.name: modern metaphysics
sources.use: Contrasts: treats mind as abstract or inferential only.

sources.name: Oedipus
sources.use: Illustrates: aided by the Light of true Chemistry to vanquish the Metaphysical Monster and enter the Temple of Truth.

sources.name: the Egyptians
sources.use: Illustrates: they placed the Sphinx in the vestibule of Isis, read as Ether guarding Wisdom.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.use: Reference for the Sphinx interpretation in ¶6.

sources.name: Laus Hermonaeus
sources.use: Reference: 'an admirable extract' concerning the Sphinx, found in Taylor's notes; cited at the end of the ¶6 Sphinx reading.

sources.name: unattributed verse
sources.quote: A nature to search out which is invisible,
sources.use: Supports: the material of the Magistry is invisible and insensible.

sources.name: Arnboldi
sources.use: Reference (with the other n2 sources) for the Latin advice 'vita vitam concipit...': work the material by itself, self to self.

sources.name: Democritus
sources.use: Reference for the same Latin advice.

sources.name: Turba Philosophorum
sources.use: Reference for the same Latin advice.

sources.name: De Lapide Physici Condit.
sources.use: Reference for the same Latin advice.

sources.name: Vaughan ("the adept")
sources.quote: as long as men continue to lick the shell after their fashion
sources.use: Supports: outward study cannot know hidden things substantially, only their outward effects.

sources.name: Vaughan ("the adept")
sources.quote: be sure to add reason to thy experience, and to employ thy mind as well as thy hands
sources.use: Supports: theory precedes practice. The text says 'So wrote Vaughan in 1650'.

sources.name: inductive sciences / modern method of experimenting
sources.use: Criticized: facts accumulated for ages have failed to yield the satisfaction reason requires.

sources.name: Genesis
sources.quote: that land of Havilah where good gold is
sources.use: Illustrates the hidden riches of Wisdom on the a priori ground.

sources.name: Job
sources.quote: Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is Wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding
sources.use: Illustrates, quoted at length: precious things hidden in the earth are brought to light, but Wisdom's place is hidden from all living and known to God; for man, it is the fear of the Lord.

sources.name: unnamed ("he ... who said")
sources.quote: the first step of philosophy is to set the mind a-going
sources.use: Supports: the search for Wisdom begins by setting the mind in motion.

sources.name: the saints and apostles
sources.use: Contrasts: their gift of healing is absent today; the reason is promised in the sequel.

sources.name: scripture ("is it not written")
sources.quote: Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in thy field; and afterwards build thy house
sources.use: Supports: the healer must first heal or be healed. The beam-and-mote saying and 'Physician, heal thyself' are also cited.

sources.name: the Paracelsians / Paracelsian Alchemists
sources.quote: The true medicine, according to the Paracelsians, is bound in man
sources.use: Supports: the medicine and fire of life ('Antimony') are in man and freed by purgation. Named in the chapter title.

sources.name: unattributed ("as is declared")
sources.quote: a pure panacea from the god of Light
sources.use: Supports: the purged life flows forth as panacea.

sources.name: Crollius
sources.quote: physic and pyrotechny, says Crollius, cannot be separated
sources.use: Supports: trial by fire, the natural inbred chemist's separation, the physician born of the light of grace.

sources.name: B. Valentine
sources.use: Reference only (n8, alongside Crollius).

sources.name: Jesus Christ and his apostles
sources.quote: the perfect doctrine of regeneration preached by Jesus Christ and his apostles
sources.use: Comparison: the Theurgic Art comes nearest to their doctrine of regeneration.

sources.name: Iamblicus
sources.use: Supports the claim that Theurgists consulted the divine intellect only on purification, liberation and salvation of life.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.use: Reference for beginners' errors (n10), the Alchemists' precepts (n11) and the gold/Mercury passage (n18, p. 97).

sources.name: Basil Valentine
sources.work: Triumphal Chariot of Antomony / Chariot of Antimony; 'Disce igitur' (n14)
sources.quote: Learn and look for the first foundation, says the monk, which nature holds concealed
sources.use: Supports the need for first-hand experience of nature's hidden first foundation. His second, 'celestial' part (separating pure from impure by spiritual reason) leads into Atwood's turn to spiritual reason. Atwood calls the advice 'Excellent'. Spelled 'B.. Valentine' in n10, 'B. Valentine' in n15, and called 'the monk'.

sources.name: Norton
sources.use: Reference only (beginners' errors).

sources.name: Lully
sources.work: Lullii Theoria et Practica, cap. 68 and 88; Arbor Scientiae, Brancha Human; Arbor 10, Scientiae, p. 99
sources.quote: Intellectus naturam habens subtilem ad intelligendum res intelligibles
sources.use: Supports: lessons of patient rational inquiry; 'intimates' Reason as a ferment; source of the Latin on Intellect (n26).

sources.name: Crollius
sources.quote: by a holy assiduity of preparations, joining thereto diligent contemplation of natural causes
sources.use: Supports: preparation, contemplation, handiwork and grace bring forth great things.

sources.name: Van Helmont
sources.quote: the attainment of the Tree of Life is laborious, and the fruit of intellectual research
sources.use: Supports the claim that the work is laborious and intellectual.

sources.name: Michael Maier
sources.use: Named among writers with specimens of the preliminary lessons; reference for the gold/Mercury passage.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.quote: Our fire is the true sulfur of Gold
sources.use: Supports. His 'internal fire of the sulfur of thy water' names the operating agent (¶13), and he supplies the account of fire, waters, menstruals, regimen and signs (¶14).

sources.name: Ripley Revived
sources.use: Reference for the Eirenaeus passage (n16) and the gold/Mercury passage (n18).

sources.name: the poet
sources.quote: reclusa resedet longius
sources.use: Illustrates how remote the discovery is.

sources.name: the Sybil / Aeneas
sources.quote: Alte vestiga oculis: et rite repertum
sources.use: Illustrates the Golden Bough: sought by looking upward, and yielding only to one the fates call.

sources.name: Orpheus
sources.quote: Mercurii ingedier spuluncam
sources.use: Illustrates prudent entry into the Cave of Mercury, which Atwood interprets hermetically.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.work: de Somniis (extract in Taylor's Proculus on Euclid)
sources.quote: Intellect above all things separates whatever is contrary to the true purity of phantastic Spirit
sources.use: Supports the claim that Intellect purifies the phantastic Spirit.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.work: Proculus on Euclid; a note to Aristotle's Metaphysics
sources.use: Transmits the Synesius extract and the Anaxagoras passage.

sources.name: Paracelsus
sources.work: book to the Athenians (First Book of the Athenians, text 9, 10)
sources.quote: Separation is the greatest miracle in philosophy
sources.use: Supports: Separation as the Art's primary object; free will as friend or foe; the sequestatrix. Atwood calls him 'our doctor'.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.work: Tract. Aureus, cap. 2 and cap. 4; Smagardine Tablet (Tabula Smaragdina hermetis); Asclepius (Aclepius, cap. 13)
sources.quote: Thou shalt separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross
sources.use: Supports: the perscrutinating Intellect, the separation precept read as Mind the Separator, man's power to effect the Causal Nature, and the One only Thing ('the great Master', n24). Called 'the same reputed author'.

sources.name: Arnold
sources.use: Named as celebrating the Head Stone.

sources.name: Bacon
sources.use: Named as celebrating the Head Stone.

sources.name: Geber
sources.use: Named as celebrating the Head Stone.

sources.name: Manget
sources.use: Reference only. n25 continues 'Sumantur Lapis in capitulis notus, etc.'

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.work: Select Works (treatise on the Gnostic Hypostasis)
sources.use: Reference only ('a very beautiful treatise').

sources.name: Anaxagoras
sources.work: lost works, as preserved by Simplicius; given in Taylor's note to Aristotle's Metaphysics
sources.quote: Intellect is infinite and possesses absolute power, and is not mingled with any thing
sources.use: Confirms Intellect's efficient, separating operation. Atwood calls him 'one of the earliest of the Greek hermetic School'.

sources.name: Simplicius
sources.use: Preserved the Anaxagoras passage.

sources.name: Anaxagoras
sources.quote: it begins from that which is small to exercise its comprehending power
sources.use: Supports. Atwood says what he describes as past, internal philosophers describe as present (¶23), and she cites his 'begins from that which is small' for starting with a small portion (¶32).

sources.name: Eudoxus in Plutarch
sources.quote: the mind and reason of the Supreme God, which in nature is invisible and dwelling in obscurity, by being put in motion becomes known
sources.use: Illustrates. The myth of Jupiter's grown-together feet freed by Isis, which Atwood reads as an allegory of the Art.

sources.name: the Magian
sources.work: Agrippa’s Third Book of Occult Phil., chap. 43
sources.quote: All is one soul, says the Magian, but reason, unless it be illuminated, is not free from error
sources.use: Supports: reason needs divine illumination.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.work: Third Book of Occult Phil., chap. 43
sources.use: Reference only (source of the Magian's words).

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.work: treatises attributed to Aristole by his Arabian compilers, as rendered by Taylor, from the Latin of A. Magnus in his Dissertation, book 3
sources.quote: That Intellect must be assumed which is most perfectly purified
sources.use: Supports: the purified Intellect is to be sought in spirit.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.use: Reference only (translator of the Aristotle passage).

sources.name: A. Magnus
sources.use: Reference only (Latin source of the Aristotle passage).

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.work: Select Works, On the Gnostic Hypostasis; Ennead 5, Lib. 8
sources.quote: a sudden Light, and this Light is from Intellect, and is also It
sources.use: Supports. Intellect's beauty and sudden Light (¶23), and approaching the universal subject through an image, a portion of gold (¶32).

sources.name: the philosopher
sources.quote: Dimidium facti qui bene coepit habet
sources.use: Supports: a good beginning is half the work.

sources.name: Homer
sources.use: Illustrates. Achilles' armour, Patroclus' death and Achilles' vow and death, read as allegory of the Art.

sources.name: Pope
sources.quote: Patroclus dead, Achilles hates to live.
sources.use: Gives the verse quoted; Atwood criticizes him for rendering the heroic tears 'unavailing'.

sources.name: Virgil
sources.quote: Hunc tegit omnis Lucus et obscures claudunt convallibus umbrae
sources.use: Illustrates. Misenus' rites before the descent, Aeneas leaving the bough, the hidden tree and the Golden Bough, and the mother's birds as guides. Atwood denies Virgil was a servile imitator of Homer.

sources.name: the Sybil
sources.use: Illustrates: enjoins peculiar rites and sacrifices to Misenus' remains, compared with those at Patroclus' pile.

sources.name: Apollonius Rhodius
sources.work: Argonaut., Lib. 2; Fawkes’ Apollonius Rhodius Argonautics, Book. 1
sources.quote: So the gloomy god/Stood mute with fearto see the golden rode
sources.use: Reference / parallel to the terror caused by Achilles' armour.

sources.name: Fawkes
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Plato, Proclus, Porphyry, Faber, Tollius, Michael Maier
sources.use: Supports. The 'golden chain of Hermetic philosophers' who traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil as their own.

sources.name: Manzoli (Palingenius)
sources.quote: Take this Arcadian slippery lad that’s apt to fly.
sources.use: Supports. His verse 'divulges the artificial method'; Atwood says the name Palingenius means 'one regenerated'.

sources.name: Capricornus 214
sources.use: Reference only. Footnote 34 has no marker in the main text.

sources.name: the great Apostle (St Paul)
sources.quote: thou sowest not that body that shall be
sources.use: Supports: what is sown must die to be quickened and rises in a better form.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: our Son, as Hermes calls him
sources.use: Supports: Hermes' 'our Son' is one more personification of the intellectual purpose.

sources.name: L. Comitibus
sources.use: Reference for 'To find the true Separator is ... the greatest difficulty'.

sources.name: Chrysopaea
sources.use: Reference for the difficulty of finding the true Separator.

sources.name: Trevisan
sources.use: Example: he worked over half a century in vain until he found the separated Light.

sources.name: Pontanus
sources.quote: seek to know this Fire with all thy soul
sources.use: Supports. He erred two hundred times; the Fire is the unrevealed key and is found only by profound meditation.

sources.name: Zachary
sources.use: Cited as another example of long searching for the key.

sources.name: Flamel
sources.use: Example: having the matter, fire and furnace from Abraham the Jew, he still wandered three years.

sources.name: Abraham the Jew
sources.use: Mentioned as the one who indicated fire and furnace to Flamel.

sources.name: Madathan
sources.work: Mus. Hermeticum, Lumen de Lumine, p. 67
sources.quote: I was entrusted with the Key of Power, by a secret revelation from Almighty God
sources.use: Example: he failed for five years and received the key by revelation after the sixth.

sources.name: Basil Valentine
sources.work: Chariot of Antimony; Stone of Fire
sources.quote: in the preparation of Antimony consists the Key of Alchemy
sources.use: Supports. The key lies in preparing Antimony (the stone of Fire) with the microcosm's corporeal fire.

sources.name: Kirchringius
sources.quote: this opens the first gate, this will also unlock the last
sources.use: Supports. The key is the principal part of the Art, and its method is called Manual Operation.

sources.name: Lucerna Salis
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Jacob Boehme
sources.quote: that they first seek God’s love and grace, and resign up themselves to become wholly one with that
sources.use: Supports: the operator must first surrender to divine grace; the divine Separator may not be given into unworthy hands. Atwood qualifies that the divine cannot exactly be given into possession.

sources.name: Boehme
sources.quote: enter in even to the Cross, then seek gold and you will not be deceived
sources.use: Supports the core operation (Sol and Luna brought through death at the cross and reconceived); Atwood says it comprehends 'the end and beginning of the Sacred Art'.

sources.name: the fables (Theseus, Ariadne, Jason, Medea, Hercules, Eurystheus, Achilles, Ulysses, Minerva, Aeneas, the Sybil)
sources.use: Illustrates: the hero never labors alone but is aided by wise counsel, as the Moon or Passive Intelligence aids the seeking Reason.

sources.name: Maria Practica
sources.quote: Istud est vas Hermetis, quod Stoici occultaverunt
sources.use: Supports or illustrates: the vessel of Hermes as the 'measure of thy fire', placed after the Passive Understanding.

sources.name: Smagardine Table
sources.quote: That which is above is as that which is below, and that which is below is as that which is above
sources.use: Supports: both the spiritual agent and the spiritual patient must be prepared.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: both need the help of the other
sources.use: Supports: equal Spirits allied, each needing the other, for the precepts demand a medium.

sources.name: Tract. Aur., Scholium
sources.quote: Que l’art imite la nature
sources.use: Supports: external fire alters, internal fire perfects.

sources.name: the sage
sources.quote: Si pariat ventum valet auri pondera centum
sources.use: Supports the superiority of the purified internal fire.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: it behooves us to mortify two Argent vives together
sources.use: Supports: two natures to be mortified together.

sources.name: Idem (Tract. Aur.)
sources.quote: Protégé me et protegam te
sources.use: Illustrates the mutual relation of Sun and Moon; the speaker is not named in the text.

sources.name: Plutarch
sources.quote: the influence of the Moon, says Plutarch, seems to reflect the works of reason
sources.use: Supports: Moon as reason and Wisdom, Sun as force.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.work: treatise on Providence (Extracts at the end of Plotinus’ Selct Workd, by Taylor, p. 531)
sources.quote: this is an enigma indicative of contemplation and action
sources.use: Supports: the two pairs of eyes of the Mysteries as alternating contemplation and action.

sources.name: Egyptian Mythology of Isis and Osiris
sources.use: The mythology Synesius is said to explain with the two-pairs-of-eyes enigma.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: Proclus on the Theology of Plato --- Scholia on the Cratylus
sources.quote: the prophetic power unfolds the simplicity of truth and takes away the variety of that which is false
sources.use: Supports: the twofold Apollonical Intellect (prophetic and arrow-darting powers), paralleling Wisdom and Power.

sources.name: the wise king
sources.quote: A wise man is strong, says the wise king, and knowledge increaseth strength
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom joined with strength; two are better than one.

sources.name: Iliad
sources.quote: By mutual confidence and mutual aid
sources.use: Illustrates mutual aid between two.

sources.name: the Master
sources.quote: Our stone comes with Light, and with Light it is generated
sources.use: Quoted after Atwood's gloss on Boehme: Nature's middle principle; the stone generated with Light, bringing forth darkness.

sources.name: Cornelius Agrippa
sources.quote: Pinge duos Angues
sources.use: Illustrates the two natures to be joined.

sources.name: his ingenious disciple (of Cornelius Agrippa; not named)
sources.quote: Take our two serpents, which are to be found everywhere on the face of the earth
sources.use: Illustrates in 'more suggestive language' the joining, siege and creature sequence of the work.

sources.name: the Kabalist
sources.quote: Unite the end to the beginning as the flame is united to the coal
sources.use: Supports: the completed work unites end and beginning.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.use: Reference for the closing passage on the uniting union and the first love; whether the words are quoted is not marked in the text.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.use: Supports: his italics, in the passage quoted before this chunk, mark latent meanings and analogies throughout the process.

sources.name: Aquarium Sapientum
sources.work: Aquarium Sapientum, in Mus. Herm., The Enigma
sources.quote: The Spirit is given to the body for a time,
sources.use: Illustrates and supports, in translated verses: spirit, soul and body in one seat, then dissolution, then reunion in the last heat. Atwood calls this 'the constant doctrine and rule of the regeneration'.

sources.name: the fable (Typhon, Osiris, Isis; the Egyptian monarch)
sources.quote: Typhon killed Osiris, his uterine brother, and scattered his members to the four winds
sources.use: Illustrates the threefold division of the ethereal hypostasis, the fire allowed to grow (the hair grown in Ethiopia), and Isis's reconciling of the opposites.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: Take, my son, the flying bird and drown it flying
sources.use: Supports two points: the volatile must be held and cleansed so that it does not depart, and the Dragon dwelling in the threefold nature is removed by dissolution. Atwood notes that Hermes 'does not speak of it openly'.

sources.name: Prosopopoeia of the Stone
sources.work: Theatr. Chem., Tome 3, p. 764; Processus Chiica, Carmen Elegans; Vaughan’s magia Adamica
sources.quote: I am not dead although my spirit’s gone,
sources.use: Illustrates the balanced state in which the principles neither die nor live during the severation.

sources.name: Lully
sources.quote: Let the heavenly power or agent be such in the place of generation, or mutation
sources.use: Supports the warning against too strong a fire and the right measure of the agent.

sources.name: Sal Lumen
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Nuysement
sources.use: Reference only (p. 133).

sources.name: Ripley
sources.work: Second Gate, of Solution; Ripley Revived; Fifth Gate, Of the Putrefaction
sources.quote: Ryght so to water minerall reduced ys our gold
sources.use: Supports and illustrates three points: the vapor running down in the vessel (n61); the sun obscured and the waters passing like Noah's flood (n63); and the purgation to a white Elixir, with gold reduced to mineral water 'by Crafte occasionate', a phrase Atwood glosses (n69).

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.work: New Light of Alch.; Discourse of Sulfur; New Light, Discourse of the Three Principles
sources.quote: Sal gave Sulfur a mortal wound
sources.use: Illustrates the fight of Sal and Sulfur, which yields white milk (n62). Per n66 he is also the source of 'the Adept's' saying that without Salt no man attains the Science.

sources.name: David
sources.quote: Abierunt in sicco flumina
sources.use: Cited within Ripley's verse on the waters passing away.

sources.name: the French adept
sources.quote: the two dragons do bite one another very cruelly
sources.use: Illustrates the two principles destroying each other and turning into a Fifth Essence.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.quote: To Saturn, Mars with bond of love is tied,
sources.use: Illustrates. Atwood finds 'a profound mystery' in it: the eclipse of the Divine Light in the circulation.

sources.name: darkness upon the Abyss (unattributed in the text)
sources.quote: as there was darkness upon the Abyss when the Divine Spirit moved upon the Water’s face
sources.use: Analogy for the eclipse of the Divine Light in the hyperphysical work.

sources.name: Isaiah
sources.quote: He shall overflow the channels, and go over all the banks
sources.use: Illustrates the overflowing of the dark power in this stage.

sources.name: book of Jehior
sources.work: the book of Jehior of the Fire and its Mystery, chap. 11
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: the Alchemists
sources.quote: nothing of an unclean nature that enters into the composition of the Stone, except One thing
sources.use: Supports. Atwood endorses the saying and explains at length that the unclean Instrument is necessary, because the philosophers are obscure about it.

sources.name: Maria
sources.quote: when this poison is resolved into a subtle water, it coagulates our Mercury into most pure silver
sources.use: Supports: the deadly poison, once resolved, is productive.

sources.name: Albert, Raymond and Arnolde
sources.use: Named in Ripley's verse as writing plainly of gold reduced to mineral water.

sources.name: Plutarch
sources.use: Supports: explains that Typhon's names Seth and Bebo import violent restraint, contrariety and subversion.

sources.name: the Mysteries
sources.use: Isis is called Athena in the Mysteries, to express the Spirit's self-motion and intelligence.

sources.name: Maier
sources.use: Reference only. The footnote marker sits within the Leviathan passage.

sources.name: Job
sources.quote: Canst thou draw out Leviathan with an hook?
sources.use: Quoted at length after the account of Typhon's subjugation, with no commentary.

sources.name: Egyptian relics
sources.use: Illustrates the rebellious Principle depicted in human semblance with emblems of grace and power, seated between his foes.

sources.name: Adepts
sources.quote: not with arrows or clubs, but with the Hand, as Adepts say
sources.use: Supports, endorsed: the Orient Animal is stripped with the Hand, not by force.

sources.name: Maier
sources.quote: Animal de Oriente pelle sua leonine spoliari debet
sources.use: Supports the stripping of the Orient Animal; Latin given untranslated; reference p. 222.

sources.name: Malden; Philalethean Lion Hunt
sources.work: The Hunting of the Greene Lyon
sources.quote: But our Lyon wanting maturity, Is called greene for unripenes trust me,
sources.use: Given 'by way of recreation' ('in part' per ¶64, though headed '[*unabridged]') as an allegorical account of the whole practice (Green Lion, Sun and Moon, black/white/red, imbibition, ferment, multiplication); Atwood does not comment on it in this chunk. Attribution: see ambiguities.

sources.name: the Cosmopolite Eirenaeus
sources.use: Named alongside the Lion Hunt; either a further piece to be given or a co-source of the poem (see ambiguities).

sources.name: noble Master (of the poem's narrator)
sources.quote: At his death he made me sweare hym to, That all the secrets I schould never undoe
sources.use: Within the poem: the reason for veiling.

sources.name: Philosophers of tyme old / olde Fathers
sources.quote: The secret of Imbibition never out tould;
sources.use: Within the poem: criticized for describing the creation of Magnesia while hiding imbibition.

sources.name: the Adept
sources.quote: known, as the Adept says, only to the Wise
sources.use: Supports, endorsed: the Corner Stone is known only to the Wise who have it in themselves.

sources.name: Greek fable (Cadmus, Jason, Orpheus, Aeneas)
sources.quote: who represent the Rational Ferment
sources.use: Decoded: the heroes represent the Rational Ferment, their associates the other faculties of the mind.

sources.name: Orpheus
sources.quote: and by the advice of the goddess, too, according to Orpheus, the subtle stratagem was contrived
sources.use: Cited for the tale that Saturn was bound in fetters, inebriated, by his son through a stratagem advised by the goddess; illustrates the satiated Opposive Principle being ensnared.

sources.name: unnamed verse
sources.quote: Saturn, with honey of the bees produced, Sunk in ebriety; fast bind the god.
sources.use: Illustrates; Atwood glosses it as Intellect cutting off the sated Saturnian Will.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.quote: For in our water is our secret fire.
sources.use: Supports: long verse on Mercury/first matter, the secret fire, Argent Vive, the menstrual, and the soul hidden in Saturn, leading into Atwood's account of the First Matter.

sources.name: Helvetius
sources.quote: that most recreant Beauty can never be blotted out from my mind
sources.use: Supports: 'the acute Helvetius' testifies to the transcendent Light and that the mystery is found, by experience, at the centre (extent of his words unclear).

sources.name: tradition (mythological antique devices)
sources.quote: Such are a very few of the games and choice spectacles which tradition commemorates as instituted by Wisdom
sources.use: Illustrates: myths (Salamander, Aeneas in Numitius, Pactolus/Midas, Medea/Jason, Hesperides, Atalanta, Hercules, Phoenix, etc.) as spectacles of the soul's liberation, made natural by art.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.quote: the Quintessence and hidden thing of our Stone is nothing else than our viscous celestial and glorious soul
sources.use: Supports: 'the Greek saint' gives the summary statement; Atwood calls these 'plain words' supporting her evidence.

sources.name: Mylius
