sources.quote: Deus, cum solus fuisset in principio, creavit unam substantiam; hanc primam materiam nominamus.
sources.use: Epigraph: God created one substance, the first matter.

sources.name: Rosenroth
sources.work: Kabbala Denudata, seu Doctrina Hebraeorum Transcendentalis et Liber Zohar Restitutus
sources.use: Reference only: recommended for study of the Kabalah.

sources.name: Franck / Ad. Franck
sources.work: La Kabbale, ou Philosophie Religieuse des Hebreux
sources.use: Recommended history of the Kabalah, read 'with no less instruction than delight'; source of the Zohar translations cited.

sources.name: Zohar
sources.quote: he begins by producing a point
sources.use: Supports: the Initial Principle as Wisdom/Supreme Crown and as the Unknown manifesting by a point of Light; its white appearance.

sources.name: Rabbi Ben Jocahi
sources.quote: From his head he shakes a dew which awakens the dead
sources.use: Supports: the hidden principle's white form and dew of light.

sources.name: Apocalypse / Revelation of St.John
sources.quote: whose hair was like wool, and white as snow
sources.use: Illustrates the white appearance of the primeval splendour (White Stone, Son of Man).

sources.name: Enoch / Book of Enoch
sources.work: Book of Enoch, chap. 46:1; chap. 46 and 41
sources.quote: the Ancient of Days, whose head was like wool
sources.use: Illustrates whiteness; and the seer's vision of the Radical Essence, winds, clouds and the cloud before creation.

sources.name: Paracelsus
sources.quote: Omnia in Dei manu alba sunt; is eas tingit ut vult
sources.use: Supports: whiteness as the simple ground of diversity whereon to recreate.

sources.name: author of the Lucerna Salis
sources.quote: Govern your fire with a great deal of care
sources.use: Supports: the whitening of the matter in the white work.

sources.name: Arnold, Lully, Artephius
sources.use: Said to agree with the Lucerna Salis description of whitening; cited earlier 'in the Theory'.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.quote: that water was as white as snow
sources.use: Supports: the Water of our Sea, not wetting the hands, white as snow, attested by sight and touch.

sources.name: Eireanaeus
sources.use: Mentioned, not quoted ('we will not enlarge').

sources.name: the old Alchemists
sources.quote: it is no common water, but an unctuous mineral vapour, universally subsisting
sources.use: Supports (endorsed): definition of the Matter; bodies to be turned into vapour, which is the Stone.

sources.name: the Arabian
sources.quote: Sumatur lais in capitulis notus
sources.use: Cited as 'the subtle phrase' on the Stone known and proven.

sources.name: unattributed quotation
sources.quote: such stuff as dreams are made of
sources.use: Illustrates the dreamlike nature of human beings, contrasted with the real discovery of the Matter.

sources.name: Orpheus
sources.use: Illustrates: recommended the Hermetic material be taken in the cave of Mercury.

sources.name: the Arabians
sources.quote: Flos Salis Albi
sources.use: Supports: name of the Matter, Flower of White Salt.

sources.name: Van Helmont
sources.use: Supports: the white sand Quellum in a vital soil never pierced.

sources.name: unattributed quotation
sources.quote: Land of Havilah, where good gold is
sources.use: Identifies the magic earth.

sources.name: H. O’Brien, author of the Round Towers
sources.work: the Round Towers of Ireland, chap. 22, p. 327
sources.use: Mildly criticized: mistook the White Paradise for his 'Emerald Home', an exclusiveness pardonable for its enthusiasm; called 'an estimable work'.

sources.name: the Platonists
sources.quote: The Platonists have declared true Being to be white
sources.use: Supports whiteness of true Being; their view of the origin of matter.

sources.name: Plato
sources.use: His Tartarus, rivers and seas are read ethically, physically and psychically via Olympiodorus.

sources.name: Olympiodorus
sources.quote: souls, in which reason does not preside as a charioteer, are changed according to the subject temperament of the body
sources.use: Supports: ethical/physical reading of Tartarus; reason's dominion over the soul.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.use: Reference only (source of the Olympiodorus passage and the Parmenides fragments).

sources.name: Reuchlin
sources.quote: Nihil est in principio nisi Sapientia.
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom as Ain in darkness; dark Aleph turned to light Aleph.

sources.name: scripture ('as it is written')
sources.quote: The night shineth as the day, the darkness and the light are all alike to Him
sources.use: Supports the conversion of darkness into light.

sources.name: unattributed Latin verse
sources.quote: Si tu, Deus meus, illuminaveris me Lux fiunt tenebrae meae.
sources.use: Illustrates darkness made light by divine illumination.

sources.name: some modern Kabalists
sources.quote: an absolute concentration of Divinity within its original identity
sources.use: Explain the nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo and the primitive Ether.

sources.name: Dionysius
sources.quote: caligo divina
sources.use: Supports: divine darkness, visible yet incomprehensible; the True Thing of negative theology, possession of the happiest life.

sources.name: author of the Lumen de Lumine
sources.work: Lumen de Lumine, the chapter on Matter
sources.quote: a certain horrible, inexpressible chasm
sources.use: Supports: Tenebrae activae beneath sense and imagination.

sources.name: Parmenides
sources.quote: Non-being, which nor mind can see
sources.use: Supports: Non-being is not the object of the mental eye; check intellectual notions on this path.

sources.name: the Oracle
sources.quote: Stoop not down, for a precipice lies below in the earth
sources.use: Warning about the infinite End of the principle.

sources.name: Boehme
sources.quote: this water is that One Thing in which all things are contained
sources.use: Supports: creation out of nothing of a cloud or darkness condensed into water, the One Thing.

sources.name: Boehme
sources.quote: is called by many the Tincture
sources.use: Supports: description of the Tincture in the Celestial Light, following Atwood's identification of the One Thing with the regenerate Identity; endorsed as agreeing with the ancient Kabalah.

sources.name: Boehme
sources.quote: the gate was opened to me
sources.use: Supports: first-person account of the method and content of his illumination; called 'modern testimony'.

sources.name: Moses and the Prophets, Christ and his Apostles
sources.use: Named by Boehme as teaching what he finds in his inner book.

sources.name: Kabalah
sources.use: Supports: Boehme's testimony said to agree 'in all particulars with the most ancient Kabalah and profound experimental divinity'.

sources.name: Van Helmont
sources.quote: I saw, as in a dream, the whole face of the earth
sources.use: Supports: another favoured individual led to perceive the simple element of nature.

sources.name: Pordage
sources.quote: Here ‘tis that God himself t’ himself displays
sources.use: Illustrates: verse on the sphere where God displays himself to himself.

sources.name: Basil Valentine
sources.quote: is the first matter of all things
sources.use: Supports: allegory of flight, fall and mountain, read by Atwood as displaying the whole metaphysico-chemical analysis; account of the first matter.

sources.name: Icarus and is father Daedelus
sources.use: Illustration within Basil Valentine's allegory.

sources.name: Georgic
sources.quote: Verum,ubi correptum minibus, vinclisque tenebis
sources.use: Illustrates: the captive held in bonds changes into varied shapes.

sources.name: the adept
sources.quote: he raises himself likewise into an infinity of forms
sources.use: Supports: the freed, purified substance's endless transformations; footnote adds 'Ubi vero spiritus excessit, etc'.

sources.name: Democritus
sources.use: Supports: hints that the alterations cease only when the Matter is brought by Art into the fixity of its Final Cause.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: The philosophers chain up their matter with a strong chain or band when they make it to contend with fire
sources.use: Supports: binding the matter by force.

sources.name: Georgic
sources.quote: vim duram et vincula capto Tende
sources.use: Illustrates: only force and bonds compel the captive.

sources.name: Reuchlin
sources.quote: the other nature or principiating substance is incorruptible, immutable, and always subsistent
sources.use: Supports: two natures in the mirific Word, changeable and immutable; said to allude to arresting the flux.

sources.name: Apuleius
sources.quote: you must pardon, as Apuleius says, the strange expression
sources.use: Cited within Reuchlin's passage to excuse an obscure expression.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.use: Reference only (footnote gives it as a further location for the Reuchlin passage).

sources.name: an ancient and much esteemed Adeptus / Grasseus
sources.quote: Within this fabric (i.e., the consecrated vessel), was a certain mass moving circularly
sources.use: Supports: eyewitness account of the world-in-miniature in the vessel, which Atwood reads as the whole Hermetic laboratory.

sources.name: Lully
sources.use: Illustrates: his Lunaria identified with the authors' quicksilver/mercury.

sources.name: Lumen de Lumine
sources.use: Reference only (parallel to the vessel vision).

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.use: Reference only (parallel).

sources.name: Paracelsus
sources.use: Reference only: his 'account of the magical separation of the Elements, and vision, in their native place'.

sources.name: Helmont / Van Helmont
sources.quote: Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury
sources.use: Supports: names the three principles into which Life is resolved; works cited as parallels (reference only).

sources.name: Scripture
sources.work: Genesis 2, Deut. 8, 9; Exodus, Moses’ Description of the Promised Land; Job 28
sources.use: Reference only (parallels to the vision of the fruitful land).

sources.name: Virgil
sources.quote: Salve Magna Parens frugum Saturnia Tellus Magna virum!
sources.use: Illustrates: verses praising the land as mother of metals, crops and men, applied to the vision though Virgil referred them to his 'native soul'.

sources.name: Hippocrates
sources.use: Illustrates: 'the Night of Hippocrates' names the end of the destructive way.

sources.name: Orpheus
sources.use: Illustrates: 'the Day of Orpheus' follows the Night.

sources.name: Kabalistic commentators and mystics of the middle ages; the Rabbis
sources.use: Supports: they hold the same ideas as German metaphysics, reached by ontological experiment.

sources.name: Hegel (the German philosopher)
sources.quote: All things, says the German philosopher (Hegel), have their commencement in pure Being
sources.use: Contrasts: abstraction reaches pure Being = non-Being, but only as a void.

sources.name: La Kabbale
sources.use: Reference only (footnote to the Hegel passage).

sources.name: Abram den Dior
sources.work: Comment. on the Zephir Jezirah, p. 67
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Kant, Fichte, Schelling
sources.use: Criticized: metaphysics ending in void non-entity and skepticism, short of objective realization; Schelling ranked above the other two.

sources.name: the learned Rassbi / the Rabbi; Ben Jochai and his disciples
sources.quote: by non-Being they mean that which is neither conceivable as cause nor as essence, but yet is in fact the Cause of causes
sources.use: Supports: creation from nothing as from the primitive non-Being, Wisdom; endorsed as Hermetic. Footnote marker (29) has no footnote in this chunk.

sources.name: Platonic theology
sources.use: Supports: agrees with the doctrine of primitive non-being.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.quote: we are accustomed likewise to call that heaven, which is composed from every natural and sensible body
sources.use: Supports: his discourses on the origin of things and on Identity accord; triple distinction of heaven. Criticized for making away with his brethren 'after the manner of the Ottomans'.

sources.name: Lord Bacon
sources.use: Supports: advice to regard the early sages with more reverence.

sources.name: Thales
sources.quote: teaches that all beings have their beginning from water
sources.use: Illustrates: names the principle water, looking to its first material manifestation; differs in expression only.

sources.name: Pythagoras, Parmenides
sources.use: Reference only: among the sages whose dogmas deserve reverence.

sources.name: Empedocles
sources.use: Illustrates: 'the physiologist' substituting elements as principles, differing in expression only.

sources.name: Anaxagoras
sources.quote: calls it Intellect
sources.use: Illustrates: names the principle Intellect, regarding the One Thing in consciousness.

sources.name: Heraclitus
sources.quote: have denominated it to be fire
sources.use: Illustrates: names the principle fire, according to essence.

sources.name: Timaeus
sources.quote: mentions a certain earth as antecedent, and the most ancient element
sources.use: Illustrates: names a certain earth as the principle.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: calls it the most ancient element within the heaven
sources.use: Supports: derives all things transcendentally; places earth within heaven, as the Hermetists do.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: On the Theology of Plato, pp. 236, 240
sources.quote: Heaven, he says, is the intellectual contact with the intelligible
sources.use: Supports: explains what 'heaven' means.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: The same is called by Hermes, a Quintessence
sources.use: Supports: names the Spirit of Universal nature the Quintessence.

sources.name: the initiated poet
sources.quote: the arising circulation of Mature from the four concentering winds
sources.use: Illustrates: an apt figure of the same celestial elements.

sources.name: Ovidii
sources.quote: Haec super imposuit liquidam et gravitate carentem, Aethera
sources.use: supports: verse placing the dreg-free Aether above the rest, introducing the Etheral Quintessence.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: the Demiurgus assumed One Whole from wholes, in all things perfect and free from old age and disease
sources.use: supports: read as alluding to the Etheral Quintessence; reported as criticized by Aristotle for explaining essence by Ideas; cited (n38) for metals reducible to water.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: on the Theology of Plato, Book 5, p. 365
sources.use: reference only (for the Timaeus passage).

sources.name: Aristotle (the Stagyrite)
sources.quote: Parmenides appears to have touched upon the One according to Reason; but Melissus, according to Matter
sources.use: supports: his perfect world read as the ethereal; his abstruse diction illustrates concealment; his criticisms of predecessors qualified as aimed at letter not spirit; his logic praised in its original intent, later degraded; cited (n38) for metals reducible to water.

sources.name: Empedocles
sources.quote: All things in union now thro’ love conspire, And now thro’ strife divulsed are borne along
sources.use: supports: twofold intelligible/sensible order; perpetual interchange; the One formed from the many.

sources.name: Anaxagoras
sources.use: supports: matter is the progeny of mind.

sources.name: the Alexandrians
sources.use: supports: explained the descent and efflux of matter, as if knowing the universe by analogy through their own.

sources.name: Alexander
sources.use: illustrates: recipient of Aristotle's avowal that only his pupils would understand the Acaomatic Ethics.

sources.name: Simplicius
sources.work: Commentary ... in Plutarch’s Life of Aristotle
sources.use: reference only (Aristotle's letter to Alexander).

sources.name: Thomas Taylor
sources.work: Dissertation; Translation of the Timaeus; Select Works of Plotinus
sources.use: supports: 'most erudite translator' who showed Aristotle's strictures misunderstood; bibliographic references.

sources.name: Pythagoras
sources.use: reported as criticized by Aristotle for explaining essence in number; his hecatomb for the right-angle theorem read as symbolical of discovering the Psychical Quintessence.

sources.name: Parmenides
sources.use: reported via Aristotle: touched the One according to Reason; saw more than Xenophanes and Melissus.

sources.name: Melissus
sources.use: reported via Aristotle: the One according to Matter; dismissed as rustic.

sources.name: Xenophanes
sources.quote: the One is God
sources.use: reported via Aristotle: first to introduce the doctrine; dismissed as rustic.

sources.name: Bacon
sources.use: illustrates: observed the Organon becoming worse than useless.

sources.name: Thales
sources.use: illustrates: his deed about the inscription of the circle read as symbolical, not a flat demonstration.

sources.name: Zeno (of Elea, not the stoic)
sources.quote: if any one should undertake to demonstrate the philosopher’s Unit, he would unfold Being
sources.use: supports: the absolute unit as ground of Being.

sources.name: the Mysteries
sources.use: illustrates: their mandate forbade communicating the revelation to the profane.

sources.name: the Alchemist / modern Alchemists
sources.use: supports: agree with the Greeks on a universal pure matter; contrasts: modern Alchemists mostly silent on the metaphysics of their Art.

sources.name: the Neoplatonists
sources.use: supports: spoke of Principles and the procedure of mind while avoiding the Practice; their images stimulate inward faith.

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.work: Select Works (of Matter, and of the Impassivity of Incorporeal Natures; p. 38, note)
sources.quote: there should be a Nature primarily vital which is also formless, indestructible and immortal
sources.use: supports: source (with Porphyry) of the summary on the Subject of bodies, analysis and pure divine Matter; n38 says he alludes to the mystical analysis.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.use: supports: co-source of the summary on pure Matter.

sources.name: Iamblichus
sources.quote: being connascent with the gods by whom it is imparted, will doubtless be an entire and fit receptacle for the manifestation of Divinity
sources.use: supports: pure Matter as receptacle of Divinity; power of the highest causes present in all.

sources.name: Albertus Magnus
sources.quote: Light, which is the formal essence of all things, and most abundant in gold, is found in the ultimate alchemical analysis of every existing thing
sources.use: supports: all things may be reduced to gold.

sources.name: Becher
sources.use: reference only (cites Albertus Magnus).

sources.name: Select Works
sources.use: reference only (footnote 40; no marker for it in this chunk's text).

sources.name: the ancients
sources.use: Supports: this life is a diminution of existence (¶50); the 'wise ancients' compared the estate of Being verging to annihilation to darkness for the eye (¶54).

sources.name: Proclus
sources.work: sixth book, on the Parmenides of Plato
sources.quote: he must raise himself to that which is most united in nature, and to its flower
sources.use: Supports: one must be assimilated to the One Principle to discover it.

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.quote: the reality is testified by reminiscence
sources.use: Supports: real beings abide in themselves, known by self-investigation and reminiscence (¶50; marker (30) has no footnote in this chunk); in ¶53 asks how the infinite is conceived: the Indefinite by the Indefinite.

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.work: treatise concerning the Descent of the Soul
sources.quote: Often when by an intellectual energy, I am roused from body and converted to myself
sources.use: Supports: inward withdrawal, union with Divine nature, the soul's middle order and the value of its fall.

sources.name: T. Taylor
sources.use: Reference only: n41 says the Descent of the Soul is the last of five Plotinus treatises 'rendered by T. Taylor'.

sources.name: These Greeks / these philosophers
sources.use: Their contrary predicates for Matter (one/all, everywhere/nowhere) are expounded and defended by Atwood, for comparison with the Hermetic adepts.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: Matter is indeed to be apprehended, and that by a sort of defective or ablative reasoning
sources.use: Supports: Matter apprehended by negative reasoning.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.work: Metaphysics (n42: Metaph., Book 9, p. 221; Book 9, p. 237)
sources.quote: I mean, he says, by Matter, that which of itself is neither essence nor quantity
sources.use: Supports: Matter is manifest only by negation; contact with it is a kind of ignorance. Called 'the logician'.

sources.name: Virgil
sources.quote: vast, endless, horrible
sources.use: Illustrates the crass, obscure vacuity of the Original of Life.

sources.name: Parmenides
sources.use: Cited with 'the rest' to prove the initial nonentity of all.

sources.name: Celsus
sources.quote: that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven
sources.use: Illustrates: the ladder is identified with the magnetic chain.

sources.name: Zoroaster
sources.quote: that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven
sources.use: Illustrates: the ladder is identified with the magnetic chain.

sources.name: the philosopher
sources.quote: By no means, says the philosopher
sources.use: Supports: in the Night of Matter the mind receives the formless rather than understanding nothing. Not named (see ambiguities).

sources.name: the motto
sources.quote: Deus, cum solus fuisset in principio, Creavit unam substantiam, Hanc primam materiam nominamus.
sources.use: Supports: the First Matter as the one substance God created in the beginning.

sources.name: the Platonist and the Kabalist
sources.use: Supports: the First Matter is unknown, or known as nothing.

sources.name: the poets
sources.quote: to the sleeping Endymion she vouchsafed her willing presence
sources.use: Illustrates: presumptuous striving repels; sleeping receptivity receives the presence.

sources.name: unattributed Latin couplet
sources.quote: Quaeres multum et non invenies; Fortasse invneies cumnon quaeres.
sources.use: Illustrates: finding comes without seeking.

sources.name: Prophyry / Porphyry
sources.work: Auxil. to the Perception of Intelligibles, sec.3
sources.quote: being established in yourself and in your own Essence, you will be assimilated to the Intelligible Universe
sources.use: Supports: adding place or relation veils the Eternal Essence; self-presence assimilates to the Intelligible; additions from selfhood impoverish.

sources.name: Trismegistus
sources.quote: is most like unto a torrent running with a violent and swift stream from a high rock
sources.use: Illustrates: the Mind of Divinity eludes understanding (footnote to Porphyry's fountain image).

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: A fat mineral nature it was, he says, bright like pearls, and transparent like crystal
sources.use: Supports: eye-witness description of 'the same Matter', identified as the First Matter.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.quote: the water of our sea, the water of life, not wetting the hands
sources.use: Supports: another name and eye-witness description of the same Matter.

sources.name: Alchemists
sources.quote: the Matter so often celebrated by the Alchemists
sources.use: Supports: their celebrated Matter is the Passive Nature.

sources.name: Plato
sources.quote: the Quintessence of Plato
sources.use: Supports: his Quintessence is identified with the Matter.

sources.name: Thales
sources.quote: the Water of Thales
sources.use: Supports: his Water is identified with the Matter.

sources.name: Parmenides
sources.quote: the Non-Being of Parmenides
sources.use: Supports: his Non-Being is identified with the Matter.

sources.name: Kabalists
sources.quote: styled also by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite
sources.use: Supports: their Abyss is identified with the Matter.

sources.name: Pierce the Black Monk
sources.use: Supports: one of the 'ecclesiastics of different orders' agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: the Benedict Valentine
sources.use: Supports: agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: Friar Bacon
sources.use: Supports: 'the experimentalist', agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: the Greek Divine
sources.use: Supports: agreed concerning the Matter. Not otherwise identified.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.use: Supports: agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: the Canon Ripley
sources.use: Supports: agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: Morien
sources.use: Supports: agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: Lully
sources.use: Supports: agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: Albertus Magnus
sources.use: Supports: agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: Calid
sources.use: Supports: one of 'the Mahomedan princes' agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: Geber
sources.use: Supports: one of 'the Mahomedan princes' agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: Avicenna
sources.use: Supports: one of 'the Mahomedan princes' agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: Paracelsus
sources.use: Supports: agreed concerning the Matter.

sources.name: the Christian brotherhood of the Rosy Cross
sources.use: Supports: agreed concerning the Matter; searched Nature experimentally, found and used it.

sources.name: the adept
sources.quote: she has no hands
sources.use: Supports: Nature cannot enter the True Light by herself.

sources.name: Madathan
sources.quote: Dost thou think, says she, to eat the oysters, crabs, shells and all?
sources.use: Illustrates: Nature rebukes him for trying to make the Stone without dissolution.

sources.name: unattributed ('as we are abundantly instructed')
sources.quote: Flesh and blood cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven, neither doth corruption inherit corruption
sources.use: Supports the dissolution of the Vital Spirit's natural bind. The text gives no attribution.

sources.name: Lucerna Salis Phil.
sources.quote: Nullo corrosivo adhibito
sources.use: Supports: the Stone is to be dissolved after the mind of the wise, without corrosive.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.use: Supports the long labours: he suffered and toiled to obtain 'the blessed Lunary of Diana'.

sources.name: the Sphinx’s fables
sources.quote: carried within the temple upon the back of an ass
sources.use: Illustrates the reduction to a simple estate of Being.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.quote: There is no creature, concludes the panegyrist, that is so able to receive divinity as an ass
sources.use: Supports: praise of the 'asinine condition' needed by a disciple of Wisdom, which Atwood applies to the Philosophic Subject.

sources.name: the Saviour
sources.use: Illustrates the honour of the ass, chosen 'on the occasion of his greatest earthly triumph'.

sources.name: Abraham
sources.use: Illustrates: 'constantly traveled with his asses'.

sources.name: Balaam
sources.use: Illustrates: his ass was clear-sighted and spoke.

sources.name: Ammonius
sources.use: Illustrates: he admitted an ass daily to his lectures, alongside Origen and Porphyry.

sources.name: Origen
sources.use: Mentioned in the Ammonius story.

sources.name: Porphyry
sources.use: 'the Greek Porphyry', mentioned in the Ammonius story.

sources.name: Apuleius of Megara
sources.use: Illustrates: he was turned into an ass before admission to the mysteries of Isis.

sources.name: Callimachus
sources.quote: All mixture of her pure and simple oil
sources.use: Supports: Divinity rejects anything mixed.

sources.name: the mysteries / the wise hierophants
sources.quote: the order in which Divinity is perceived
sources.use: Illustrates: the Aspirant leaving the statues to behold the Adytum shows the mind leaving all images.

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.quote: separate body from the man and its defilements
sources.use: Supports: union as a true experimental ingress to the source, and how to approach it (establish oneself in Intellect, separate from the body).

sources.name: Book of Enoch
sources.work: Book of Enoch, c. xl., v. 1.
sources.quote: Wisdom is poured forth like water, and glory faileth not before Him for ever.
sources.use: Epigraph: wisdom as water.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: In chains of liquid pearl did fall
sources.use: Illustrates: Hyanthe's tears as the shed Water (Tears of Isis); also the work in which the Benedictine Monk (Mehung) passage is cited.

sources.name: Theatrum Chemicum
sources.quote: Terra mihi corpus, vires mihi praestitit ignis
sources.use: Supplies the 'Prosopoiae of the Stone', called 'instructive' and 'elegant'.

sources.name: Khunrath
sources.quote: Seek Three in One, and again seek One in Three, dissolve, congeal
sources.use: Supports: threefold secret, separation, no manual labour, Azoth; and the colour sequence ending in the glorified Stone.

sources.name: the adept (unnamed)
sources.quote: Lux manifeste et visibilis ad oculum
sources.use: Supports: the Light becoming visible and subject to the artist.

sources.name: Mystere de la Croix
sources.work: Mystere de la Croix, chap. 13 (n10 spells 'Mystere de la Crois')
sources.quote: Cet ouvrage s’appelle Aimantique
sources.use: Supports: conjunction of Mars and Venus yielding solar sulphur; repeated cooking until rainbow colours; the magnetic work.

sources.name: Orpheus Eucharisticus
sources.quote: Cui scelerum viru mens moribunda tumet
sources.use: Supports: the corrupt mind cannot draw the healthful waters.

sources.name: the ancients
sources.quote: This is the marriage, by the ancients so many times prefigured
sources.use: Illustrates: Peleus and Thetis, Earth and Heaven, Bacchus and Ariadne, Jason with Medea as prefigurations of the union of Mind and Universe.

sources.name: the Adept (unnamed)
sources.quote: the bridegroom crowneth the bride in the North!
sources.use: Glossed by Atwood as the Light arising out of the crucifixion of cerebral life.

sources.name: Pierce, the Black Monk
sources.quote: In Arsenic sublimed there is a way straight
sources.use: Illustrates: verse recipe for the Stone with the Water of Might.

sources.name: the adept (unnamed)
sources.quote: Our golden water, says the adept, is not found in wells
sources.use: Supports: the water is taken from higher places.

sources.name: Proverbs of Solomon
sources.quote: Exalt her, and she shall promote thee
sources.use: Applied to Mercury/the water: exalted, she crowns.

sources.name: the Hermetic Master
sources.work: Tract. Aur., cap. 2, and Ripley Revived
sources.quote: henceforth thou art a Crowned King, resting over the Fountain
sources.use: Supports: the accomplished operator crowned.

sources.name: the Adepts
sources.quote: they who sow in tears shall reap in joy
sources.use: Maxim Atwood expands into the sacrifice of Self-Will.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.quote: Never grudge, then, that thou hast destroyed thye gold
sources.use: Supports: destruction of gold as sowing seed for increase; glossed as the first fruits of reason.

sources.name: the Apostle
sources.quote: that which is sown is not the body that shall be, but mere grain
sources.use: Answers how what is destroyed increases: law of resurrection, natural then spiritual body, leaven; closing 'sown in corruption'.

sources.name: the Benedictine Monk
sources.work: Mehung in Vaughan’s Coelum Terrae, p. 122.
sources.quote: For I have my heavenly fire, which excites and stirs up the elemental one
sources.use: Supports: solve et coagula, the gross body as vessel, the heavenly fire, work without tools.

sources.name: Jacob Boehme
sources.quote: It cometh forth from anguish into the meekness of the light
sources.use: Supports: Christ's power in the motion of contrition; tincture; fire drawing Light into Water; Blood; the Spirit born of the Soul entering God.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: the sure quality of the golden m,atter and the nature thereof is not sweetness
sources.use: Footnote to Boehme's 'mortifying anguish': the golden matter's quality is not sweetness.

sources.name: the Platonic Successor
sources.quote: he will again, says the Platonic Successor, be elevated
sources.use: Supports: the soul's ascent from image to Archetype and recovery after falling from the vision of God.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: These three, being but One substantially, admit of a perfect hypostatic union
sources.use: Supports (Atwood: 'has well described'): the Hypostatic Metamorphoses, the descending series of Light, and union into immortality.

sources.name: the Aristotle
sources.quote: Behold I show you a mystery, says the Aristotle, we shall not all sleep, but we shall be changed
sources.use: Supports: change of the corruptible into incorruption. Footnote: 'ibid., 15: 51, etc.'

sources.name: Roger Bacon
sources.quote: it is impossible for you to attain this immortal essentiality, unless you become sanctified in mind and purified in soul
sources.use: Supports: moral/spiritual requirements of the operator; knowledge of the whole work by meditation.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.quote: who knows how to congeal water with heat, and to join a spirit thereto
sources.use: Illustrates (called enigmatic): separation, putrefaction and rejoining of spirit and water, as conversion of the elements.

sources.name: Khunrath
sources.use: Reference only (cited with Sendivogius).

sources.name: Michael Maier
sources.quote: Fac ex mare et foemina circulum; inde quadrangulum
sources.use: Illustrates: geometric symbol of the procedure (circle, square, triangle, circle) yielding the Stone; Atwood: 'epigrammatically symbolized by Michael Maier'.

sources.name: the author of Lucerna Salis
sources.work: Lucerna Salis, p. 39; from the Latin verse, Aurum Sapientum
sources.quote: the gold of the Wise to be by no means vulgar gold
sources.use: Supports: the gold of the Wise as pure water; its dissolution and reunion into One inseparable Thing.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.quote: by Ripley called tetraptive
sources.use: Supports: his name for the consummating Conjunction.

sources.name: Pythagoras
sources.quote: that so highly commended fountain of Pythagoras, and Divine Tetractys
sources.use: Supports: the Conjunction identified with the Tetractys.

sources.name: Iamblichus
sources.quote: Whence all our Wisdom springs, and which contains Perennial nature’s fountain, cause, and root
sources.use: Source of the verse praising the Tetractys.

sources.name: Enigma Philosophicum
sources.quote: There is no sun but which is twice begot
sources.use: Supports: Nature and Art as parents; twofold yet indivisible work; fixed fixing the unfixed.

sources.name: Poemander and Book of Wisdom
sources.quote: The whole world is before thee, O God! As a little grain of the balance
sources.use: Illustrates: the whole world held before the divine vision, as before the one who has the Principle.

sources.name: unnamed Latin verse
sources.quote: Mundum mente gerens, similique in imagine formas
sources.use: Illustrates: the world formed after a supernal exemplar held in mind; carries footnote (27).

sources.name: Paracelsus and Van Helmont
sources.quote: by separation of their parts the specific impress is to be perceived in the vessel containing the decomposed spirit
sources.use: Corroborates the appearance of the Universal Idea; Atwood qualifies it as only a secondary witness.

sources.name: Marcus
sources.quote: Quid quaesco dicerunt hi tanti philosophi, si plantam quasi momento nasci in vitreo case viderent
sources.use: Source of the words on the impress and on a plant born, dying and reborn in a glass vessel.

sources.name: Hesiod
sources.work: Epic Cycle, The Weeks and the Days
sources.quote: First of all existed Chaos
sources.use: Supports: his theogony, compared with alchemical descriptions, is 'very regular and correct'; accepted by ancient philosophers.

sources.name: the Platonists
sources.use: Reported as saying the Epic Cycle includes the true philosophic secret of creation.

sources.name: the Mosaic (Scripture)
sources.quote: the Mosaic was the only revealed truth of all
sources.use: Contrast: some learned judged it the only revealed truth; Atwood would still reverence Scripture if all cosmogonies share one divine source.

sources.name: the Kabalistic Interpreter
sources.quote: the Divine Will, then alone operating, says the Kabalistic Interpreter, produces itself into a material form and recreation
sources.use: Supports: creation as the Divine Will producing itself into form from inane Identity.

sources.name: the Memphian prophet
sources.use: Illustrates: teacher of the hidden mysteries of creation to the young Aspirant, probably by inward evolution rather than words.

sources.name: Ovid
sources.quote: he was inspired, as he declares, by that same universal deity of the two-faced Janus
sources.use: Illustrates: an 'initiated poet' inspired, as he declares, by the same universal deity of the two-faced Janus; the chunk ends here.

sources.name: Ovid
sources.quote: Me Chaos antiqui, nam res sum prisca, vocabant.
sources.use: Illustrates (per our translation of the Latin): Chaos as the primeval thing, opening the cosmogony.

sources.name: Ovid
sources.quote: Ille opifex rerum, mundi melioris origo
sources.use: Illustrates (per our translation of the Latin): man made from divine seed or from earth holding seeds of heaven.

sources.name: the metropolitan of Memphis
sources.quote: And know, consecrated Youth, adds the metropolitan of Memphis
sources.use: Illustrates: cosmogony of Chaos, Hyle, Eros, the spirit's breath stirring the mass, separation of congenial from heterogeneous parts; footnoted to Blackwell's Mythology.

sources.name: Blackwell
sources.use: Reference only (source of the cosmogony passage).

sources.name: Ecclesiasticus
sources.quote: He created her and numbered her, and poured her out upon all his works.
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom is created by God, poured on all his works, given to those who love him.

sources.name: Solomon
sources.quote: For Wisdom, which is the Worker of all things, taught me.
sources.use: Supports: knowledge of creation comes by Conscious Intuition, taught by Wisdom; Wisdom's spirit described.

sources.name: the mysterious adeptest
sources.work: Khunrath, Amphiteatr. Sap. Etern., Isag. in fig.
sources.quote: The philosopher’s stone, says the mysterious adeptest, is Ruach Elohim
sources.use: Supports: defines the Stone as embodied Ruach Elohim, Salt as its principle and named Wisdom; Atwood then concedes such definitions explain the unknown by the more unknown.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: Conceive well the Light in thy Mind, and Know It.
sources.use: Supports/illustrates: testimony of the inward experience of regeneration — the Mind/Light and Word, self-knowledge, purity as condition, and the ascent to Intellect. The speaker Poemander is also spelled 'Pymander' (III.3 ¶54).

sources.name: Poemander
sources.work: The Divine Poemander of Hermes Trismegistus, book 2
sources.quote: For the sleep of the body was the sober watchfulness of the mind
sources.use: Supports: testimony of the operative revelation of Intellect, to which Atwood says nothing can be added.

sources.name: St John’s Gospel
sources.quote: thou blasphemest, because I said I am the Son of God
sources.use: Supports: those to whom the Word of God came are called gods; set against unbelief.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.quote: under the Bark of the Law
sources.use: Supports: no one now reads Scripture beneath its literal surface.

sources.name: the Apostle
sources.quote: the veil shall be taken away
sources.use: Supports: the veil over reading Moses lifts on turning to the Lord/Spirit; beholders are transformed.

sources.name: Moses
sources.quote: when Moses is read, the veil is upon their heart
sources.use: Within the Apostle's text: the Law read under a veil.

sources.name: the Kabalist
sources.quote: The story of the Law is the vestment of the Law
sources.use: Supports (endorsed): the Law's narrative clothes a sublime mystery, its Soul.

sources.name: Frank
sources.use: Reference only (p. 165), for the Kabalist passage.

sources.name: Origen
sources.use: Reference only, for the Kabalist passage.

sources.name: St. Paul
sources.quote: and that rock was Christ
sources.use: Cited: the Fathers baptized in cloud and sea, eating spiritual meat and drinking from the spiritual rock; its application is not stated.

sources.name: Synesius
sources.work: True Book concerning the Philosopher’s Stopne
sources.quote: labour only for that Water which burns to blackness, dissolves and congeals
sources.use: Supports: practical instruction on coction of the one Water, unity of operations, extraction and the luminaries; Atwood calls it the Experiment of the Fathers.

sources.name: Lumen de Lumine
sources.use: Reference only, for part of ¶60.

sources.name: Norton
sources.use: Reference only, for parts of ¶60.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.work: Eirenaeus’s Experiments, at the end of his Ripley Revived, p. 6
sources.use: Reference only, for sealing the vessel (¶60).

sources.name: Democritus
sources.use: Atwood names the Experiment 'the Art of Democritus', as commemorated by Bacon.

sources.name: Lord Bacon
sources.work: Bacon’s Wisdom of the Ancient, Fable of Proteus
sources.quote: lays hold of and works upon matter in the extremest degrees
sources.use: Supports (endorsed, quoted before and repeated): matter forced to extremity runs through all forms and restores itself; Atwood glosses the extremity as the last exigence of life.

sources.name: the Adepts
sources.quote: her birth, according to the Adepts, is singular and not without a miracle
sources.use: Supports: the miraculous birth of the Matter.

sources.name: the Greeks
sources.quote: by the Greeks called Myrionymous
sources.use: Supports: Isis's name 'goddess with a thousand names'.

sources.name: the initiated, who celebrated her Mysteries in the Eleusian fane
sources.use: Illustrates: the multinominal goddess as they described her.

sources.name: fraternity of the Rosy Cross
sources.work: Latin original of the Fraternity, as given in the Coelum Terrae of Vaughan
sources.quote: I am a Goddess for beauty and extraction
sources.use: Supports/illustrates: speeches of the Matter as Goddess (First Matter, Eagle and Lion, five gates) and as Dragon/Mercury.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.use: Reference only: source for the Rosicrucian passages.

sources.name: Aelia Laelia Crispis
sources.quote: No male, nor female, nor hermaphrodite,
sources.use: Unattributed riddling inscription: a thing none of the opposites yet all, nowhere particular yet everywhere; follows the claim that the Matter is one Identity.

sources.name: Lucius Agatho Priscus
sources.quote: Both corpse and sepulcher the same!
sources.use: Companion inscription: corpse and sepulcher, contained and container, are the same.

sources.name: Scripture ('as it is written')
sources.quote: Thou hast disposed all things, in number, weight, and measure.
sources.use: Supports: number, weight and measure as Nature's three dimensions.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.quote: That ‘t is a fountain sealed, Which one thing only can unlocke;
sources.use: Supports/illustrates: long verse on the signs, stages, timing and results of the work, and the one key to the sealed Art.

sources.name: Gentile Mythology
sources.use: Illustrates: carries in symbol the tradition of the manifold powers and preservation of the One Thing.

sources.name: Arkite Mysteries
sources.use: Supports: refer to the physical secret of regeneration.

sources.name: Cadmillus, Atys, Adonis, Osiris
sources.use: Illustrate the god dead and revived, among the Cabiri, in Phrygia, in Lydia and among the Egyptians.

sources.name: Proclus
sources.quote: The heart of Bacchus, swiftly slaughtered king, Was saved in Aether
sources.use: Illustrates the god torn apart, preserved and renewed, and the demiurgic impulse in the mind.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.use: Reference only: the Proclus hymn is given 'by Taylor, in his Sallust'.

sources.name: Cadmus, Deucalion, Osiris, Bacchus, Hercules, Orpheus
sources.use: Heroes who passed the same ordeal; their adventures read as records of the soul's struggle with her inner enemies.

sources.name: Poemander
sources.quote: do force the inwardly placed man to suffer sensibly
sources.use: Supports: language for the real suffering passions cause in the revealed light.

sources.name: Noah
sources.quote: as Noah in the Ark
sources.use: Illustrates the principle preserved in the water through destruction, which renews all things.

sources.name: the Alchemists
sources.quote: called by the Alchemists, for certain accurate reason, Altitude, Latitude and Profundity
sources.use: Source of the names for the three periods of the threefold Law.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: And this shall stand, said that noble clerke, For the Water within our werke
sources.use: Supports: verse on the never-wasting Water of the work, citing Democrit and Hermes for its names.

sources.name: Democrit
sources.quote: Lux umbra caresn, Water most orient;
sources.use: Reported within Norton's verse as naming the Water.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: no liquor so necessary, As was water of crude Mercury:
sources.use: Reported within Norton's verse as naming the Water.

sources.name: Ashmole
sources.quote: Blessed be thou, Experience!
sources.use: Supports: verse 'Tablet' erected by Philosophy to Experience, on the One Thing, the first Material Mother and the Three Powers in one seat, which III.3 ¶77 glosses as Sulphur, Mercury and Salt.

sources.name: the Rabbi in Zohar
sources.quote: Thought is the Principle of all that is; but it is as first Unknown and shut up in itself.
sources.use: Supports: Thought as hidden Principle unfolding into Spirit/Intelligence and articulate voice; Atwood takes it up as her theme, calling it a 'Magnificent, yet impervious assertion'.

sources.name: Frank.
sources.use: Reference only (n50: 'Frank. Part 2, p. 101').

sources.name: Poemander
sources.quote: for the like is intelligible by the like
sources.use: Supports, introduced with 'Yet' against her stated impossibility: enlarge the self beyond body and time to understand God; self-limitation is the obstacle; knowing, willing, hoping are the way.

sources.name: the Kabalah
sources.use: Supports: in the Divine I Am is signified the Substant Unity of all that is.

sources.name: the Sybil in Boissard
sources.quote: Verbum invisible fiet palpabile et germinabit ut Radix.
sources.use: Supports: the recreation as a birth of the invisible into the palpable.

sources.name: the philosopher
sources.use: Supports: work faithfully until it be the Divine pleasure to make it appear. Not named.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: Wherefore old Fathers, conveniently, Called this science Holy Alkimy
sources.use: Supports: epigraph on the few chosen; closing verse on Alchemy as a holy gift of grace, taught orally under oath only to the proven and virtuous, kept secret because of the danger of evil men.

sources.name: Ashmole
sources.use: Reference only (where Norton's Ordinal, chap. 1, is cited).

sources.name: Geber
sources.quote: Natural Impotency, he asserts, is manifold
sources.use: Supports: foundation list of bodily and mental impediments; his 'necessary charges' is reinterpreted by Atwood as abandonment of selfhood.

sources.name: Paradise Lost (author not named)
sources.quote: for e’en in heaven his looks and thoughts Were always downward bent
sources.use: Illustrates Mammon as the downward-looking spirit leading the depraved operators.

sources.name: the prophet
sources.quote: They have discovered secrets, and these are they who are to be judged
sources.use: Supports: those who discover secrets and turn them to ill account are judged; Atwood identifies them with Geber's avaricious.

sources.name: story of an Arabian Magician
sources.quote: the story of an Arabian Magician, who must needs steal a little boy
sources.use: Illustrates that wickedness bars approach to the material.

sources.name: the pious author of the Aquarium
sources.quote: this art will vanish from under thy hands
sources.use: Supports: pride or covetousness after possession makes the art vanish; endorsed by Atwood.

sources.name: Job
sources.quote: If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence
sources.use: Supports accountability of moral evil and condemnation of trusting gold; n6 accompanies Adam hiding his iniquity in his bosom.

sources.name: Holbein
sources.quote: The pictures, of Holbein are not less beautiful for all the covetous spirit that reigned with their conception
sources.use: Contrasts: in ordinary arts the maker's moral state does not appear in the product, unlike Alchemy.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: For this reason are the philosophers said to be envious, declares Hermes
sources.use: Supports: the philosophers' secrecy withholds truth from the vicious, for whom they are accountable to God.

sources.name: more experienced observers
sources.use: Supports: their testimony that very few are naturally disposed to the research.

sources.name: Geber
sources.use: Supports: his ranking of the unfit (Skeptics condemned next above the Covetous) and his 'impediments of body' are followed. Also named as an era ('Geber’s and Norton’s time') and as read by those in darkness in Eirenaeus' allegory.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: Scarcely seven men maie this science finde.
sources.use: Supports: the science is granted by God to few faithful, lowly men and withheld from proud clerks who trust their wits and then call it fable. Also named as an era in III.4 ¶15.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: But some Lords be of stable wit, Such only be apt to finish it
sources.use: Supports: the unfit should cease; the fit proceed mightily and suavely; only those of stable wit finish.

sources.name: the hermetic Master
sources.quote: to free himself from the usurpation of vice, and to be good, just, and of sound reason
sources.use: Supports: moral qualifications for one to be introduced into the hidden Wisdom.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.quote: there was any water in our sea
sources.use: Illustrates: friends, who would be accounted philosophers, disbelieved his word-by-word explanation of the Art.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.quote: that darkness I now perceived had a false fore of its own
sources.use: Illustrates (in 'outward application'): the light of Alchemy is not perceptible to the gross understanding, which has its own false light.

sources.name: Rhasis
sources.use: Named in Eirenaeus' allegory as read by those sitting in darkness.

sources.name: Galileo
sources.use: Contrasts: Atwood would as soon have lived in Galileo's days as see the recovered secret sink into obloquy through modern skepticism.

sources.name: the wise / adepts
sources.quote: As the adepts indeed foretold, their records have proved like a curious two-edged instrument
sources.use: Supports: they declare none attain without right intention and God's blessing, that the pursuit is dangerous to the ill-informed, and that their records are two-edged.

sources.name: this holi letter
sources.quote: Attingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter, Disponens omnia suaviter;
sources.use: Cited within Norton's verse as the sentence to follow; unattributed in the text.

sources.name: Revelations, Open Entrances, New Lights and True Lights, Sunshine and Moonshine, Auroras, Dawns, Manuals, Introductory Lexicons, Triumphal Chariots, Banners, Gates, Keys, Guides
sources.use: Illustrates: generic titles of alchemical books, all directing to the Royal Road once found but useless to most modern readers.

sources.name: the royal artist
sources.quote: this treasure is not to be bought with money; and as it cannot be bought, so neither can it be sold
sources.use: Supports: the art is for those who understand, and cannot be bought or sold.

sources.name: Geber
sources.quote: Ye sons of Avarice and Ignorance, cries Geber, and ye of evil manners, avaunt and fly from this science
sources.use: Supports deliberate veiling: the unworthy are excluded; the writing is intelligible only to the wise by pursuit.

sources.name: the preacher
sources.quote: The words of the wise are as goads
sources.use: Illustrates the pointed, veiled nature of the wise writings.

sources.name: the prince
sources.work: Epilogue to the Invest. Of Perfection
sources.quote: let the sapient artificer, concludes the prince, studiously peruse our books, collecting our dispersed intention
sources.use: Supports: the student must collect the dispersed teaching and test it by experiment.

sources.name: Ricardus
sources.quote: I beg of thee, my son, says the adept Ricardus, to examine the writings of the philosophers
sources.use: Supports: study of theory precedes practice; study overthrows ignorance.

sources.name: Zachary
sources.quote: for no one ever acquired this art by chance, but by prayer rather than by other means
sources.use: Supports: read the philosophers and pray before the Work, yet means must be used.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.quote: Pray, says Sendivogius, pray; but work.
sources.use: Supports: prayer joined with work and knowing how and when to use understanding.

sources.name: Arnold
sources.quote: three requisites, viz., subtlety of mind, manual skill, and a free will for the operation
sources.use: Supports: requisites of the operator.

sources.name: Lully
sources.work: Lullii Theor. Test. Ch. 31.; Theatr. Chem., vol. 2, p.419
sources.quote: a sufficiency of the Divine Favour, and books to open the understanding and give it zest for truth
sources.use: Supports: adds Divine Favour and books to Arnold's requisites.

sources.name: Ricardi Anglici Libellus
sources.use: Reference only (cited with Lully).

sources.name: The author of the Lucerna Salis
sources.quote: He does not either grant it immediately to any person, but always by mediate dispositions, to wit, by instructions and the labour of the hands
sources.use: Supports: study, meditation and prayer are needed; God grants the art only through instruction and labour, and without prayer obstructs or spoils it. Also cited in n16 for 'many passages to the same effect' as Ricardus.

sources.name: Digby
sources.work: Digby's Translation of the Lucerna Salis
sources.use: Reference only (translation cited).

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: this science I have obtained by the sole gift of the living God inspiring me
sources.use: Supports: love of God is the strength of the undertaking; the science is God's gift.

sources.name: the Scripture
sources.quote: the Lesser is blessed by the Greater
sources.use: Supports: blessing and increase come from God. Atwood also quotes 'Every good gift and every perfect gift comes from the Father of Lights' and 'Paul may plant and Apollos may water, but God alone giveth the increase', and says the talent is taken from him who does not use it.

sources.name: Pierce, the Black Monk
sources.work: on the Elixir, in Ashmole's Theatr.
sources.quote: Therefore there ys no other waye But to take thee to thy beades and pray:
sources.use: Supports: the subject is a seed from a body, not common gold and silver; the seeker must be pious, charitable and prayerful; covetous men never find it.

sources.name: Ashmole
sources.use: Reference only (collection containing Pierce's verse).

sources.name: Kirchringius
sources.work: Annotations of Kirchringius on Basil Valentine, sub init., p. 5
sources.quote: even in the midst of the operations of Vital Chemistry, full of labour and toil, they prayed, says Kirchringius
sources.use: Supports: efficacy of prayer in the work and in solving enigmas; prayer as desire plus cooperation yielding revelation.

sources.name: Basil Valentine
sources.use: Reference only (subject of Kirchringius's annotations).

sources.name: the oracles
sources.quote: Thus piety is available for all things, as the oracles declare
sources.use: Supports: piety, and prayer as its principal exercise, are profitable for great undertakings.

sources.name: St. Paul
sources.use: Reference only (compared with supplication interceding as a mediator).

sources.name: Iamblicus
sources.quote: Prayer, according to Iamblicus, was divided into three classes
sources.use: Supports Atwood's defence of prayer: three classes of prayer, its necessity in sacred operations, and its purifying effects on the soul.

sources.name: the authorities
sources.use: Supports: the three terms of adoration contain all the Divine measures.

sources.name: the Psalmist
sources.quote: I called upon the Lord, exclaims the Psalmist, and He heard me out of His holy temple
sources.use: Supports: prayer from the inner temple is heard and brings understanding and the Spirit of Wisdom.

sources.name: the Preacher
sources.quote: Behold, two are better than one, says the Preacher
sources.use: Supports: the work needs a companion, a medium and a bond. One alone labours endlessly.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset, and that is glasse
sources.use: Main authority on the practical requisites: vessels (chap. 6, p. 94), ministers (Second Concord), furnaces, instruments and places (Fourth Concord). Atwood calls his description of the Preparatory Practice naive and 'without much envy'.

sources.name: my good Master (Norton's)
sources.quote: Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset
sources.use: Cited within Norton's verse as disclosing the secret that the vessel is glass.

sources.name: Albertus Magnus
sources.quote: And this sheweth best Albertus Magnus, In his Boke De Mineralibus
sources.use: Cited within Norton's verse as best showing the right figure of vessels.

sources.name: Charnocke
sources.quote: One within another, it is a pretty feate, The Third without them to guide up the heate
sources.use: Illustrates the nested vessels and the need to instruct the potter (chap. 1), and the trouble with indifferent assistants and the value of a faithful servant (chap. 3, 'Idem').

sources.name: Solomon
sources.quote: A good servant, saith Solomon, let him be unto thee, As thine own hearte,in each degree
sources.use: Cited within Charnocke's verse on the value of a faithful servant.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: thou mayst easily carry it, says Vaughan, in one of thy Hands
sources.use: Supports: the true furnace is small and simple, the glass one, the work no trouble, and women fitter for it than men.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: the excitation of the Fire is a very trivial, slight, almost a ridiculous thing
sources.use: Supports: exciting the Fire is slight, yet it contains all the secrets of corruption and generation.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.use: Reference only (p. 118).

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.use: Reference only (chap. 8 and 24).

sources.name: Geber
sources.quote: Geber calls this furnace Athanor
sources.use: Gives the name Athanor for the furnace. Atwood criticizes others who, following his example, described it 'with a misleading subtlety'.

sources.name: the Arcadia
sources.quote: a lady may read the Arcadia
sources.use: Within Vaughan: illustrates that the work does not occupy the attention.

sources.name: Argo / Apollo (classical allusion)
sources.quote: like the planks of Argo, on occasion, are still oracular
sources.use: Illustrates that the philosophic vessels 'speak for themselves'.

sources.name: Philosophers / Astrologers / Auctors (in Norton)
sources.quote: Philosophers said, by their engine, How it should be wrought within locks nyne
sources.use: Cited within Norton's verse on working 'within locks nyne' and on the importance of a fitting place.

sources.name: Virgil
sources.use: Illustrates: the locality he appointed for his Bees, with its allegorical exclusions of corrupt and evil associates, as the desirable working-place.

sources.name: adepts
sources.use: Supports: said to 'well testify' that imaginative impressures linger and pollute the ether of a place.

sources.name: Cornelius Agrippa
sources.use: Supports: said to expound diffusely that imaginative impressions linger and pollute the ether of a place.

sources.name: unnamed verse
sources.quote: It is a grace - To finde a fitting working-place.
sources.use: Supports the need for a fitting working-place.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: consider well with thyself what manner of man thou art, and what it is that thou wouldst do
sources.use: Supports: 'an English Adept, neither antique nor envious'; his lessons on self-examination, moderate heat, charity, piety, solitude and perseverance are quoted at length and offered 'in conclusion of the rest'.

sources.name: Zeno
sources.quote: Nature gave us one tongue and two ears, that we might hear much and speak little
sources.use: Cited within Vaughan's lessons: supports listening much and speaking little.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.quote: according to God and the angels, rejecting all things that are dissimilar to the heaven
sources.use: Cited within Vaughan's lessons: a heavenly life is the condition of communion with superiors.

sources.name: Anima Magia Abscondita
sources.use: Reference only (p. 51, etc.), footnote to the Vaughan passage.

sources.name: Coelum Terrae
sources.use: Reference only (p. 137), footnote to the Vaughan passage.

sources.name: Arcanum Ignis Aquae
sources.quote: Dii sudoribus vendunt Artes
sources.use: Chapter epigraph; sets the theme of labor (arts bought by sweat).

sources.name: the Monk Basil (B. Valentine)
sources.quote: more is learned by once seeing the work done, than can be taught by the writing of many pages
sources.use: Supports: preparation of the subject by manual operation, which draws out the hidden nature; experience and seeing over writing.

sources.name: maxim 'Physician, heal thyself'
sources.quote: Physician, heal thyself
sources.use: Cited within Basil's passage: the praise of the science consists in experience.

sources.name: Kirchringius
sources.use: Reference only (cited 'in Basil, idem').

sources.name: Antiquity
sources.use: Source of the celebrated image of the Brazen Wall.

sources.name: Albertus (Alberti mag.)
sources.work: Secret. Tact. Alberti mag.; Ars Aurifera, p. 130
sources.quote: Take the occult Nature, which is our Brass
sources.use: Supports: purification of the occult Nature (our Brass) by successive dissolution and coagulation, beginning with perfect solution.

sources.name: Lully (R. Lully)
sources.quote: comes not but by help of ingenuity, and the Manual operations of man
sources.use: Supports: the hand as instrument; the Mercury of the philosophers needs manual operation.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: nature is not moved by theory alone, but by sagacious Handicraft and human assistance
sources.use: Supports: necessity of handwork and human assistance.

sources.name: the author of the Filum Ariadne
sources.quote: Nature cannot of herself enter into the dissolution
sources.use: Supports: the dissolution needs hands, which Nature lacks.

sources.name: Van Helmont (Helmont)
sources.quote: The Hand, says Van Helmont, is the instrument of instruments
sources.use: Supports: the Hand as the soul's instrument (¶5); learners must buy coals and fire and labor as philosophers did (¶7).

sources.name: Norton
sources.use: Cited in n3; in ¶9 his and his brother Adepts' advice on the choice of servants and their qualifications illustrates the need for assistants.

sources.name: Crollius
sources.quote: these Chemical Secrets will never be fingered by those slothful or sottish despisers of them
sources.use: Supports operator requirements: the slothful and profane are unfit for the work.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.work: Introit. Apert., cap. 8; Introitis Apertus, cap. 7
sources.quote: there is no work more tedious than our First Operation
sources.use: Supports: the First Operation is literal, tedious labor needing attention and sagacity; distinguishes it from the Second, where Nature works alone by external fire.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: I spared no labor either of mind or body
sources.use: Cited by Eirenaeus: supports the necessity of labor.

sources.name: Solomon
sources.quote: The desire of the idle shall cause him to perish
sources.use: Proverb cited by Eirenaeus against idleness.

sources.name: Morien
sources.use: Cited by Eirenaeus: warned King Calid that many philosophers were overcome by the fatigue of this work.

sources.name: Arnold (Arnoldi)
sources.quote: The work of philosophers, says Arnold, is to dissolve the Stone in its own mercury
sources.use: Supports: the work is dissolution of the Stone in its own mercury to first Matter.

sources.name: Urbigeranus, the author of the Hermetic Secret
sources.use: Styles the labor a labor of Hercules; with 'these Adepts', holds it impossible without the Theory of their Arcanum.

sources.name: the wise author of the Rosarium
sources.quote: Tere, coque, et reitera, et non te taedeat
sources.use: Supports: grind, coct, and repeat without weariness.

sources.name: the Spirit to Dr Dee
sources.quote: to fight against the Powers of Darkness requires great force
sources.use: Supports steadfast continuance of labor to the end.

sources.name: Digby
sources.use: Reference for kings and powerful princes setting their hand to the work.

sources.name: Ovidii
sources.quote: Ardua prima via est
sources.use: Illustrates the steepness of the first way.

sources.name: the wise poet, in his Georgics
sources.use: Said to teach the repeated labor of ploughing and clearing the field.

sources.name: Zachary (Zacharius)
sources.quote: there is indeed but one way of working, in one matter, one linear way throughout
sources.use: Supports: despite many furnaces and vessels, one method, one matter, one vessel.

sources.name: the Adept
sources.quote: the advantages of the Spirit preparing its body and extracting from it the tinging spirit
sources.use: Describes the Preparing Spirit and the cleansing of the Argent vive.

sources.name: Norton’s Ordinal
sources.work: Ordinal, chap. 4 (n14); Norton’s Ordinal, cap. 4 (n17); Ordinal, cap. 4 (n22, n23)
sources.quote: Excess of one half quarter of an hour May destroy all
sources.use: Supports: main verse authority for balanced unhasty feeding, cost, patience, simmering, the three-year Gross Work, and the Gross Work as foul, perilous handicraft needing experience, uniformity and able ministers.

sources.name: Avicen
sources.quote: Comedas ut bibas, et bibas ut comeda;
sources.use: Cited within the Ordinal for balanced feeding of the matter.

sources.name: Rasis
sources.quote: Non tamen comedat res festinanter,
sources.use: Cited within the Ordinal: 'set the dietary'; the matter must not eat hastily.

sources.name: the prophet
sources.quote: Visitasti terram et inebriasti eam,
sources.use: Cited within the Ordinal as wondrous mention of the feeding of the matter, 'If ye apply it to this intention'.

sources.name: Arnolde
sources.quote: Esto longanimus et suavis
sources.use: Cited within the Ordinal: the Art belongs to great men, so poor men beware; be patient and gentle.

sources.name: Oedipus
sources.use: Illustrates: his lameness signifies not hastening to solve the Sphinx's riddle.

sources.name: Alciatus
sources.quote: Festina Lente
sources.use: Illustrates: emblem of a dolphin wreathed about an anchor, applied to slow trituration.

sources.name: Basil
sources.work: Kirchringius in Basilio, Latin, 12 mo., p. 160
sources.quote: permit it not to fly suddenly
sources.use: Supports: the winged Matter must be accustomed to flying gradually under Mercury and bound, lest like Icarus it fly too near the Sun.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: Take the flying bird, says Hermes, and drown it flying
sources.use: Supports: drowning the flying bird so it lives by forbearing to fly, and repeatedly withdrawing its corrupt redness.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.quote: of a vulgar ignoramus I became a true Adept
sources.use: Illustrates a favored case: the Arcanum revealed in two and a half years; also cited as promising and describing a guide.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.quote: Ab actionibus procedit speculatio
sources.use: Supports: speculation proceeds from action (¶18); one deliberates about means, not ends, analyzing back to the first Cause as with a diagram (¶30).

sources.name: Kelly
sources.quote: by grace it is obtained
sources.use: Supports: the Art is obtained by grace, not reading or will.

sources.name: Pope’s Homer’s Odyssey
sources.quote: In wondrous ships self-moved, instinct with mind;
sources.use: Illustrates: the Phoeacian ships and Alcinous' court as the dominion of Intellect; the vast sea as the barrier before the goal.

sources.name: Taylor
sources.use: Supports: has shown the whole Odyssey to be an allegory of latent meaning and the recondite Wisdom of antiquity.

sources.name: Perseus, Theseus, Bacchus, Ulysses, Hercules, Jason
sources.use: Illustrates: heroes' labors before reward, as the toil required for Wisdom.

sources.name: Anaxagoras
sources.quote: Nemo prima fronte reperitur discretus
sources.use: Cited within the Ordinal: no one is discreet at first.

sources.name: Flamel
sources.use: Illustrates: learned discretion from his Second Book.

sources.name: Khunrath
sources.quote: What was wrong taught me what was right
sources.use: Supports: indefatigable labor at own expense, learning from error, book interpreting book, note-keeping, constant meditation.

sources.name: Hermetical Triumph
sources.quote: the Stone of Philosophers, which is a pure petrification of the Spirit
sources.use: Supports: the Stone is prepared with the Lunar Vulcan, which Atwood glosses as the first prepared Subject.

sources.name: Cheiron (Latin verse, unattributed)
sources.quote: Ille pius Cheiron justissimus omnes Inter Nubigenas et Magni Doctor Achillis.
sources.use: Illustrates: Atwood identifies Cheiron as Power and Motive in alliance, educating the Heroic Fire.

sources.name: Dactyli Idaei (fable)
sources.quote: Such were those Dactyli Idaei, literally the Fingers of Mount Ida
sources.use: Illustrates: hand and fiery artifice exhibiting the metallic veins, as the hand expresses premeditated thought.

sources.name: Bell
sources.use: Reference only (for the Dactyli Idaei).

sources.name: the wise Adept
sources.quote: the Association is ominous
sources.use: Warns that Pluto's Palace exposed with Minerva's Artifice, or Vulcan with her at the Altar, is ominous.

sources.name: Oracula Chaldeor
sources.quote: Vitifer Ignis
sources.use: Illustrates: Latin verse on 'Vitifer Ignis' and a Centre.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.work: Preface to the Fame and Confession of the R.C.
sources.quote: one of the greatest subtleties of the Art
sources.use: Supports: the Second part of the Gross Work is among the hardest; reports Agrippa's failure and, apparently continuing, Lully's and Ripley's. n28 cites the Lully Latin passage as quoted in his Preface.

sources.name: Cornelius Agrippa
sources.use: Contrasts: knew the First Preparation but not the Solution of the Salt, as shown by his practice at Malines; confessed he could not increase the transmutative virtue.

sources.name: Natalius
sources.use: Would not teach Agrippa despite his entreaties.

sources.name: his disciple (Agrippa's)
sources.quote: This was it, adds his disciple, that made his necessities so vigorous and his purse so weak
sources.use: Illustrates Agrippa's poverty resulting from his failure.

sources.name: Raymond Lully
sources.quote: Nos, says he, de prima illa nigedine a paucis cognita ebnigmum Spiritum extrahere affectantes
sources.use: Example: first followed the tedious common process, later performed the Solution in nine days with the secret from God; also cited (¶39) that only God can reveal it.

sources.name: Arnold
sources.use: Lully did not receive the mystery from him.

sources.name: Ripley
sources.use: Contrasts: tried to putrefy his Red Salt by alternate heat and cold, a 'singular' method.

sources.name: Faber
sources.quote: Faber is so wise that he will not understand him
sources.use: Aside on Ripley's method.

sources.name: Khunrath
sources.quote: In the first act of the physico-chemical works, explains Khunrath
sources.use: Supports: detailed account of the first act and the Second Operation.

sources.name: the philosopher
sources.quote: who is he that is bale to untie it, enquires the philosopher?
sources.use: Frames the question of who can untie the Gordian Knot.

sources.name: Latin verse (unattributed)
sources.quote: Janua clausa est, vah quae lamentabilis haec vox;
sources.use: Illustrates: the door is shut and hands cannot force it.

sources.name: Van helmont
sources.quote: Not every messenger, says Van helmont, approacheth to the mine of Sontes
sources.use: Supports: requirements of the operator; the dissolving virtue is specific, not corrosive.

sources.name: Scripture ('the Scriptural phrase', unnamed)
sources.quote: He that hath clean hands and a pure heart
sources.use: Supports: purity is required; Atwood says she quotes it because it is apt, 'proved on the Divine Ground', not because it is popular.

sources.name: the Hermetic Master
sources.quote: Wisdom was with thee, says the Hermetic Master; it was not gotten by thy care
sources.use: Supports: wisdom is not gotten by human care or study.

sources.name: 1 Corinth.
sources.quote: neither he that watereth, but God, that giveth the increase
sources.use: Supports: God gives the increase.

sources.name: the Apostle
sources.quote: the weapons of this warfare are not carnal, as the Apostle teaches
sources.use: Supports: the purification of the operator is a spiritual, not carnal, warfare.

sources.name: Basil Valentine ('the monk')
sources.quote: Our Antimony, says Basil Valentine, which is fixed, searcheth out fixed diseases
sources.use: Supports: Antimony must be freed of venom (glossed by Atwood as purging self-will from the mind); separation by Fire, Vulcan as sole master.

sources.name: Kirchringius
sources.use: Reference only.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: There is one operation of heat, says Vaughan, whose method is vital and far more mysterious than all other
sources.use: Supports: the vital, mysterious heat-operation and placing the Moon of the Firmament equally in two elements. Work assigned from n35, which lists 'Coelum Terrae; Flamelli Summula' in the order Vaughan, Flamel are quoted.

sources.name: Flamel
sources.quote: a bright shining fire like the Sun itself, whose heat must neither be excessive, but always of one and the same degree
sources.use: Supports: the nature of the fire (not coal or wood; sun-like, constant) for cherishing the Solar and Lunar Mercury.

sources.name: Morien
sources.quote: Our operation, concludes Morien, is nothing else but extracting water from the earth and returning it again
sources.use: Supports: alternating extraction and return of moisture leading to putrefaction; Atwood then glosses it as action and reaction.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.quote: For what one doth concoct t’other will drive away;
sources.use: Supports: two contrary works to be done apart and then reconciled (verse).

sources.name: the same author
sources.quote: Hence comes the Chamelion which is our Chaos
sources.use: Illustrates: 'an explanation of the whole difficulty' — Fiery Dragon, Lodestone, purgation, the Chamelion/Chaos. 'The same author' follows the n37 verse (Eirenaeus); n38 names no author.

sources.name: Nuysement
sources.work: Sal Lumen, the latin of Combachius
sources.quote: sed potius solis terrestris innatus calor
sources.use: Supports: the effective heat is innate (terrestrial sun), not external.

sources.name: Democritus
sources.work: In Flamelli Summula, Quae ex Democrito colleguntur
sources.quote: Drawing the fixed Brass out bodily, instructs this Abderite
sources.use: Illustrates: Atwood says Democritus 'before all, and as it were pyrographically, portrays' the Vulcanic action; called 'this Abderite'.

sources.name: Paris (Venus, Juno, Minerva)
sources.quote: Perchance it was when Paris gazed on such a Venus, he did prefer her both to Juno and Minerva
sources.use: Illustrates: the beauty of the golden Venus (Paphia) of the Democritus passage; speaker unclear (see ambiguities).

sources.name: the philosopher
sources.quote: Labor to know causes
sources.use: Supports: rational inquiry into causes as the condition of success; endorsed by Atwood.

sources.name: unattributed Latin maxim
sources.quote: Sie finis ab origine pendet.
sources.use: Supports: the end depends from the beginning (the Motive governs the result).

sources.name: the apostle
sources.quote: the Fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is
sources.use: Supports: the one foundation, trial of every work by Fire, and man as Temple of God; attached to the call to press on to Divine Perfection.

sources.name: Oedipus / the Sphinx
sources.quote: like Oedipus, is able to solve the Enigma of the Sphinx
sources.use: Illustrates: solving the riddle as rational penetration of one's own natural understanding.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: The philosopher’s worke doe not begin Till all things be pure without and within
sources.use: Supports: the Work begins only after complete purity (verse).

sources.name: Khunrath
sources.quote: Omnia in omnibus primum, omni Tertio traditit
sources.use: Chapter epigraph ('Enigma') on a first-second-third transmission; introduces the threefold order.

sources.name: the Adepts
sources.quote: Natus est jam Elias Artista
sources.use: Concealed the three operations (¶3); witnesses with Plutarch to the fable's meaning (¶7); their saying that Elias the artist is born (¶12).

sources.name: Eudoxus
sources.quote: the practice of our Art is the most difficult thing in the world, not in regard to its operation
sources.use: Supports: the difficulty lies in learning the Art from books; the seeker needs profound knowledge of Nature.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: Greate neede hath he to be a clerke
sources.use: Supports the need for learning (¶5); gives the white medicine, the shared vessel and the change of operation, and cites Hermes (¶13).

sources.name: our author of The Triumph
sources.quote: you must make the conversion of the Elements
sources.use: Supports: lists the fixed principles (Elements, Three Principles, white and citrine Mercury, fixed Sulphur as the Stone).

sources.name: Egyptian Fable of Isis and Osiris
sources.use: Illustrates Intellect bringing itself into natural effect by begetting a supernatural offspring; Horus's birth represents the metaphysical offspring.

sources.name: Plutarch
sources.use: Cited, with the Adepts, as witness to the fable's meaning.

sources.name: Aristotle
sources.use: Reference (n1) for the fourfold doctrine of causes ('ancient Metaphysics'), applied to the Art.

sources.name: the Stagyrite
sources.quote: is good, according to the words of the Stagyrite, and the end of spiritual generation
sources.use: Supports: the self-perceiving final object is good and the end of spiritual generation; within the 'Peripathetic scheme'.

sources.name: unattributed Latin verse
sources.quote: Primus dicatur in quo sensus dominatur.
sources.use: Illustrates the four principles and their relations, graded against the senses.

sources.name: the Adept
sources.quote: they should be quickly lighted
sources.use: Supports: the three fires lit quickly, the Fourth supervening.

sources.name: Aquarium Sepientum
sources.work: Aquarium Sepientum in Mus. Herm., p. 112
sources.quote: Triuna universalis essentia, quae Jehovah appellatur
sources.use: Illustrates the triune and fivefold divine-human essence, placed after the birth of Horus.

sources.name: Malachi
sources.quote: Behold I will send you Elijah, the prophet
