sources.use: The Elijah prophecy frames Elias the artist (¶12); the Refiner's-Fire messenger closes the chunk without comment (¶14).

sources.name: Introit. Apertus
sources.use: Reference for the Elias Artista saying.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: Ignis et Azoth tibi sufficient
sources.use: Cited inside Norton's verse: fire and Azoth suffice.

sources.name: the Brethren
sources.quote: Master mason, of Grand Architects
sources.use: Their phrase for the only builders who 'erect structures in the air'.

sources.name: the Master
sources.quote: O blessed watery Form! That dissolveth the Elements!
sources.use: Supports: dissolution by Water, fire on the Foliated Sulphur, the King's Tincture and revival.

sources.name: Book of Enoch
sources.quote: ye that are capable to comprehend the Elect One
sources.use: Rain and dew; metal mountains melting before the Elect One. Given without comment.

sources.name: St. John
sources.quote: That which was from the Beginning, which they had heard, and seen with their eyes
sources.use: Supports: Christ as the Word of Life made manifest, the one awaited by prophets and philosophers.

sources.name: St Matthew
sources.quote: He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with Fire
sources.use: Illustrates: baptism by Water versus by the Holy Ghost and Fire; purging the floor and burning the chaff.

sources.name: the Bishop of Alexandria (footnote: Clemens Alexandrinus)
sources.quote: It is the Lord himself who is the Hierophanta.
sources.use: Supports: the Mysteries continued in Christianity, with the Lord as Hierophanta illuminating the Adepts. Footnote link depends on reading marker (2) as n12.

sources.name: De Septchenes
sources.use: Reference only (given with Clemens Alexandrinus).

sources.name: St Paul
sources.quote: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in times past unto the Fathers by the prophets
sources.use: Supports: revelation in the Son surpasses every earlier revelation of the Light.

sources.name: the Theosophist (footnote: Khunrath)
sources.quote: reduce the Ternary by the Quaternary, through the rejection of the Binary, to the simplicity of the Monad
sources.use: Supports: states the formula of reduction to the Monad, which Atwood then expounds.

sources.name: Trismegistus
sources.work: the Divine Poemander, Sermon on the Mont of Regeneration
sources.quote: the seed of his own regeneration
sources.use: Supports: each of the two principles carries the seed of its own regeneration.

sources.name: the Adept (footnote: Lumen de Lumine)
sources.quote: Salvation is nothing else but a Transmutation
sources.use: Supports: invisible Artist, operator only keeps the heat, Water and Spirit perform all, Three and Four make seven, salvation is transmutation. Atwood completes and extends the statement.

sources.name: Ancient Schools of Divinity
sources.use: Their meaning of metempsychosis is set against the common, erroneous one.

sources.name: St John's Gospel
sources.quote: The True Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world
sources.use: Supports: the True Light perfected in the Saviour, whose ray cleanses life.

sources.name: Hermetic Riddle
sources.quote: The First all things in all gave the First Second all things in all, from the all in the First Second to the Third all
sources.use: Illustrates the circulation that manifests the Flower of Intellect back to its Archetypal Source.

sources.name: Chaldaic oracle
sources.quote: For the mind of the Father said that all things be cut into Three
sources.use: Supports: pursues the same Art of Reason (Monad, Duad, Triad, the Matrix and the Prester of Fire).

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.use: Cited (within the Adept's words) for the menstruum in the sphere of Saturn that can calcine gold, identified with the Salt.

sources.name: the Adept / the philosopher (footnote: Introitus Apertus)
sources.quote: The Wise will rejoice, adds the Adept
sources.use: Supports: the loadstone, Salt, Pole and Fire imagery, the Genesis analogy, and the union of agent and patient. Footnote link depends on reading marker (10) as n19.

sources.name: the Wise
sources.quote: their work may be likened to the creation of the world
sources.use: Supports: the work likened to creation, reported as their unanimous view.

sources.name: Genesis
sources.quote: And the Spirit of God moved upon the Face of the Waters.
sources.use: Illustrates: the work likened to the creation of the world.

sources.name: Maria
sources.work: Maria Practica; Ars Aurifera, vol. 2, p. 208
sources.quote: Gummis cum binis fugitivum figit in imis,
sources.use: Illustrates: Latin verse on fixing the fugitive and binding in three hours; given without comment.

sources.name: book of Jezirah
sources.quote: with the Fiery Letters of the Law, He engraved the empty, and the void, and the obscure mind
sources.use: Illustrates: compared with the building of Solomon's Temple and the threefold completion of the Stone.

sources.name: Homer
sources.quote: Be silent, repress your intellect, and do not speak.
sources.use: Supports: quietude and cessation of mental energy are needed to receive divinity.

sources.name: Trismegistus
sources.quote: the knowledge of it, says Trismegistus, is a most Divine Silence, and a rest of all the senses
sources.use: Supports: knowledge of the First Cause as silence that draws the soul from the body into God's Essence.

sources.name: Schelling
sources.quote: We awaken from the Intellectual Intuition, says Schelling, as from a state of death
sources.use: Supports: after the intuition only the remembered vision remains, because human reason is limited.

sources.name: Norton
sources.quote: The last concord is well known to Clerkes Between the sphere of Heaven and our Subtil Werkes
sources.use: Supports: astrological election for the work, the four virtues, and the Elixir as a thing of Second Intention.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: a first and second sublimation, of a double nativity, visible and invisible
sources.use: Illustrates: further operations alluded to but withheld.

sources.name: the schoolmen
sources.quote: bad news (as the schoolmen phrase it)
sources.use: Phrase borrowed within Vaughan's quotation.

sources.name: Bloomfield
sources.work: Camp of Philosophy (Conclusion), in Theatrum Chemicum Brit
sources.quote: Our magistery is Three, Two, and One
sources.use: Supports: the threefold magistery, the Dragon, the blackness and the appearing of Phoebus.

sources.name: Callimachus
sources.quote: Apollo’s eyes endure None but the good, the perfect, and the pure.
sources.use: Illustrates: the coming of the God of Light and the purity required to behold him.

sources.name: the philosopher (unnamed)
sources.quote: Fit thy roof to thy God in all thou canst
sources.use: Supports: self-preparation, invitation and sudden illumination.

sources.name: Anima Magia Abscond.
sources.quote: Eritque in te cum Lumine, Ignis
sources.use: Reference for the Latin sequence of illumination in the philosopher's passage.

sources.name: Plotinus
sources.quote: For the Light is with Power, and is God.
sources.use: Supports: sudden Light as sign of God's presence in the soul.

sources.name: unattributed Latin verse
sources.quote: Nec Sentire Deum nisi qui pars ipse Dei sit.
sources.use: Supports: only what is part of God perceives God (our translation).

sources.name: Scriptures (of the ancestors)
sources.quote: which their neglected Scriptures everywhere testify of
sources.use: Supports: the ancestors' finding of the Word of Life.

sources.name: Thrice Great Hermes
sources.quote: That which is above is as that which is below
sources.use: Supports: quoted in full as summary instruction in the Mystery.

sources.name: Eudoxus
sources.work: The Six Keys of Eudoxus, Opening Into the Most Secret Philosophy
sources.use: Named in the chapter heading; the first-person text of the chunk is presented as his.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: In the caverns of the metals there is hidden the Stone, which is venerable, bright in colour, a mind sublime, and an open sea.
sources.use: Supports: demonstrates the operation of the First Key.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: What is born of the Crow is the beginning of this Art.
sources.use: Supports: beheading the Raven/Black Dragon belongs properly to the First operation.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: the Stone, which, according to Hermes, is the vine of the Wise
sources.use: Supports: the Stone as vine that becomes Wine.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: power of it is not integral until it be turned into earth
sources.use: Supports: the earthy residue must not be discarded.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: For Water is the strongest Nature which surmounts and excites the fixed Nature in the Body, that is, rejoices in it
sources.use: Supports: union of water/spirit with body.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: The first of all is the water which issueth out of this Stone.
sources.use: Supports: the water from the Stone is the foundation of the Art.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: When I saw that the water by degrees did become thicker and harder I did rejoice
sources.use: Supports: thickening water as sign of success at the end of the second Work.

sources.name: Artefius
sources.use: Cited, with Trevisan and Flammel, among 'the sincerest' who passed the Preparation of Mercury in silence.

sources.name: Trevisan
sources.use: As Artefius.

sources.name: Flammel
sources.use: As Artefius.

sources.name: John Pontanus
sources.quote: he who pretends to separate anything from our subject knows nothing of philosophy
sources.use: Supports: nothing in the subject is to be discarded; superfluities are converted into essence by the Fire.

sources.name: Cosmopolite
sources.quote: All things must therefore being purged make Fire and Water to be Friends, which they will easily do in their earth, which had ascended with them.
sources.use: Supports: the manner of reconciling fire and water.

sources.name: philosophers
sources.quote: the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam
sources.use: Supports: spirit and body must be joined for generation.

sources.name: Senior
sources.quote: the highest fume should be reduced to the lowest
sources.use: Supports: union of volatile with fixed; called a precept 'which deserves attention'.

sources.name: Geber
sources.quote: a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur
sources.use: Supports: definition of the compound of Art as volatile and fixed.

sources.name: Eudoxus
sources.use: Not named in this chunk. The chapter heading identifies him as the first-person speaker of the whole quoted text, which Atwood presents as instruction on the practice.

sources.name: Flammel
sources.quote: one must make use of the citrine Mercury to make the Imbibition of the Red
sources.use: Supports: said 'more particularly' than others about the two Mercuries; warns that he was himself deceived until the Jew informed him.

sources.name: the Jew
sources.use: Mentioned as the one who informed Flammel of the truth on this point.

sources.name: Cosmopolite
sources.quote: if you shall give our old man gold and silver to swallow, that he may consume them, and at length he also dying may be burnt
sources.use: Supports and illustrates: his 'ingenious allegory' of the old man (Mercury) on the purification of the Mercury and the whole magistery; his naming of the Mercury as water, steel and lodestone; gold coupling eleven times and the Chalybes. Offered as confirmation of the secret of the two mercuries.

sources.name: Hermes
sources.quote: there is so much sympathy between the purified bodies and the spirits, that they never quit one another when they are united together
sources.use: Supports: permanent union of purified bodies and spirits (¶10); the mercurial water gaining all its virtues when turned to earth (¶12); the ferment/bread comparison, 'put a ferment to them and make the water earth' (¶14).

sources.name: Faith
sources.quote: there shall be no more separation or death
sources.use: Illustrates: the soul's permanent union with the glorified body as analogy for the union of spirits and purified bodies.

sources.name: Others (unnamed philosophers)
sources.quote: the White Mercury is the bath of the Moon, and that the Red Mercury is the bath of the Sun
sources.use: Reported teaching on the two Mercuries as baths, which the speaker does not dispute but supplements.

sources.name: the philosophers / the Adepts
sources.use: Contrasted: none shows how to get the two mercuries; they pass over the point 'very slightly' and the preparation of Mercury 'in silence'; the Adepts are less reserved about the last operations than the First. Reading them alone will hardly suffice.

sources.name: the most enlightened philosophers
sources.use: Supports: the difference between common and natural calcination.

sources.name: all artists
sources.quote: This truth is acknowledged by all artists
sources.use: Supports: that knowledge of the Magistery comes rather by Inspiration of Heaven.

sources.name: Eudoxus
sources.quote: The Keys of Eudoxus open no more
sources.use: Atwood notes its last Keys, on Multiplication and Projection, are avowedly defective, so she turns to another source.

sources.name: Author of the Open Entrance; E. Philalethes
sources.quote: you will no longer be able to calculate the strength of the medicine
sources.use: Supports: provides the Multiplication (¶18, attributed in text to the Author of the Open Entrance) and Projection (¶20, footnoted n1 to the Introitus Apertus of E. Philalethes) procedures. Treating the two as one rests on our translation of the title; the text does not state it.

sources.name: Sendivogius
sources.work: Praxis; footnoted as New Light of Alchemy, treatise 11
sources.quote: thou takest not common gold or silver, for these are dead; take Ours which are living
sources.use: Supports/illustrates spiritual fermentation: living vs common metals, the philosophers' Water/Mercury, radical moisture, color signs, iron test. Atwood calls him 'the wary Artist', who admits his experience stopped there.

sources.name: Vaughan
sources.quote: this dust is the Arabian Elixir
sources.use: Supports: nature of the finished medicine, bodily fermentation in gold used only to temper its power, the Arabian Elixir.

sources.name: Norton
sources.use: Reference only (cited in n3 alongside Vaughan).

sources.name: Marrow of Alchemy
sources.quote: And it sufficeth in one glasse to put
sources.use: Illustrates (verse): a small quantity of composition sealed in one glass.

sources.name: Author of Lucerna Salis; Digby
sources.work: Lucerna Salis, cap. 8 (footnoted as Digby’s Lucerna Salis)
sources.quote: one drachm of gold is sufficient for the fermentation in the red
sources.use: Supports: fermenting with pure gold or silver before projection, purifying the metals, tenfold multiplication by dissolving and coagulating.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.work: Marrow of Alchemy, Book 3, v. 45, etc.
sources.quote: But one at last ting’d ninety thousand more
sources.use: Illustrates (verse): multiplication by reiteration, the projection steps, the rennet image, an eyewitness claim of the Red medicine's power.

sources.name: Author of the Rosary
sources.use: Cited for inexhaustible abundance won by industry, patience and one's own labor; followed by 'continues Eirenaeus' within a passage footnoted to Introitus Apertus cap. 35. Part of the testimony Atwood then says is not literally true.

sources.name: Eirenaeus
sources.work: Introitus Apertus, cap. 35. De Multiplici hujus Artis.
sources.quote: even one Adept, were he permitted, might impart health to the whole world
sources.use: Cited for transmutation, perfected precious stones and a universal medicine; Atwood then tells gold-seekers to disregard such testimony.

sources.name: Kabalah
sources.quote: that which in the Kabalah is denominated the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God
sources.use: Supports: its union of man with God is identified with Fermentation.

sources.name: Gospel tradition of the Life of Christ
sources.use: Illustrates: the Adepts compare the phenomena of their work to it and to human redemption.

sources.name: Khunrath
sources.work: Amph. cap. 9; Amph. Sap. Etern., cap. 8
sources.quote: It is the universal medium of restoration and preservation
sources.use: Supports: named among Adepts linking the work to the Creed; main authority for the Stone's universal virtues, the Azoth, and (per n9) the fermentation with its metal; rightly conceiving the azoth is half the work.

sources.name: Boehme
sources.use: Supports: named among Adepts comparing the work to the Christian Creed.

sources.name: Freher
sources.use: Supports: named among Adepts comparing the work to the Christian Creed.

sources.name: Grasseus
sources.use: Supports: named among Adepts comparing the work to the Christian Creed.

sources.name: Julian
sources.work: Oration to the Extra-Mundane Mother; Julian’s Orations II
sources.quote: health is a certain symmetry or equilibrium of nature
sources.use: Illustrates vital rectification: the purified soul receives Divine Light and strengthens its connate spirit; disease comes from erroneous motion of the spirit.

sources.name: the oracles
sources.quote: through purifying ceremonies bodies become worthy of receiving divine assistance and health
sources.use: Supports Julian's claims; the Latin verse in ¶31 is cited with them.

sources.name: Petris, the Persian
sources.quote: this man is the prince of divine knowledge
sources.use: Illustrates: narrative of Hippocrates' divine nature and healing (footnoted to Helmont, Tumulus Pestis).

sources.name: Hippocrates
sources.use: Illustrates: the divinely endowed physician who imparts healing to others.

sources.name: Aesculapius
sources.use: Hippocrates' paternal ancestor; honored with Hercules; a demigod only among the Greeks, modern Mesmerism's only just pride.

sources.name: Praxithea
sources.use: Hippocrates' mother, of the race of the Heraclides.

sources.name: Triptolemus
sources.use: Simile: Hippocrates dispersed the succours of Aesculapius as Triptolemus the seed of Ceres.

sources.name: Iliad
sources.quote: Such as sage Chiron, sire of pharmacy, First taught Achilles, and Achilles thee
sources.use: Illustrates the handing on of healing virtues.

sources.name: Hercules
sources.use: Hippocrates was honored by the Athenians with the same gifts as Hercules and Aesculapius.

sources.name: Solomon
sources.quote: Honor the physician with the honor due unto him
sources.use: Supports (within Helmont's text): the physician is created by the Lord.

sources.name: Helmont
sources.quote: But a physician chosen by God
sources.use: Supports: requirements of the God-chosen physician and the decline of medicine through ambition and gain; called by Atwood 'one of its brightest ornaments'.

sources.name: Van Helmont
sources.use: Illustrates: his reported cures of some 10,000 people yearly without diminishing his medicine.

sources.name: Galen
sources.quote: being allured with the facility of the art of Galen
sources.use: Criticized (in Helmont): measuring all diseases by degrees of heat and cold.

sources.name: Greek temples to Ceres, Minerva, Apollo, Bacchus
sources.use: Illustrates: institutions ministering to defects of mind and disciplining the understanding for Wisdom.

sources.name: Mesmerism
sources.use: Mentioned: Aesculapius is its only just pride (praise or limitation; see ambiguities).

sources.name: Eccles.
sources.quote: Her secret is with the Faithful
sources.use: Supports: honor the physician; Wisdom's secret is with the Faithful (the prophet; chunk's close).

sources.name: the Scriptures
sources.quote: I will put enmity between thee and the woman
sources.use: Supports throughout: a faith bestowing Wisdom; God's sentence on the Serpent; promises of Wisdom and material fruits; read as obscure and mystical.

sources.name: the theosophist
sources.quote: Herein the Philosophers’ Stone or tincture lyeth.
sources.use: Supports, endorsed: Adam and the fall, the two fires, the tincturing of Mercury, the Two Natures, the Mercury as worker and the Artist's role.

sources.name: D.A. Freher
sources.work: Of the Analogy in the Process of the Phil. Work with the Redemption of Man through Jesus Christ
sources.use: Reference for the theosophist's account in ¶38.

sources.name: Revel.
sources.quote: he that hath the Key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth
sources.use: Supports the qualifications of the competent minister.

sources.name: Solomon
sources.quote: Or what man is he, asks Solomon, that can know the counsel of God?
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom must be given from above; illustrates Wisdom preserving the righteous.

sources.name: Isaiah
sources.quote: Line upon line, Precept upon precept
sources.use: Supports gradual purifying and perfecting.

sources.name: Habbakuk
sources.quote: he had horns coming out of his hand, and there was the hiding of his power
sources.use: Illustrates power acting through the hand of the wise.

sources.name: Revel.
sources.use: Reference only (footnote placement possibly shifted; see ambiguities).

sources.name: Proverbs
sources.quote: I love them that love me, and those that seek me early shall find me
sources.use: Supports the worth and promises of Wisdom; introduced in ¶47 'as Solomon says'.

sources.name: Revel.
sources.quote: To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the Tree of Life
sources.use: Supports promises of material fruits with Wisdom; ¶41-45 apparently from these chapters (footnote numbering unclear).

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.quote: Clausum est Armarium
sources.use: Supports reading Scripture as obscure and mystical yet significant in material promises.

sources.name: the disciple
sources.quote: then he sends us these things as tokens and pledges of his love
sources.use: Supports, endorsed: material gifts as tokens of the Spirit's love.

sources.name: Midas
sources.use: Contrasts: one who preferred an earth-born harmony to the music of the spheres and was dishonored by the god.

sources.name: prophecies
sources.quote: Many prophecies there are of times to come
sources.use: Reported: they foretell the Fourth Monarchy; Atwood notes them but does not tarry on them.

sources.name: unattributed verse
sources.quote: Begin today, nor end till evil sink In its due grave
sources.use: Illustrates: keeping the completed work ever in mind as aim and model and persevering.

sources.name: unattributed verse
sources.quote: Then shall the reign of Mind commence on earth
sources.use: Illustrates: the hoped-for reign of Mind and man's second birth.

sources.name: Palingenius
sources.quote: Invenere artem, qua non ars dignior ulla est, Fingendi Lepidem Aetherium
sources.use: Supports: the art of fashioning the Ethereal Stone is found only after long trial and cost, is barred to the profane, and is granted to few.

sources.name: Theat.Chem.
sources.use: Reference only (location of the Palingenius verse).

sources.name: unattributed maxim
sources.quote: Ne tu augeas fatum
sources.use: Supports: warning to the would-be practitioner against presumption; given with the English 'Enlarge not thy destiny'.

sources.name: the Pythagoric precept
sources.quote: Neither break a superficies
sources.use: Supports: warning to would-be practitioners, parallel to 'Enlarge not thy destiny'.

sources.name: the Lawgiver
sources.quote: Beware that thou forget not the Lord thy God
sources.use: Illustrates and supports: the Israelites' suffering for rebellion and the warning against presumption and forgetting God in prosperity, applied by analogy to those favoured in the work. Footnote: Deuteronomy 8:10.

sources.name: Jacob
sources.quote: Wherefore I abhor myself, cries Jacob
sources.use: Supports: self-renunciation as the way to union. The text attributes these words to Jacob.

sources.name: Job
sources.quote: THEN WILL I ALSO CONFESS UNTO THEE THAT THINE OWN RIGHT HAND CAN SAVE
sources.use: Supports: humbling of the proud followed by the promise of saving power. Footnote marker (27) follows the end of the quotation in ¶58–59; how far back the citation extends is not stated.

sources.name: the Kabalah
sources.quote: Egredere et regredere, et propterea pactum praecisum est
sources.use: Supports: going forth and returning, with closed-eye meditation, as part of the final passage into accord.

sources.name: Apollo
sources.use: Illustrates: the truth is so enveloped it 'might puzzle Apollo himself to explicate the whole Enigma'.

sources.name: individuals of various ages and nations, whose names are renowned in philosophy
sources.use: Supports: the witnesses gathered for the Inquiry, many attesting the Stone from personal experience.

sources.name: unnamed ('as it is narrated')
sources.use: Supports the claim that man has mind and manual efficacy by the Divine Will to effect all things.

sources.name: adepts
sources.use: Supports: their vital analysis found man's life a pure fire in an ethereal vapour containing the Universal Efficient; reported 'as they profess', presented by Atwood as shown.

sources.name: the Ancients
sources.use: Supports: authority for regarding the Mysteries as real inductions; discovered their whole philosophy in the vital experiment; their philosophy weighed against Physical science.

sources.name: Mysteries celebrated at Eleusis and the rest
sources.use: Reinterpreted as real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source, connected with Alchemy.

sources.name: the Sphinx
sources.use: Illustrates the barrier at the vestibule that perplexes intruders and admits only philosophers.

sources.name: the Greek Ontologists
sources.use: Supports: their course guided Atwood in following Nature to her Initial Source.

sources.name: Prometheus, Vulcan, Minerva
sources.use: Illustrates the method of ascent as the artistic fabrication of the Fire which Prometheus received from Vulcan and Minerva disseminated.

sources.name: Hermetic Tradition
sources.use: The body of tradition Atwood says she has run cursorily through.

sources.name: defunct philosophers
sources.use: The sole evidence on which Alchemy may be imagined real.

sources.name: disappointed chemists
sources.use: Criticized: their 'learned cavils and clamours' against Alchemy.

sources.name: unnamed ('Alchemy has been declared')
sources.quote: the only true glass of the mind
sources.use: Supports: Alchemy as the means to enter and discover Truth.

sources.name: the Alchemists and Greek physicians
sources.use: Supports: they assert an immutable Being pre-existent to sensibles, provable in intellect and confirmed in phenomena.

sources.name: the ancients
sources.use: Supports: they insisted on means for removing barriers to the Divine Light; their Wisdom was acquired by discipline and transcends but does not contradict reason.

sources.name: metaphysicians, inductively arguing
sources.use: Criticized: their attempt to reduce the Idea of Cause to mere antecedence is opposed by human instinct.

sources.name: unattributed verse
sources.quote: The beams pour in, and truth and skill may couch the blind.
sources.use: Illustrates: the divine faculty is confined from birth, yet light can enter.

sources.name: philosophers
sources.use: Supports: they anciently excavated the saving Salt and exalted it by circulating media.

sources.name: Job
sources.quote: no one by searching can find out the Almighty to perfection
sources.use: Objection answered: true of man searching by his own will, but not of one conditionating in obedience to the Divine Will.

sources.name: St Paul
sources.quote: to him that esteems a thing unclean, as St Paul says, it is unclean
sources.use: Supports: the impurity lies in the thought of the accuser, not in the Art.

sources.name: Hone soit qui mal y pense (unattributed)
sources.quote: Hone soit qui mal y pense.
sources.use: Supports the same point against the charge of impiety.

sources.name: Adepts
sources.quote: He has always revealed them to his elected children
sources.use: Supports: God has always revealed the means of assimilation to his elect.

sources.name: Heraclitus
sources.use: Illustrates: the Wisdom is 'that Well of Heraclitus' where Truth lies hidden; 'whence also those philosophic tears'.

sources.name: Socrates
sources.use: Supports: the Wisdom is the Nothing Socrates knew.

sources.name: the oracle
sources.use: Supports: pronounced Socrates the wisest of mankind on account of that Nothing.

sources.name: Democritus
sources.use: Illustrates: beholding it, he laughed at other things.

sources.name: Friar Bacon
sources.use: Illustrates: it warned him 'from the error of his ways'.

sources.name: Agrippa
sources.quote: to know Nothing was the most happy life
sources.use: Supports: convicted of the vanity and confusion of his youth, he came in manhood to know this.

sources.name: the Platonic successors
sources.use: Supports: their 'highly elevated philosophy' agrees in the same divine tradition.

sources.name: the Hebrew Kabbalah
sources.use: Supports: 'profound yet simple metaphysics', 'partially transmitted'; agrees in the same tradition.

sources.name: the Hermetic and Chaldaic Fragments
sources.use: Supports: their 'soul-stirring syllables' agree in the same divine tradition.

sources.name: the Middle Age Adeptists
sources.use: Supports: their 'refined enthusiasm' agrees in the same divine tradition.

sources.name: the Gospel
sources.use: Supports: 'the Christian doctrine of fulfillment' is added to all these as agreeing in the same tradition.

sources.name: the bards and hallowed sages of Asia Minor
sources.use: Contrasts: they knew their Creator under the same sun, while moderns remain blind.

sources.name: Lord bacon
sources.use: Criticized and used: leader of the 'exterminating chase' of experimental philosophy, yet he recommended the pursuit of Causes and inquiry after the ancients' hidden Wisdom, 'though he knew it not'.

sources.name: the wise Adepts
sources.use: Supports: their enigmas, fables, parables and maxims all tend to one discovery; to be studied with the Key.
